That is, matter is never a necessary being while motion exists; nor while motion does not exist and gravitation is necessarily present; nor while motion does not exist, gravitation is not necessarily present, and the world is not merely material. If we now write u=wz, and then eliminate the symbols w and z by the general problem of Chap. IX., we find xu+xyu‾=0, and from this u=10xy+0xy‾+00x‾; and so wz=00x‾ with xy=0. That is: If the world is merely material, and without a presiding intelligence, and at the same time motion exists, matter is not a necessary being.

Now we have already shown that if motion exists, matter is not a necessary being. So this conclusion actually tells us less than we had already found (by inference) to be true. All the same, it is the proper and complete answer to the question that was asked, which was simply to find the consequences of a certain complex hypothesis.

4. So even from the limited set of premises before us, it would be easy to deduce a great variety of further inferences, taking as the given condition any combination of the elementary propositions we like. If the condition is inconsistent with the premises, the form of the solution will show it: the method will assign the value 0 to the combination of symbols that expresses the proposed condition. If, on the other hand, the condition puts no restriction at all on the propositions whose relation we are looking for, so that every combination of those propositions is equally possible, the form of the solution will show that too. Here are examples of each case.

Suppose we look, in the usual way, for the consequences of the condition that matter is a necessary being and at the same time motion exists, as they bear on the propositions The world is merely material, and without a presiding intelligence, and Gravitation is necessarily present. We get the equation xw=0, which shows that the proposed condition is inconsistent with the premises, and so can never be met.

Now suppose we look for the consequences of the condition that Matter is not a necessary being and at the same time Motion does exist, with respect to the same elements as above, namely the absence of a presiding intelligence and the necessity of gravitation. We get the following result, (1−x)w=00yz+00y(1−z)+00(1−y)z+00(1−y)(1−z), in which every one of the four constituents carries the indefinite coefficient, so that each of them may or may not hold. Read literally, it says this:

If matter is not a necessary being, and motion exists, then either the world is merely material and without a presiding intelligence, and gravitation is necessary; or one of these two holds without the other; or both fail to be true. So of the four possible combinations, one of which must be true and only one of which can be true, we are told that any one may be true. Such a result is a truism, a merely necessary truth. Still, it is the only answer that can be given to the question asked.

I do not think I need to defend these applications against the charge of laborious trifling. To build confidence in general principles and methods, it may be necessary to go fairly fully into details that are useless in themselves. When that end has been reached in the subject of this inquiry, let everything that helped to reach it, but later proved unnecessary, be forgotten.

Chapter 15: Of the Aristotelian Logic

1. The logical system of Aristotle, altered in its details but unchanged in its essentials, holds such an important place in university education that this book ought to give some account of it, and briefly discuss the main problems it raises. I hope I come to the task in no narrow or harshly critical spirit. My aim is not to set up a direct comparison between the time-honoured system of the schools and the system of this book. It is, putting truth above every other consideration, to show what the ancient doctrine really is, and to clear away one or two common misunderstandings about how far it reaches and whether it is sufficient.

What is essential in the spirit and method of Aristotle's logic, and of every system related to it, is this: it tries to classify the allowable forms of inference, and it refers those forms, together or one by one, to some general principle that is taken as an axiom. One such principle is the "dictum of Aristotle:" Whatsoever is affirmed or denied of the genus may in the same sense be affirmed or denied of any species included under that genus. About such general principles I think we can say this. Either they state directly, but in abstract form, the very argument they are supposed to explain, and in stating it declare it valid; or they use technical terms which, once defined, bring us back to the same place, namely the abstract statement of the forms of inference that are supposed to be allowed. So the idea of classification runs all through these systems. They also divide logic into two great branches. One deals with categorical propositions, the other with hypothetical or conditional ones. This distinction is nearly the same as the one this book draws between primary and secondary propositions. In all the ordinary textbooks of logic, the theory of categorical propositions is treated far more fully and carefully than the theory of hypothetical ones. Part of that treatment is taken up with old scholastic distinctions, and part with the rules of deductive inference. Only the second part needs our attention here.

2. Categorical propositions are sorted under the following four heads:

Type
1st.Universal affirmativePropositions:All Y’s are X’s.
2nd.Universal negative"No Y’s are X’s.
3rd.Particular affirmative"Some Y’s are X’s.
4th.Particular negative"Some Y’s are not X’s.

Four more forms have recently been added to these, making eight in all (see the next article). The eight can, however, be reduced to six, and the relations among them have been discussed very fully and ably by Professor De Morgan in his Formal Logic. Sir W. Hamilton has published a somewhat different scheme, and has made it the basis of a method of syllogistic inference that authorities on logic speak of with very high respect.12

The textbooks describe the processes of formal logic, as applied to this system of propositions, as being of two kinds, "Conversion" and "Syllogism." Conversion means stating a proposition of one of these kinds in an equivalent form, but with its terms in reverse order. Syllogism means taking two such propositions that share a common term, whether as subject or as predicate, and deducing from them a third proposition that the two contain between them, called the "conclusion." Most writers on logic hold that these two processes, or, according to some, the single process of syllogism, provide the universal patterns of all reasoning. On their view, in any chain of proof the mind's business is to conform itself, knowingly or not, to the particular models of these processes that logicians have classified in their books.

3. What I mean to do is this. First, I will show how syllogism and conversion can be carried out in the most general way on the principles of this book. Then, viewing them as part of a system of logic whose foundations, I believe, have been laid in the ultimate laws of thought, I will try to settle their true place and their essential character.

In the language of symbols, the eight basic types of proposition are written as follows:

1.All Y’s are X’s,y=vx.
2.No Y’s are X’s,y=v(1−x).
3.Some Y’s are X’s,vy=vx.
4.Some Y’s are not-X’s,vy=v(1−x).
5.All not-Y’s are X’s,1−y=vx.(1)
6.No not-Y’s are X’s,1−y=v(1−x).
7.Some not-Y’s are X’s,v(1−y)=vx.
8.Some not-Y’s are not-X’s,v(1−y)=v(1−x).

When we refer to these forms, it will be convenient to use the old words for logical quantity, "universal" and "particular," and for quality, "affirmative" and "negative," in a sense I will explain in a moment. But we will apply them to the terms of propositions, not to the propositions themselves. So we will call the term "All Y’s" universal-affirmative; the term "Y’s," or "Some Y’s," particular-affirmative; the term "All not-Y’s" universal-negative; and the term "Some not-Y’s" particular-negative. "No Y’s" is not really a term of a proposition at all. For the true meaning of "No Y’s are X’s" is "All Y’s are not-X’s." The subject of that proposition is therefore universal-affirmative, and its predicate particular-negative. That there is a real difference between the ideas "men" and "not men" is obvious. That difference is all I have in mind when I call terms affirmative and negative in this way; I do not insist that the words are etymologically the right ones for terms. The words positive and privative would have fitted better, but "positive" is already used in a fixed sense elsewhere in this book.

4. The laws of conversion follow at once from these symbolic forms. Take the equation y=vx, which stands for the proposition "All Y’s are X’s." Eliminating v, we get y(1−x)=0, that is, nothing is a y that is not an x. Solving this for 1−x gives 1−x=00(1−y); and this reads All not-X’s are not-Y’s.

This is an example of what is called "negative conversion." In the same way, the equation y=v(1−x), which stands for "No Y’s are X’s," gives x=00(1−y), and this reads "No X’s are Y’s," since every x falls among the things that are not y. This is an example of what is called simple conversion, though in reality it is the same kind of conversion as the one in the previous example. Every example of conversion that logicians have noticed is of one of two kinds. Either it is of the kind just shown, or it simply swaps the terms of a proposition around without changing their quality, as when we change vy=vx, representing, Some Y’s are X’s, into vx=vy, representing, Some X’s are Y’s; Or else it combines these processes with a further step of limitation, as when from the equation y=vx, representing, All Y’s are X’s, we multiply both sides by v and deduce vy=vx, representing, Some Y’s are X’s, and from this vx=vy, representing, Some X’s are Y’s. In this example the limitation (narrowing "all" to "some") comes first, and the swapping of terms second.

Editor's note: Here Boole passes from "All Y's are X's" to "Some Y's are X's", the step traditional logic calls conversion per accidens, or conversion by limitation. Modern logic does not allow it. It counts "All X are Y" as true even when there are no X's at all, so the statement cannot imply that any X exist. For the same reason some of Aristotle's moods (Darapti, Felapton, Bramantip, Fesapo, and the weakened moods) need an extra premise saying that the class in question is not empty. Boole's v quietly supplies it: to read v times y as "some Y's" is already to assume there are Y's to take some of.

These cases show that conversion is one particular use of a much more general process in logic, a process this book has illustrated many times. Its aim is to find any element of any proposition, however complex, as a logical function of the remaining elements. We need not confine ourselves to the subject and the predicate, treated as simple terms. We can take any element, or any combination of elements, appearing in either of them; make that element or combination the "subject" of a new proposition; and work out what its predicate must be from the data we are given. Even the simple forms of proposition listed above leave room for using such a method beyond what the accepted laws of conversion seem to recognise. So the equation y=vx, representing, All Y’s are X’s, gives us, besides the proposition we deduced from it before, the following three:

1st.y(1−x)=0.There are no Y’s that are not-X’s.
2nd.1−y=00x+(1−x).Things that are not-Y’s include all things that are not-X’s, and an indefinite remainder of things that are X’s.
3rd.x=y+00(1−y).Things that are X’s include all things that are Y’s, and an indefinite remainder of things that are not-Y’s.

These conclusions, it is true, only put the given proposition into other, equivalent forms. But that, and no more, is exactly what the accepted method of "negative conversion" does.

Furthermore, these processes of conversion are not elementary. They are combinations of simpler processes, which depend more directly on the ultimate laws and axioms that govern the use of the symbolic instrument of reasoning. The same remark applies to syllogism, which we now go on to consider.

5. The nature of the syllogism is best seen in a particular case. Suppose we have the propositions All X’s are Y’s,All Y’s are Z’s.

From these we can deduce the conclusion All X’s are Z’s. This is a syllogistic inference. The terms X and Z are called the extremes, and Y is called the middle term. We can now define what a syllogism does in general. We are given two propositions of the kinds listed in (1), sharing one middle or common term Y. In one proposition it is connected with an extreme X, in the other with an extreme Z. We are asked for the relation connecting the extremes X and Z. The term Y may appear in its affirmative form, as All Y’s or Some Y’s, or in its negative form, as All not-Y’s or Some not-Y’s, in either proposition, whatever form it takes in the other.

Nothing is easier than to resolve a particular syllogism by the method of this book. Resolving it is in fact just one application of the process for reducing systems of propositions. Taking the example above, we have x=vy,y=v′z; so, substituting, x=vv′z, which reads All X’s are Z’s. Or, keeping strictly to the method set out in (VIII.7), we deduce x(1−y)=0,y(1−z)=0. Adding these equations and eliminating y, we get x(1−z)=0; so x=00z, or All X’s are Z’s. Any other case can be handled in the same way.

6. But let us leave particular examples aside and examine the general forms to which every syllogism can be reduced.

Proposition I.

To deduce the general rules of Syllogism.

By the general rules of syllogism I mean here the rules that apply to premises in which the subjects and predicates may have every variety of quantity and quality, except that no proposition may join two universal terms. The forms of proposition allowed are therefore those set out in the table at (1).

Let X and Y be the things in the first premise, and Z and Y those in the second. Two cases, fundamentally different in character, then arise. The terms involving Y will be either of like or of unlike quality. They are of like quality when both speak of "Y’s," or both of "Not-Y’s"; of unlike quality when one speaks of "Y’s" and the other of "Not-Y’s." Any pair of premises of the first sort can be written as the equations vx=v′y,(1)wz=w′y;(2) For we can use the symbol y to stand either for "All Y’s" or for "All not-Y’s," since what the symbol means is purely a matter of convention. If we let y stand for "All not-Y’s," then 1−y will stand for "All Y’s," and nothing else changes. We have the same freedom with the symbols x and z. So by choosing the meanings of x, y, and z properly, equations (1) and (2) can be made to represent every combination of premises that depends on the quality of their terms. Again, by giving suitable meanings to the symbols v, v′, w, w′ in those equations, every variety of quantity can be represented as well. For instance, if we take v=1, and let v′ stand for an indefinite class, equation (1) will represent a universal proposition in the ordinary sense of the word, that is, a proposition with a universal subject and a particular predicate. In fact we may give the subject and the predicate in either premise whatever quantities we like (using the word in its scholastic sense), except that, as we assumed, they must not both be universal. The system (1), (2) therefore represents, in complete generality, every possible combination of premises with like middle terms.

7. So that our analysis is as general as the equations it works on, let us eliminate y from (1) and (2) by the method of this book, and look for the expressions for x, 1−x, and vx in terms of z and the symbols v, v′, w, w′. These cover every possible form of the subject of the conclusion. The form v(1−x) is left out, because the premises give us the reading vx= Some X’s, and that does not let us read v(1−x) as Some not-X’s. When the symbol v is used to mean "some," it applies only to the term it is attached to in the premises.

The results of the analysis are these: x=[vv′ww′+00{vv′(1−w)(1−w′)+ww′(1−v)(1−v′)+(1−v)(1−w)}]z+00{vv′(1−w′)+1−v}(1−z),(I.) 1−x=[v(1−v′){ww′+(1−w)(1−w′)}+v(1−w)w′+00{vv′(1−w)(1−w′)+ww′(1−v)(1−v′)+(1−v)(1−w)}]z+[v(1−w)w′+00{vv′(1−w′)+1−v}](1−z),(II.) vx={vv′ww′+00vv′(1−w)(1−w′)}z+00(1−w′)(1−z).(III.)

Each of these expressions has two terms on its right-hand side: one with z as a factor, the other with 1−z. But syllogistic inference, as a matter of form, does not allow opposite classes in its conclusion, such as Z’s and not-Z’s together.

So, to find the rules of that kind of inference, we must find out under what conditions the right-hand side of any of our equations shrinks to a single term.

The simplest is (III.), and it shrinks to a single term if w′=1. The equation then becomes vx=vv′wz,(3) Its left-hand side is the same as the extreme in the first premise. Its right-hand side has the same quantity and quality as the extreme in the second premise. Here is why. Since w′=1, the right-hand side of (2), which contains the middle term y, is universal. So, by our assumption, the left-hand side of (2) is particular; and so the right-hand side of (3), which has the same symbol w in its coefficient, is particular too. From this we get the following law.

Condition of Inference.—One middle term, at least, universal.

Rule of Inference.—Equate the extremes.

Examining equations (I.) and (II.) further shows that this is the only condition of syllogistic inference when the middle terms are of like quality. The right-hand side of (I.) shrinks to a single term if w′=1 and v=1; the right-hand side of (II.) shrinks to a single term if w′=1, v=1, w=1. In each of these cases w′=1 is required, and that is the one sufficient condition already found.

Consider next the case in which the middle terms are of unlike quality. The premises can then be written in the forms vx=v′y,(4)wz=w′(1−y);(5) and if, as before, we eliminate y and find the expressions for x, 1−x, and vx, we get x=[vv′(1−w)w′+00{ww′(1−v)+(1−v)(1−v′)(1−w)+v′(1−w)(1−w′)}]z+[vv′w′+00{(1−v)(1−v′)+v′(1−w′)}](1−z).(IV.) 1−x=[ww′v+v(1−v′)(1−w)+00{ww′(1−v)+(1−v)(1−v′)(1−w)+v′(1−w)(1−w′)}]z+[v(1−v′)+00{v′(1−w′)+(1−v)(1−v′)}](1−z).(V.) vx={vv′(1−w)w′+00vv′(1−w)(1−w′)}z+{vv′w′+00vv′(1−w′)}(1−z).(VI.)

Now the right-hand side of (VI.) shrinks to a single term in z if w=1, giving vx={vv′w′+00vv′(1−w′)}(1−z); and the right-hand side of this is opposite, in both quantity and quality, to the corresponding extreme wz in the second premise. For since w=1, wz is universal. But the factor vv′ shows that the term it is attached to is particular, since by our assumption v and v′ are not both equal to 1. From this we get the following law of inference in the case of unlike middle terms:

First Condition of Inference.—At least one universal extreme.

Rule of Inference.—Change the quantity and quality of that extreme, and equate the result to the other extreme.

Again, the right-hand side of (V.) shrinks to a single term if v′=1, w′=1; it then gives 1−x={vw+00(1−v)w}z. Now since v′=1, w′=1, the middle terms of both premises are universal, and so the extremes vx, wz are particular. But in the conclusion, the extreme involving x is opposite in both quantity and quality to the extreme vx in the first premise, while the extreme involving z agrees in both quantity and quality with the corresponding extreme wz in the second premise. From this we get the following general law:

Second Condition of Inference.—Two universal middle terms.

Rule of Inference.—Change the quantity and quality of either extreme, and equate the result to the other extreme unchanged.

When the middle terms are unlike, there are no other conditions or rules of syllogistic inference than these. Equation (IV.), for instance, can be brought to the form of a syllogistic conclusion when w=1 and v=1, but that does not give a new condition of inference, since, by what we have already seen, the single condition v=1, or w=1, would be enough.

8. The following examples will be enough to illustrate the general rules of syllogism just given: 1. All Y’s are X’s. All Z’s are Y’s. This belongs to the first case, like middle terms. All Y’s is the universal middle term. Equating the extremes gives the conclusion

All Z’s are X’s;

with the universal term, All Z’s, as the subject, and the particular term, (some) X’s, as the predicate. 2. All X’s are Y’s. No Z’s are Y’s. The proper way to express these premises is All X’s are Y’s.All Z’s are not-Y’s. They belong to the second case, unlike middle terms, and they satisfy the first condition of inference. The middle term Y’s in the first premise is particular-affirmative; the middle term not-Y’s in the second premise is particular-negative. If we take All Z’s as the universal extreme and change its quantity and quality as the rule says, we get the term Some not-Z’s. Equating this with the other extreme, All X’s, gives

All X’s are not-Z’s, that is, No X’s are Z’s.

If we start from the other universal extreme and do the same, we get the equivalent result

No Z’s are X’s.

3. All Y’s are X’s. All not-Y’s are Z’s. Here too the middle terms are unlike in quality. So the premises belong to the second case, and since both middle terms are universal, the second condition of inference is met. If, following the rule, we change the quantity and quality of the first extreme, (some) X’s, we get All not-X’s, and equating this with the other extreme gives

All not-X’s are Z’s.

Going the other way round would give the equivalent result

All not-Z’s are X’s.

The scholastic system of logic would not accept the conclusions of these last two examples as valid, because in effect it requires the subject of a proposition to be affirmative. They are, however, perfectly legitimate in themselves, and the rules that produce them are without doubt the most general rules of syllogistic inference. The investigation that led to them will probably look needlessly complicated. Certainly they could have been reached more easily, and without any symbolic instrument at all. But my aim was to carry out the investigation in the most general way, by an analysis that left nothing out. With that aim, whether the method is short or long does not matter. Indeed the analysis is not really an analysis of the syllogism, but of a much more general combination of propositions, since we are free to give the symbols v, v′, w, w′ any class-meanings we like. To illustrate this, I will apply the solution (I.) to the following imaginary case.

Suppose a number of pieces of cloth, striped in different colours, were brought for inspection, and the following two observations were made about them:

1st. Every piece striped with white and green was also striped with black and yellow, and vice versâ (and the other way round).

2nd. Every piece striped with red and orange was also striped with blue and yellow, and vice versâ. Suppose we are then asked how the pieces marked with green stand with respect to the colours white, black, red, orange, and blue.

Here, if we take v= white, x= green, v′= black, y= yellow, w= red, z= orange, w′= blue, our premises are written vx=v′y,wz=w′y, which matches the system (1) (2). Equation (I.) then leads to the following conclusion:

Pieces striped with green are of one of these kinds. Either they are striped with orange, white, black, red, and blue all together, and every piece with that combination is among those striped with green. Or they are striped with orange, white, and black, but not with red or blue. Or they are striped with orange, red, and blue, but not with white or black. Or they are striped with orange, but not with white or red. Or they are striped with white and black, but not with blue or orange. Or they are striped with neither white nor orange.

Given what kind of conclusion this is, neither the symbolic expression (I.) that conveys it nor the analysis that produced that expression can fairly be called needlessly complicated.

9. The way the doctrine of the syllogism has been presented in this chapter leads to an important observation. We have seen that in each of its two great divisions the whole discussion, at least as far as finding rules and methods goes, comes down to analysing a pair of equations: the system (1), (2) when the premises have like middle terms, and the system (4), (5) when the middle terms are unlike. Moreover, that analysis was actually carried out by a method founded on certain general laws. Those laws were drawn directly from the structure of language, Chap. II., confirmed by the study of the operations of the human mind, Chap. III., and proved to apply to the analysis of every system of equations whatever by which propositions, or combinations of propositions, can be represented, Chap. VIII. So here we have the means of settling definitely whether the syllogism really is the fundamental type of reasoning, that is, whether the study of its laws covers the whole of deductive logic. For if it does, some sign of that must show up in the systems of equations we have been analysing. It is impossible to believe that the syllogism could be the one essential process of reasoning and yet, when the process is laid out, show nothing of that high rank. But no such sign appears. Nothing suggests that the treatment of every system of equations expressing propositions is contained in the treatment of the particular system examined in this chapter. And yet writers on logic have been all but unanimous in claiming for syllogistic inference not just supremacy in deductive reasoning, but complete sufficiency. Archbishop Whately, whose language is always clear and definite, and who deserves special attention on the subject of logic, is very explicit on this point. "For Logic," he says, "which is, as it were, the Grammar of Reasoning, does not bring forward the regular Syllogism as a distinct mode of argumentation, designed to be substituted for any other mode; but as the form to which all correct reasoning may be ultimately reduced." And Mr. Mill, in a chapter of his System of Logic entitled "Of Ratiocination or Syllogism," lists the ordinary forms of syllogism and then remarks, "All valid ratiocination, all reasoning by which from general propositions previously admitted, other propositions, equally or less general, are inferred, may be exhibited in some of the above forms." And again: "We are therefore at liberty, in conformity with the general opinion of logicians, to consider the two elementary forms of the first figure as the universal types of all correct ratiocination." In line with these views, it has been argued that the science of logic is exempt from the imperfection and the progress to which every other science is subject. Its birth from the labour of one mighty mind of long ago has even been compared, in a rather daring metaphor, to the mythological birth of Pallas (the goddess Athena, who sprang fully armed from the head of Zeus).13,14

Since the syllogism is a kind of elimination, the question before us clearly splits into two. First, can all elimination be reduced to syllogism? Second, can deductive reasoning properly be regarded as consisting of elimination and nothing else? After careful examination, I believe the true answer to the first question is this. In theory it is always possible to break down and recombine propositions so that the elimination can then be done by the rules of the syllogism. But in many cases that reduction would be forced and unnatural, and it would involve operations that are not syllogistic. To the second question I answer that reasoning cannot be confined to elimination, except by arbitrarily narrowing what the word means. No definition will do that makes reasoning anything less than the whole collection of methods founded on the laws of thought as they apply to propositions. Among those methods elimination, important as it is, holds only one place.

Much of what I can only regard as error about the nature of the syllogism and the scope of its work seems to come from a habit of mind. It is the habit of treating as primary every truth in logic that is simple and intuitively certain, without asking how it stands to the other truths of the science, or to the general methods of the art, of reasoning. Aristotle's dictum de omni et nullo is a self-evident principle. But it is not one of those ultimate laws of the reasoning faculty to which all its other laws, however plain and self-evident, can be traced back, and from which they can be deduced in strict scientific order. In every science the fundamental truths are usually the simplest to grasp. Yet that simplicity is not the test by which we judge their claim to be fundamental. The test must be found in the nature and size of the structure they can support. On this view, Leibnitz seems to me to have judged rightly when he gave the "principle of contradiction" a fundamental place in logic. For we have seen the consequences of the law of thought of which that principle is the axiom-like statement (III. 15). But enough has been said about the nature of deductive inference and its elements. The subject of induction will perhaps get some attention in another part of this work.15

10. I remarked earlier in this chapter that the ordinary treatment of hypothetical propositions is much more defective than that of categorical ones. What is usually called the hypothetical syllogism seems, in fact, to be no syllogism at all. Take the argument

If A is B, C is D,
But A is B,
Therefore C is D,

and put it in the form

If the proposition X is true, Y is true,
But X is true,
Therefore Y is true;

where X means the proposition A is B, and Y the proposition C is D. We then see that the premises contain only two terms or elements, while a syllogism essentially involves three. The following would be a genuine hypothetical syllogism:

If X is true, Y is true;
If Y is true, Z is true;
∴If X is true, Z is true.

After the discussion of secondary propositions earlier in this book, it is clear that the forms of hypothetical syllogism must match those of categorical syllogism exactly, in every respect. Particular propositions, such as "Sometimes if X is true, Y is true," can be brought in, and the conditions and rules of inference worked out in this chapter for categorical syllogisms can be read, without any loss, to cover the corresponding cases among hypotheticals.

11. What final conclusions, then, are we led to about the nature and reach of the scholastic logic? I think these. It is not a science, but a collection of scientific truths, too incomplete to form a system by themselves, and not fundamental enough to serve as the foundation on which a perfect system can rest. It does not follow, however, that because the logic of the schools has been credited with qualities it has no right to, it does not deserve our regard. A system that has been bound up with the very growth of language, and has left its stamp on the greatest questions and the most famous proofs of philosophy, cannot be wholly unworthy of attention. Memory, too, and habit, it must be admitted, have a great deal to do with how the intellect works; and some of the rules of the ancient logic have become almost woven into the very fabric of thought in educated minds. But are the memory-aid forms in which the particular rules of conversion and syllogism have been set out of any real use? Might not the very skill they are supposed to give be gained, with more benefit to the powers of the mind, by the unaided efforts of a mind left to its own resources? These are questions that might still be worth examining. As for the particular results worked out in this chapter, it should be noted that they are meant only to help the inquiry into the nature of the ordinary or scholastic logic, and into its relation to a more perfect theory of deductive reasoning.

Chapter 16: On the Theory of Probabilities

1. Before another year is out, exactly two centuries will have passed since Pascal solved the first known question in the theory of probability. In solving it he laid the foundations of a science with an unusual share of the charm that belongs to the more abstract kinds of mathematical thought. The problem came from the Chevalier de Méré, a man known as a gambler, who put it to the recluse of Port Royal. Pascal had not yet been drawn away from the interests of science by the more absorbing contemplation of "the greatness and the misery of man." That problem was the first of a long series. The series was destined to call new methods of mathematical analysis into being, and to give real service in the practical business of life. Nor does the interest of the subject lie only in its links with mathematics, or in its usefulness. The theory of probability repays the attention we give it as an object of study in its own right. It repays study of the basic ways in which it has been conceived; of the great secondary principles that have gradually been added to it, as they were to mechanics, a science of the same age; and, last, of how near it has actually come to perfection. By perfection I mean unity of conception and harmony of methods. In this chapter I mean to consider a few of these points, very briefly.16

2. A distinguished writer has stated the basic definitions of the science like this:17

"The probability of an event is the reason we have to believe that it has taken place, or that it will take place."

"The measure of the probability of an event is the ratio of the number of cases favourable to that event, to the total number of cases favourable or contrary, and all equally possible" (that is, all equally likely to happen).

It follows from these definitions that the word probability, in its mathematical sense, refers to the state of our knowledge about the circumstances under which an event may happen or fail to happen. How much reason we have to think an event will occur depends on how much we know about its circumstances. Call that reason, in a single word, our expectation of the event: it varies with what we know. Probability is expectation founded on partial knowledge. If we knew all the circumstances that affect whether an event occurs, expectation would turn into certainty, and there would be neither room nor need for a theory of probability.

3. Our expectation of an event grows stronger as the number of known cases favourable to it grows, compared with the whole number of equally possible cases, favourable or not. Even so, it would be unphilosophical to claim that the strength of that expectation, taken as a feeling in the mind, can be measured against any numerical standard. The hopeful man builds high hopes where the timid man despairs and the undecided man is lost in doubt. As subjects for scientific study, opinion and sensation are somewhat alike. A thermometer, or a carefully prepared photographic plate, does not show how intense our sensations of heat and light are. It shows certain physical circumstances that go along with producing those sensations. In the same way, the theory of probability studies the numerical measure of the circumstances on which expectation is founded, and that aim covers the whole range of its proper uses. The rules we use in life insurance, and in the other statistical uses of the theory, have nothing to do with expectation as a mental phenomenon. They rest on the assumption that the future will resemble the past: that under the same circumstances the same event will tend to recur with a definite numerical frequency. They do not rest on any attempt to calculate the strength of human hopes and fears.

Now experience really does show that events of a given kind, under given circumstances, tend to recur with a definite frequency, whether or not we know their true causes. Of course this tendency usually shows itself only when the field of observation is large enough. The court records of a great nation, and its registers of births and deaths by age and sex, and so on, are remarkably uniform from year to year. In a given language, or family of languages, the same sounds and sequences of sounds recur with fixed frequencies; and if the language is written, so do the same letters and sequences of letters. The key to the rough Ogham inscriptions found in various parts of Ireland, in which at first no division into words could even be made out, was recovered by strictly applying this principle. The same method, I understand, has been applied to deciphering the cuneiform records recently dug out of the ruins of Nineveh through the enterprise of Mr. Layard.18,19

4. Let us try, from these statements and definitions, to form an idea of the proper aim of the theory of probability.

Probability, we have said, is expectation founded on a particular kind of knowledge, namely the knowledge of how often events occur relative to one another. So the probabilities of events, or of combinations of events, are always our data. It makes no difference whether we work them out from knowing how things are made, in the circumstances where the events happen, or get them from long observation of a past series of the events' occurrences and failures. The probability of some connected event, or combination of events, is then the quæsitum, the thing sought. Now in the most general, yet still strict, meaning of the word "event," every combination of events is also an event. Two or more events happening together is still an event. So is an event happening under given conditions, or in any connection we can imagine with other events. Using the word with this freedom, we could define the aim of the theory of probability like this. Given the probabilities of any events, of whatever kind, to find the probability of some other event connected with them.

5. Events can be divided into simple and compound. A compound event is one that consists of a combination of simple events (I. 13). In these terms, we could say that the practical aim of the theory is this: to find the probability of some event, simple or compound, from the given probabilities of other events, simple or compound, to which it is connected by the way it is defined.

For example, suppose we know from the way a die is made that the probability that any particular throw will give an ace (a one) is measured by the fraction 16. And suppose we are asked for the probability of getting one ace, and only one, in two throws in a row. We can set the problem out in the order of its data and its quæsitum, like this:

First Datum.—The probability of the event that the first throw gives an ace =16.

Second Datum.—The probability of the event that the second throw gives an ace =16.

Quæsitum.—The probability of the event that either the first throw gives an ace and the second does not; or the first does not give an ace and the second does.

Here the two data are the probabilities of simple events: the first throw giving an ace, and the second throw giving an ace. The quæsitum is the probability of a compound event, a particular "either-or" combination of the simple events contained or implied in the data. When the numbers in a problem can be worked out, as they are here, from the way things are made, I suspect it will usually turn out that the data are the probabilities of simple events and the quæsitum is the probability of a compound event that depends on them. That is the case with one class of problems that has taken up, perhaps, more than its fair share of the attention of students of probability, namely games of chance and games of skill. In a game of chance some physical circumstance, such as the way a die is made, fixes the probability of each possible step in the game, and the outcome is some definite combination of those steps. In a game of skill the players' relative ability, assumed to be known à priori, fixes that same element. But in statistical problems our knowledge comes not from studying how things are made but from recorded observations of Nature or of human society, and then there is no reason why the data these observations give us should be the probabilities of simple events. On the contrary, when events or conditions turn up together in striking combinations, which hints at some hidden causal connection, that very fact suggests that we should keep a numerical record of how often such combinations occur, so that they can teach us something for the future. And the data that observations of this kind give us are the probabilities of compound events. So a general method for solving problems with data like these is needed for more than the complete development of the theory of probability. It is also, perhaps, a necessary condition for applying the theory to a large and practically important class of questions.

6. Before we ask how far known methods can solve problems like these, it will help to notice that there is another way of looking at every question in the theory of probability. It is this. In place of events, we put the propositions that assert that those events have occurred, or will occur. And we take the numerical probability to refer to the truth of those propositions, not to the occurrence of the events they make assertions about. So instead of taking the fraction p to express the probability that an event E occurs, let us take it to stand for the probability that the proposition X is true, the proposition that asserts that the event E will occur. In the same way, suppose some probability q refers to a compound event, such as the events E and F happening together. Instead, let it stand for the probability that the proposition is true which asserts that E and F will both occur. And let the same exchange be made everywhere: "either-or" combinations and "if" combinations of events become disjunctive and conditional propositions. This new use of probability goes necessarily hand in hand with the old one. But adopting it brings a practical advantage, because we have already worked out the theory of propositions. We have defined their main kinds, and we have set up methods for finding, in every case, how far and in what way they depend on one another. Any general theory of probability must rest on this foundation, or on something equivalent to it. I do not say that other considerations may not sometimes be needed when the theory is applied. The data may not be enough for a definite solution, and someone may think it necessary to supply the gap by a hypothesis. Or, where large numbers are involved, difficulties of that origin may arise after the solution, and they need special methods of their own. But in every case some form of the general problem stated above (Art. 4) is involved, and the real, distinctive work of the theory lies in dealing with that problem. I want it noticed that the following chapters are devoted mainly to this aim. I do not intend to take up questions that involve extra hypotheses, except in passing. Even for those questions (I. 17), the first thing that matters is to establish a general method, founded on a solid and sufficient basis of theory.

Editor's note: This is the idea modern probability theory is built on. In 1933 the Russian mathematician Andrei Kolmogorov set probability on events treated as sets, combined by "and", "or" and "not" exactly as Boole combines classes. In today's terms, a probability is a measure on a Boolean algebra of events: a rule that gives each event a number between zero and one, and adds the numbers of events that cannot happen together.

7. Here is a summary, taken mainly from Laplace, of the principles that have been used to solve questions of probability. They follow from the basic definitions already given, and they show how far it has proved possible to put those definitions to use.

Principle 1st. If p is the probability that an event occurs, 1−p is the probability that it does not occur.

2nd. The probability that two independent events both occur is the product of their probabilities.

3rd. The probability that two dependent events both occur is the probability of one of them multiplied by the probability that, if that one occurs, the other will occur too.

4th. The probability that, if an event E takes place, an event F will also take place, equals the probability that E and F both occur, divided by the probability that E occurs.

5th. The probability that one or the other of two events occurs, when the two cannot both occur, equals the sum of their separate probabilities.

6th. Suppose an observed event can only have come from one of n different causes, which are equally probable à priori. Then the probability of any one of those causes is a fraction. Its numerator is the probability of the event, assuming that cause is present. Its denominator is the sum of the same probabilities for all the causes.

7th. The probability of a future event is found by taking each cause, multiplying its probability by the probability that, if that cause is present, the future event will take place, and adding up all these products.

8. About how far these principles reach, and how far they are enough, we can make the following remarks.

First, by combining these principles properly, we can always express the probability of a compound event that depends in any way on independent simple events whose separate probabilities are given. A very large share of the problems that have actually been solved are of this kind. The difficulty in solving them has not come from any gap in what the theory of probability tells us to do. It has come from the need for an analysis that can carry out those instructions when they bring in functions of large numbers, or series with many complicated terms. So it can be fully granted that every problem whose data are the probabilities of independent simple events falls within the reach of the existing methods.

Second, some of the principles listed above, especially the sixth and seventh, do not assume that all the data are probabilities of simple events. But when they are applied, as they particularly are, to questions of causes, they do assume that the causes they take into account exclude one another, so that no two of them can combine to produce an effect. Now let us move the numerical probabilities, as explained above, from the events to the propositions that express those events. Then the most general problem to which these principles apply can be set out in the following order of data and quæsita (things sought).

Data.

First, the probabilities of the n conditional propositions:

If the causeA1exists, the eventEwill follow;
"A2"E"
⋮⋮
"An"E"

Second, the condition that the antecedents of those propositions (their "if" parts) conflict with one another, so that no two can be true together.

Requirements.

The probability that the proposition is true which declares that the event E occurs; and also, when that proposition is known to be true, the probabilities that the several propositions are true which assert that each of the causes A1,A2…An is present.

Here we see that the data are the probabilities of a series of compound events, expressed by conditional propositions. But the system is plainly a very limited and special one. Its antecedents must exclude one another, and there is only one consequent in the whole system, the event E. Being able to handle a system like this does not mean we can solve problems whose data are the probabilities of any system of conditional propositions. Still less does it mean we can solve problems whose data are the probabilities of any system of propositions whatever. And if we look at the subject from the side of its content rather than its form, it is clear that the hypothesis of exclusive causes, causes that never act together, is seldom true of the actual world. The phenomena of the world seem usually to be the products of complex causes, working together to an extent and in a way we do not know. That is surely the case in nearly every field of natural or social inquiry where the theory of probability promises any new and useful applications.

9. To these principles we may add one more, stated in the following terms by the Savilian Professor of Astronomy at the University of Oxford.20

"Principle 8. If there be any number of mutually exclusive hypotheses, h1,h2,h3,… of which the probabilities relative to a particular state of information are p1,p2,p3,… and if new information be given which changes the probabilities of some of them, suppose of hm+1 and all that follow, without having otherwise any reference to the rest; then the probabilities of these latter have the same ratios to one another, after the new information, that they had before, that is, p′1:p′2:p′3…:p′m=p1:p2:p3…:pm, where the accented letters denote the values after the new information has been acquired."

In plain terms: if new information bears only on some of the hypotheses, the others keep their old proportions to one another. This principle seems more basic than most of those listed before it, and perhaps, as Professor Donkin has suggested, it could be treated as an axiom. Indeed it seems to be founded in the very definition of the measure of probability, as "the ratio of the number of cases favourable to an event to the total number of cases favourable or contrary, and all equally possible." For on this definition it is clear that if the number of equally possible cases is cut down in some proportion, while the number of favourable cases stays the same, then the probabilities of any events those cases bear on go up in exactly that proportion. The new hypothesis, namely that the number of possible cases shrinks without changing how many of them favour the events in question, raises the probabilities of all those events by the same factor. So their sizes relative to one another stay the same. If, then, the principle is bound up in the very definition of probability, as it appears to be, it can hardly, by itself, take us any further in solving problems than careful study of the definition alone would. From these considerations it seems doubtful whether we can hope for any real advance, either in the theory of probability as a branch of knowledge or in the practical solving of its problems, without help of a different kind from anything we have looked at so far. And it seems impossible to build, solely on a set of principles like those above, a method that applies to every problem, whatever the number or the nature of the propositions that express its data. Reaching that goal needs other elements, and they will be the subject of the next chapter.

Chapter 17: General Method in Probabilities

1. We defined it earlier (XVI. 2): “the measure of the probability of an event is the ratio of the number of cases favourable to that event, to the total number of cases favourable or unfavourable, and all equally possible.” In the investigations that follow, the word probability will be used in this sense, meaning the “measure of probability.”

From this definition we can draw the following conclusions.

I. When it is certain that an event will occur, the probability of that event, in this mathematical sense, is 1. The reason is that here the cases favourable to the event and the cases possible are one and the same.

So, also, if p is the probability that an event x will happen, 1−p will be the probability that it will not happen. To get this result straight from the definition, let m be the number of cases favourable to the event x, and n the number of cases possible. Then n−m is the number of cases unfavourable to the event x. So, by definition, mn= probability that x will happen.n−mn= probability that x will not happen. But n−mn=1−mn=1−p.

II. The probability that two events both occur is the probability of either one of them, multiplied by the probability that, if that one occurs, the other will occur too.

Let m be the number of cases favourable to the first event, and n the number of equally possible cases unfavourable to it. Then the probability of the first event is, by definition, mm+n. Of the m cases favourable to the first event, let l cases be favourable to the first and second events together. Then, by definition, lm is the probability that if the first event happens, the second will happen too. Multiplying these fractions together, we have mm+n×lm=lm+n. Now look at the resulting fraction lm+n. Its numerator is the number of cases favourable to both events together, and its denominator is the number m+n of possible cases. So it is the probability that the two events happen together.

So, if p is the probability of any event x, and q the probability that if x occurs y will occur, the probability of the combination xy, both together, will be pq.

III. The probability that if an event x occurs, the event y will occur, is a fraction. Its numerator is the probability that both occur; its denominator is the probability that the event x occurs.

This follows at once from Principle 2nd.

IV. The probability that some one of a series of exclusive events will occur is the sum of their separate probabilities. (Exclusive events are events no two of which can both occur.)

For let n be the number of possible cases; m1 the number of those cases favourable to the first event; m2 the number favourable to the second, and so on. Then the separate probabilities of the events are m1n, m2n, and so on. Again, since the events exclude one another, no case favourable to one of them is favourable to another. So the number of cases favourable to some one of the series will be m1+m2…, and the probability that some one of the series happens will be m1+m2…n. But this is the sum of the earlier fractions, m1n, m2n, and so on. That makes the principle plain.

2. Definition.—Two events are said to be independent when the probability that either of them happens is unaffected by our expectation that the other will occur or fail.

From this definition, combined with Principle II., we get the following conclusion:

V. The probability that two independent events both occur is the product of their separate probabilities.

For let p be the probability of an event x, and q that of an event y regarded as quite independent of x. Then q is also the probability that if x occurs y will occur. So, by Principle II., pq is the probability that x and y both occur

Under the same circumstances, the probability that x will occur and y will not occur will be p(1−q). For p is the probability that x will occur, and 1−q the probability that y will not occur. In the same way, (1−p)(1−q) will be the probability that both events fail to occur.

3. There is one more principle we need. It is different in kind from those above, but the investigations later in this chapter depend on it. Before I state it outright, I want to make one or two preliminary remarks.

My first remark is that the distinction between simple and compound events is not founded in the nature of the events themselves. It rests on the way, or the connection, in which they are presented to the mind. Think of the phrases “To be in health,” “To prosper,” and so on. How many separate particulars does each of them imply? Yet each could still be regarded as expressing a “simple event.” Language, by custom, has given single and definite names to some combinations of events, and has left countless other combinations to be expressed by combining separate words or phrases. That custom is essentially arbitrary. So when we call events simple because they are expressed by a single verb, or by what grammarians call a simple sentence, we do not mean that the events themselves are really simple. We use the term only with reference to how they are expressed in grammar.

4. Now if the distinction between simple and compound events is not founded in their real nature, but rests on the accidents of language, it cannot affect the question whether they depend on one another or are independent. Suppose all I know about two simple events is this one fact: the probability that one of them occurs is p, and the probability of the other is q. Then I regard the events as independent, and on that basis I say that the probability that they both occur is pq. But my ground for saying so is not that the events are simple. It is that the data give no information whatever about any connection or dependence between them. When the probabilities of events are given, but all information about their dependence is withheld, the mind regards them as independent. And this way of thinking is just as correct whether the events, judged by how they are actually expressed, are simple or compound: that is, whether each of them is expressed by a single verb or by a combination of verbs.

5. Suppose, however, that along with the probabilities of certain events we have some definite information about the ways they can combine. For example, suppose we know that certain combinations are ruled out, so that only the remaining combinations are possible. The same general principle still applies. How we use this information to calculate the probability of any outcome we can imagine does not depend on the nature of the events whose probabilities, and whose limits of possible connection, are given. It does not matter whether they are simple or compound. It makes no difference from what source, or by what methods, we came to know their probabilities and the relations connecting them. We must regard the events as independent of any connection other than the one we have information about. And it makes no difference whether that information was stated to us outright in the data or was deduced from the data by logical inference. This brings us to the general principle in question, namely:

VI. The events whose probabilities are given are to be regarded as independent of any connection except what is either expressed, or necessarily implied, in the data; and the way we use our knowledge of that connection does not depend on the nature of the source that knowledge came from.

The practical importance of this principle is as follows. Whatever the nature of the events whose probabilities are given, and whatever the nature of the event whose probability is sought, we can always do two things by applying the Calculus of Logic. We can express the event sought as a definite combination of the given events. And we can state in full all the relations, implied in the data, that connect the given events with one another. In other words, we can determine which combination of the given events is the one whose probability is required, and which combinations of them are the only ones possible. It then follows from the principle above that we can reason about those events as if they were simple events, whose conditions of possible combination had been given to us directly by experience, and of which we are seeking the probability of some definite combination. The possibility of a general method in probabilities depends on this reduction.

6. The investigations we are about to begin rest on the Calculus of Logic, so I must first explain certain terms and ways of speaking that come from using it here.

By the event x, I mean the event such that the proposition asserting that it occurs is expressed in symbols by the equation x=1. By the event ϕ(x,y,z,…), I mean the event whose occurrence is expressed by the equation ϕ(x,y,z,…)=1. Such an event may be called a compound event, in relation to the simple events x, y, z, which go into its conception. For instance, let x stand for the event “It rains,” and y for the event “It thunders.” The occurrence of each of these events on its own is then expressed by the logical equations x=1,y=1, Then x(1−y)+y(1−x) will stand for the event, or state of things, described by the proposition “It either rains or thunders, but not both;” and that state of things will be expressed by x(1−y)+y(1−x)=1. For short, let the function ϕ(x,y,z,…), taken in this sense, be written V. It is then clear (VI. 13) that the law of duality, V(1−V)=0, will be satisfied identically, that is, whatever values the symbols in it take.

The simple events x, y, z will be called “conditioned” when they are not free to occur in every possible combination: in other words, when some compound event that depends on them is ruled out. For example, the events described by the propositions “It rains” and “It thunders” are “conditioned” if the event described by the proposition “It thunders, but does not rain” is ruled out. Then the range of possible combinations is smaller than the range of combinations we can imagine. Simple unconditioned events are, by definition, independent.

A compound event is likewise called conditioned if it is assumed that it can occur only under a certain condition: that is, only in combination with some other event whose presence makes up that condition.

7. We shall go in the natural order of thought, from simple and unconditioned events to compound and conditioned ones.

Proposition I.

First. If p, q, r are the probabilities of any unconditioned simple events x, y, z respectively, the probability of any compound event V will be [V]. This function [V] is formed by changing, in the function V, the symbols x, y, z into p, q, r, and so on.

Second. Under the same circumstances, the probability that if the event V occurs, some other event V′ will also occur, will be [VV′][V]. Here [VV′] stands for the result of multiplying together the logical functions V and V′, and then changing x, y, z, and so on in the result into p, q, r, and so on.

Let us look first at the possible combinations of just two simple events, x and y, whose probabilities are p and q. The basic combinations of those events (V.11), the constituents, and their probabilities, are as follows: Events.Probabilities.xy, Concurrence of x and y, pq.x(1−y), Occurrence of x without y, p(1−q).(1−x)y, Occurrence of y without x, (1−p)q.(1−x)(1−y), Conjoint failure of x and y, (1−p)(1−q). We see that in each of these cases the probability of the compound event that a constituent stands for is the same function of p and q as the logical expression of that event is of x and y. The probability of “x and y both,” for instance, is p times q, just as the event is x times y. And clearly this remark holds however many simple events there are whose probabilities are given, and whose joint existence or failure makes up the compound event whose probability we are seeking.

Next, consider any disjunctive combination of these constituents, that is, any “either-or” combination of them. Take the compound event described in ordinary language as “either the event x without the event y, or the event y without the event x.” In symbols it is written x(1−y)+y(1−x), and its probability, found by Principles IV. and V., is p(1−q)+q(1−p). The second expression is the same function of p and q as the first is of x and y. And clearly this too is one instance of a general rule. The events expressed by any two or more constituents exclude one another. The only way they can be combined is disjunctively: in ordinary language by the word or, in the language of symbolic logic by the sign +. Now the probability that some one of a set of events that exclude one another will occur is the sum of their separate probabilities, and it is written by joining the expressions for those separate probabilities with the sign +. So the law illustrated above turns out to be general. The probability of any unconditioned event V will be found by changing, in V, the symbols x,y,z,… into p,q,r,…

8. Again, by Principle III., the probability that if the event V occurs, the event V′ will occur with it, is a fraction. Its numerator is the probability that V and V′ both occur, and its denominator the probability that V occurs.

Now the expression for the event, or state of things, made up of V and V′ occurring together is formed by multiplying the expressions V and V′ together by the rules of the Calculus of Logic. This is because every constituent found in both V and V′ will appear in the product, and no others will. Next, by what we have just shown, the probability of the event that this product stands for is found by changing x,y,z in it into p,q,r,… So the numerator we want is exactly what [VV′] stands for by definition. And the denominator will be [V]. Therefore Probability that if V occur, V′ will occur with it =[VV′][V].

9. For example, suppose the probabilities of the simple events x,y,z are p,q,r respectively, and we are asked for the probability that if either x or y occurs, then either y or z will occur. The logical expressions of the antecedent and the consequent are 1st. Either x or y occurs, x(1−y)+y(1−x).2nd. Either y or z occurs, y(1−z)+z(1−y). (Here “either-or” means one but not the other, as everywhere in this algebra.) If we now multiply these two expressions together by the rules of the Calculus of Logic, we get the expression for antecedent and consequent occurring together: xz(1−y)+y(1−x)(1−z). In words: either x and z occur without y, or y occurs alone. Changing x,y,z in this result into p,q,r, and transforming the expression of the antecedent in the same way, we find that the probability sought is pr(1−q)+q(1−p)(1−r)p(1−q)+q(1−p). In a case like this, the particular job of the calculus is to do the work of reasoning: it finds which combinations of events belong at once to the consequent and to the antecedent. But the advantage of using it here lies almost entirely in the future. It will become plain in a later proposition.

Proposition II.

10. We know that the probabilities of certain simple events x,y,z,… are p,q,r,… respectively when a certain condition V is satisfied, V being written as a function of x,y,z,…. Required: the absolute probabilities of the events x,y,z,…, that is, the probabilities that each of them occurs apart from the condition V.

Let p′, q′, r′, and so on be the probabilities required: that is, the probabilities of the events x, y, z, and so on, regarded not only as simple but as independent events. Then by Prop. I., the probabilities that these events will occur when the condition V, expressed by the logical equation V=1, is satisfied, are [xV][V],[yV][V],[zV][V], &c., where [xV] stands for the result of multiplying V by x, by the rules of the Calculus of Logic, and then changing x, y, z in the result into p′, q′, r′, and so on. But by hypothesis these conditioned probabilities are equal to p,q,r,… respectively. So we have [xV][V]=p,[yV][V]=q,[zV][V]=r, &c., a system with as many equations as there are unknowns p′,q′,r′,…, from which the values of those unknowns can be found.

Now xV consists simply of those constituents of V that have x as a factor. Let this sum be written Vx, and in the same way let yV be written Vy, and so on. Our equations then take the form [Vx][V]=p,[Vy][V]=q, &c.;(1) where [Vx] stands for the result of changing, in Vx, the symbols x, y, z, and so on into p′, q′, r′, and so on.

To make the meaning of the general problem, and the principle of its solution, clearer, let us take an example. Suppose balls are being drawn from an urn. Attention has been paid only to the cases in which the ball drawn was either of a particular colour, “white,” or of a particular material, “marble,” or had both these features. No record was kept of the cases in which the ball drawn was neither white nor marble. Suppose it was found that whenever this condition was satisfied, there was a probability p that a white ball would be drawn, and a probability q that a marble ball would be drawn. From these data alone, we are asked to find the probability that on the next drawing, with no reference at all to that condition, a white ball will be drawn; and also the probability that a marble ball will be drawn.

Here, if x stands for drawing a white ball and y for drawing a marble ball, the condition V will be expressed by the logical function xy+x(1−y)+(1−x)y. That is: white and marble, or white and not marble, or marble and not white. So we have Vx=xy+x(1−y)=x,Vy=xy+(1−x)y=y; and so [Vx]=p′,[Vy]=q′; and the final equations of the problem are p′p′q′+p′(1−q′)+q′(1−p′)=p,q′p′q′+p′(1−q′)+q′(1−p′)=q; Each says that the absolute probability of white (or of marble), divided by the probability that the condition holds, must equal the probability observed under the condition. From these we find p′=p+q−1q,q′=p+q−1p.

We see that p′ and q′ are proportional to p and q respectively, as Professor Donkin’s principle says they should be. In fact, problems of this class could be solved by applying that principle directly.

To meet a possible objection, I should say here that this reasoning does not require the drawing of a white ball and the drawing of a marble ball to be independent because of the way the balls are physically made. The assumption that they are independent is indeed part of the solution. But it does not rest on any earlier assumption about the nature of the balls, or about the relations, or lack of relations, among their shape, colour, structure, and so on. It is founded on our total ignorance of all these things. Probability always refers to the state of our actual knowledge, and its numerical value varies with varying information.

Editor's note: Boole later saw that this example was wrong. In the Note printed at the front of the book (set after the Preface in this edition) he withdrew this solution, gave the true answer to the urn problem as he had stated it (one that contains a constant the data do not fix), and restated the principle behind his method: treat the simple events as independent, with whatever probabilities make them agree with the data under the given condition. That principle was the most criticised step in his theory; Henry Wilbraham attacked it in 1854, and Boole defended it in print for years. Theodore Hailperin later showed (1976) that Boole's problems are best read as finding the range of values the data allow, which is a problem in what is now called linear programming.

Proposition III.

11. In any question of probabilities, to determine the logical connection of the quæsitum with the data: that is, to express the event whose probability is sought as a logical function of the events whose probabilities are given.

Let S, T, and so on stand for any compound events whose probabilities are given, S and T being written as known functions of the symbols x, y, z, and so on, which stand for simple events. In the same way, let W stand for any event whose probability is sought, W also being a known function of x, y, z, and so on. Since S,T,…W must satisfy the fundamental law of duality, we may replace them by single logical symbols, s,t,…w. So let s=S,t=T,w=W.

By the definition of S,T,…W, these will be a series of logical equations connecting the symbols s,t,…w, with the symbols x,y,z…

By the methods of the Calculus of Logic, we can eliminate from this system any of the symbols x,y,z,… that stand for events whose probabilities are not given. We can then find w as a developed function of s, t, and so on, together with any of the symbols x, y, z, and so on, if there are any, that stand for events whose probabilities are given. The result will be of the form w=A+0B+00C+10D, where A, B, C, and D between them take in all the possible constituents that can be formed from the symbols s, t, and so on: that is, from all the symbols that stand for events whose probabilities are given. Read in the usual way, this says: w includes all of the cases in A, none of those in B, an indefinite part of those in C, and the cases in D cannot occur at all.

This is clearly the complete expression of the relation we are looking for. It fully determines the event W, written as the single symbol w, as a function or combination of the events written as the symbols s, t, and so on. And by the laws of the Calculus of Logic it assigns the condition D=0, as connecting the events s, t, and so on among themselves; that is, the combinations in D never happen. So, by Principle VI., we may regard s, t, and so on as simple events, of which both the combination w, and the condition D attached to it, are definitely determined.

Since it is desirable for the logical steps of reduction to be uniform, I shall state here the order that will generally be followed.

12. By (VIII. 8), the original equations can be brought into the forms s(1−S)+S(1−s)=0;t(1−T)+T(1−t)=0;(1)⋯w(1−W)+W(1−w)=0; and in these forms they can be added together without losing any of their meaning. (Each one says, in effect, that there is nothing which is s without being S, and nothing which is S without being s.) We can then eliminate the symbols x, y, z, either one at a time or all together. If we eliminate them together, we must first add up the equations of the system, then develop the result with respect to all the symbols to be eliminated, and set equal to 0 the product of all the coefficients of the constituents (VII. 9).

Since w is the symbol whose expression we are looking for, we may also, by Prop. III. Chap. IX., put the result of elimination in the form Ew+E′(1−w)=0.

E and E′ are found in turn by putting, in the general system (1), first w=1 and then w=0, and each time eliminating the symbols x, y, z, … So the single equations from which E and E′ are to be found are s(1−S)+S(1−s)+t(1−T)+T(1−t)…+1−W=0;s(1−S)+S(1−s)+t(1−T)+T(1−t)+W=0. From these it only remains to eliminate x, y, z, &c., and then to find w by developing the result. In the elimination we may, where it helps, use the shortcuts of Props. I. and II. Chap. IX.

13. Sometimes the data do more than tell us the probabilities of the events. They may also lay down some explicit connection among them. Any such connection must be written in logical form, and the equation or equations that express it must be added to the general system.

Proposition IV.

14. Given the probabilities of any system of events; to determine by a general method the consequent or derived probability of any other event.

As in the last Proposition, let S, T, &c., be the events whose probabilities are given, and W the event whose probability is sought. All of these are known functions of x, y, z, &c. We write the data like this: Probability of S=p;Probability of T=q;(1) and so on, where p, q, &c., are known numbers. Now let the compound event S be represented by s, T by t, and W by w. Then by the last Proposition we find w=A+0B+00C+10D;(2) where A, B, C, and D are functions of s, t, &c. Read aloud, this says: w happens in every case of A, never in a case of B, in some indefinite part of the cases of C, and the cases of D cannot happen at all. At the same time the data (1) turn into Prob. s=p,Prob. t=q, &c.(3)

Now equation (2) can be broken into the system w=A+qCD=0,}(4) where q is a symbol for an indefinite class (VI. 12). But by the properties of constituents (V. Prop. III.), we have A+B+C+D=1, that is, the constituents together make up everything that can happen. So the second equation of the system above can be written in the form A+B+C=1.

If we call the function A+B+C by the single letter V, the system (4) becomes w=A+qC;(5)V=1.(6)

Let us stop for a moment and look at this result. V is a sum of constituents of s, t, &c. So it stands for a compound event made up of the simple events denoted by s, t, &c. Equation (6) therefore shows something important. The events denoted by s, t, &c., whose probabilities are p, q, &c., do not have these probabilities as independent events. They have them as events bound by a certain condition, namely V. Equation (5) then expresses w as a combination of the same events, bound by the same condition.

Now by Principle VI., the way we came to know this connection between the events makes no difference to the way we must use it once we know it. We must reason on it as if experience had shown us the events s, t, &c., as simple events, free to combine in every possible way, which, when they are actually bound by the condition V, have the probabilities p, q, &c.

So let p′,q′,…, be the probabilities these events would have if the restriction V were taken away. Then by Prop. II. of this chapter, these quantities are fixed by the system of equations, [Vs][V]=p,[Vt][V]=q, &c.;(7) and by Prop. I., the probability of the event w under the same condition V will be Prob. w=[A+cC][V];(8) Here Vs stands for the sum of those constituents in V that have s as a factor, and [Vs] for what that sum becomes when s,t,…, are replaced by p′,q′,…, respectively. The constant c stands for the probability of the indefinite event q. It is therefore arbitrary, a constant whose value the data do not fix, and it may have any value from 0 to 1.

Notice now that we work out the values of p′, q′, &c., from (7) only so that we can put them into (8), and so make Prob. w a function of the known quantities p, q, &c. Clearly, then, instead of the letters p′, q′, &c., we could use any other letters, such as s, t, &c., taken in the same number sense. This step would simply change the meaning of the symbols s, t, &c.: they would stop being logical symbols and become number symbols. The systems (7) and (8) would then become VsV=p,VtV=q, &c.;(9)Prob. w=A+cCV.(10) To use these, we only need to solve (9) for s, t, &c., now taken as number symbols, in terms of p, q, &c., and put the values we get into (10). Since s, t, &c., now stand for probabilities, they will clearly be positive fractions less than 1.

The system (9) can be written more symmetrically in the form Vsp=Vtq…=V.(11) Or we can write (9) and (10) together in the single symmetrical system Vsp=Vtq…=A+cCu=V;(12) where u stands for Prob. w.

15. It remains to interpret the constant c, which we took to stand for the probability of the indefinite event q. Now the logical equation w=A+qC, read in the reverse direction, means this: if either the event A happens, or the event C happens together with the event q, then the event w will happen, and not otherwise. So q stands for the condition under which, if the event C happens, the event w will happen. But the probability of q is c. So c= the probability that if the event C happens, the event w will happen.

So by Principle II., c=Probability of concurrence of C and wProbability of C. In words, c is the probability that C and w both happen, divided by the probability of C. From this we can see what new experience would give us the actual value of c. Take C, and put back, in place of s, t, &c., their original expressions as functions of the simple events x, y, z, &c. This gives the expression of the event whose probability is the denominator of the value of c above. Multiply that expression by the original expression of w, and we have the expression of the event whose probability is the numerator of c. Then the ratio of how often this second event occurs to how often the first one occurs, found by new observations, will give the value of c. Notice that the constant c does not necessarily appear in the solution of a problem. This arbitrary element turns up only when the data are not enough to fix the probability sought. And in that case, as we have just seen, the final logical equation (2) or (5) tells us how it is to be determined.

Suppose the new experience that would fix c cannot be had. We can still give c its extreme values 0 and 1, and so find the limits of the probability of w, the smallest and largest values it can have. These limits are Minor limit of Prob. w=AV.Superior limit =A+CV. The probability sought is certain to lie between these limits, whatever new experience may bring, so long as that experience does not flatly contradict the past.
