Suppose the expression of the event C is made up of many constituents, so that the logical value of w has the form w=A+00C1+00C2+ &c., Then, instead of lumping them together as above, we can give the final solution in the form Prob. w=A+c1C1+c2C2+ &c.V.

Here c1= the probability that if the event C1 occurs, the event w will occur, and so on for the others. Which form to use is a matter of convenience.

16. This is the complete theoretical solution of the problem we set. We may add that it applies just as well when some of the events named in the original statement are conditioned. Suppose, for instance, that one of the data is the probability p that if the event x occurs, the event y will occur, and that the probability of x itself is not given. Then we must assume Prob. x=c (an arbitrary constant), so that Prob. xy=cp, and these two conditions must be put into the data and used by the method already given. Again, suppose we want the probability that if an event x occurs, an event y will occur. Then the solution will take the form Prob. sought =Prob. xyProb. x, and the numerator and the denominator must each be found separately by the general method above.

17. What we have found lets us lay down a general rule for solving questions in probability.

General Rule.

Case I.—When all the events are unconditioned.

Write the symbolic expressions of the events whose probabilities are given or sought.

Set those expressions that stand for compound events equal to a new series of symbols, s, t, &c. Treat each of these symbols as standing for the event whose expression it has been set equal to, now regarded not as compound but as simple.

From the equations so formed, eliminate every logical symbol except those that stand for the events s, t, &c., whose probabilities p, q, &c. are given, and the event w, whose probability is sought. Then find w as a developed function of s, t, &c. in the form w=A+0B+00C+10D. Let A+B+C=V. Let Vs stand for the sum of those constituents in V that contain s as a factor, Vt for the sum of those that contain t as a factor, and so on for all the symbols whose probabilities are given.

Then, passing from logic to algebra, form the equations Vsp=Vtq=V,(1)Prob. w=A+cCV,(2) From (1), find s, t, &c. as functions of p, q, &c., and put their values into (2). The result will be the solution required.

Or form the symmetrical system of equations Vsp=Vtq…=A+cCu=V1,(3) where u stands for the probability sought.

If c appears in the solution, its interpretation will be c=Prob. CwProb. C, and this interpretation shows what kind of experience is needed to find it.

Case II.—When some of the events are conditioned.

Suppose we are given the probability p that if the event X occurs, the event Y will occur, and the probability of the antecedent X is not given. Then break this statement into the following two, namely: Probability of X=c,Probability of XY=cp. If what is sought is the probability that if the event W occurs, the event Z will occur, find separately, by the previous case, the top and bottom of the fraction Prob. WZProb. W, and the fraction itself will be the probability sought.

In this case it is understood that X, Y, W, Z may be any compound events whatever. The expressions XY and WZ stand for the products of the symbolic expressions of X and Y, and of W and Z, formed by the rules of the calculus of logic.

Finding the single constant c may in some cases be broken into, or replaced by, finding a series of arbitrary constants c1,c2… as convenience suggests, as explained above.

18. It was said earlier (I. 12) that there are two distinct definitions, or ways of conceiving probability, on which the theory can be made to rest. One is tied more closely to number, the other more directly to logic. We have now followed out the consequences of the number definition. We have shown how it leads us to a point where the need for a connection with logic plainly suggests itself. We have seen, to some extent, what that connection is. We have seen, too, how the special processes of logic and the more familiar processes of the algebra of quantity both enter into the same general method of solution. Each does its own job, so that the two processes may be thought of as completing each other. What remains is to run the inquiry in the reverse order. We start from a definition of probability in which the logical relation is more directly involved. We then show how the number definition would arise from it, and how the same general method, resting equally on both elements, would in the end be established, though by a different route.

I have often pointed out in this book that there is a close analogy between the symbolic expressions of the logical calculus and those of algebra. One might even say that they share their forms and, to a very large degree, their laws. With a single exception among the laws, they differ only in how they are interpreted. (The exception is the law of duality, which holds for logical symbols and not for numbers in general.) So the same expression can be read logically or as a quantity, depending on the meaning we give to its symbols. Read the first way, the expression xy stands for the events denoted by x and y both occurring. Read the second way, it stands for the product of the numbers or quantities denoted by x and y. In the same way, every expression that denotes an event, simple or compound, has, under another system of interpretation, a purely numerical meaning. This raises a question. Is there some principle of transition by which the logical meaning and the numerical meaning of the same symbolic expression are connected in a way that makes sense? The following considerations answer that question.

19. Let it be granted that there is such a feeling as expectation: a feeling whose object is the occurrence of events, and which can be more or less intense. Let it also be granted that this feeling of expectation goes along with our knowledge of the circumstances under which events are produced, and that it changes with the amount and kind of that knowledge. We need not assume, openly or quietly, that the intensity of expectation, taken as a feeling in the mind, can be measured exactly in numbers. Even so, it is perfectly fair to ask whether there could be a way of estimating it in numbers that meets at least these conditions: the number it gives should go up when the known circumstances of an event are felt to justify a stronger expectation, go down when they call for a weaker one, and stay the same when they plainly call for the same degree of expectation.

These conditions at least will be met if we take the fundamental principle of expectation to be the following. The laws for expressing expectation, taken as a number, are to be the same as the laws for expressing the expected event, taken as a logical element. So if ϕ(x,y,z) stands for any unconditioned event made up in any way of the events x, y, z, then by this principle the same expression ϕ(x,y,z) is to stand for the expectation of that event; but now x, y, z stand no longer for the simple events themselves but for the expectations of those events.

For, first, it is clear that on this hypothesis the probability that some one of a set of events that exclude one another will occur is the sum of the separate probabilities of those events. Suppose the set of alternatives in question consists of n events that exclude one another, whose expressions are ϕ1(x,y,z),ϕ2(x,y,z),…ϕn(x,y,z), Then the expression of that set of alternatives, the statement that one of them happens, will be ϕ1(x,y,z)+ϕ2(x,y,z)…+ϕn(x,y,z)=1; where the letters x, y, z are logical, and stand for the simple events of which the three alternatives are made up. And by hypothesis, the expression of the probability that some one of those alternatives will occur is ϕ1(x,y,z)+ϕ2(x,y,z)…+ϕn(x,y,z), where x, y, z now stand for the probabilities of those simple events. Now this expression grows, cæteris paribus (other things being equal), as the number of alternatives grows, and shrinks as their number shrinks. That agrees with the condition we laid down.

Further, if we start from this hypothetical definition of the measure of probability, we shall be led to the received number definition. We get there either by necessary inference or by steps of suggestion that might perhaps themselves be called necessary. We are at once led to recognise unity (1) as the proper number for certainty. For it is certain that any event x or its contrary 1−x will occur. The expression of this proposition is x+(1−x)=1, so, by hypothesis, x+(1−x), the measure of the probability of this proposition, becomes the measure of certainty. But the value of that expression is 1, whatever the particular value of x may be. So on this hypothesis, unity, or 1, is the measure of certainty.

Next, let there be n events that exclude one another but are equally possible, which we will write as t1,t2,…tn. The proposition that some one of them must occur is expressed by the equation t1+t2…+tn=1; When we pass, by the reasoning of the last section, to probabilities as numbers, this equation still holds in form. And since the probabilities t1,t2…tn are equal, we have nt1=1, so t1=1n, and in the same way t2=1n, tn=1n. Suppose we then want the probability that some one event of the shorter series t1,t2…tm will occur. The expression we need is t1+t2…+tm=1n+1n…to m terms=mn. So if there are m cases favourable to some set of alternatives out of n possible and equally likely cases, the probability that one of those alternatives occurs is the fraction mn.

Now if an event can happen in several equally possible ways, its happening really amounts to the happening of one of a set of alternatives. So the probability of any event can be written as a fraction: the top is the number of cases favourable to it, and the bottom is the total number of equally possible cases. But this is exactly the strict number definition of the measure of probability. That definition is therefore contained in the more distinctly logical definition whose consequences we have been trying to trace.

20. From these inquiries two things are clear. 1st, it makes no difference which definition we start from. We may start from the ordinary number definition of the measure of probability. Or we may start from the definition that gives the number measure of probability whatever law of value makes the logical expressions of events formally identical with the algebraic expressions of their values. Either way we are led to the same system of practical results. 2ndly, either definition, followed out to its consequences and taken together with the relations it necessarily involves, leads us, by inference or by suggestion, to the other. For a scientific view of the theory of probability, it is essential to see both principles together, each bearing on the other and depending on it.

Chapter 18: Elementary Illustrations of the General Method in Probabilities

1. My aim here is to illustrate, with elementary examples, the general method proved in the last chapter. Most of the examples are chosen because they are simple enough for their solutions to be checked easily. But there will also be hints of a higher class of problems, to be treated more fully later. The analysis of those problems would be incomplete without a separate method. That method must find the conditions the data have to satisfy if they are to represent a possible experience, and it must fix the corresponding limits of the final solutions. A fuller treatment of that method, and of its uses, is kept for the next chapter.

2. Ex. 1.—The probability that it thunders on a given day is p, and the probability that it both thunders and hails is q. Nothing more is supposed to be known about the connection between the two phenomena of thunder and hail. Required: the probability that it hails on that day.

Here what is given is the chance of thunder and the chance of thunder and hail together; what is sought is the chance of hail. Let the symbols stand for the events like this: Let x represent the event—It thunders.Let y represent the event—It hails. Then xy will represent the event "It thunders and hails," and the data of the problem are Prob. x=p,Prob. xy=q. Only one compound event, xy, is involved here. So, following the rule, we give it a single letter of its own and assume xy=u.(1) Our data then become Prob. x=p,Prob. u=q;(2) and we are required to find Prob. y. The first step is to express y in terms of the letters whose probabilities are known. Now (1) gives y=ux=ux+10u(1−x)+0(1−u)x+00(1−u)(1−x). This is the development of y into its compartments, the four combinations of u and x, each with its coefficient. From it (XVII. 17) we find V, the sum of the compartments the data allow (those whose coefficient is not 1/0), together with the parts of it that contain x and that contain u: V=ux+(1−u)x+(1−u)(1−x),Vx=ux+(1−u)x=x,Vu=ux; and the equations of the General Rule, namely Vxp=Vuq=V.Prob. y=A+cCV become, once we substitute, and note that A=ux, C=(1−u)(1−x), and that V reduces to x+(1−u)(1−x), xp=uxq=x+(1−u)(1−x),(3)Prob. y=ux+c(1−u)(1−x)x+(1−u)(1−x),(4) Here A is the compartment whose coefficient is 1, and C the one whose coefficient is 0/0, the indefinite one. From these, by eliminating x and u, we easily deduce Prob. y=q+c(1−p).(5) In this result c stands for the unknown probability that if the event (1−u)(1−x) happens, the event y will happen. Now (1−u)(1−x)=(1−xy)(1−x)=1−x, as we find by actually multiplying it out. So c is the unknown probability that if it does not thunder, it will hail.

So the general solution (5) can be read as follows. The probability that it hails equals the probability that it thunders and hails, q, plus the probability that it does not thunder, 1−p, multiplied by the probability c that if it does not thunder it will hail. Ordinary reasoning confirms this result.

If c cannot be given a numerical value, we can give it its extreme values 0 and 1, and we then find the following limits of Prob. y, namely: Inferior limit =q.Superior limit =q+1−p. That is, the chance of hail is at least the chance of thunder with hail, and at most that plus the chance of no thunder.

3. Ex. 2.—The probability that one or both of two events happen is p, and the probability that one or both of them fail is q. What is the probability that only one of them happens?

Let x and y stand for the two events. Then the data are these: Prob. xy+x(1−y)+(1−x)y=p,Prob. x(1−y)+(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y)=q; and we are to find Prob. x(1−y)+y(1−x). Read aloud: given the chance of "both, or the first alone, or the second alone," and the chance of "the first alone, or the second alone, or neither," we want the chance of "exactly one." Since all the events concerned here are compound, we give each its own letter and assume xy+x(1−y)+(1−x)y=s,x(1−y)+(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y)=t,x(1−y)+(1−x)y=w. Then we eliminate x and y, and work out w as a developed function of s and t. We find w=st+0s(1−t)+0(1−s)t+10(1−s)(1−t). So A=st,C=0,V=st+s(1−t)+(1−s)t=s+(1−s)t,Vs=s,Vt=t; and the equations of the General Rule (XVII. 17) become sp=tq=s+(1−s)t,(1) Prob. w=sts+(1−s)t; and from these, eliminating s and t, we find Prob. w=p+q−1. So p+q−1 is the measure of the probability we want. The result can be checked like this. Since p is the probability that one or both of the events occur, 1−p will be the probability that they both fail. And since q is the probability that one or both fail, 1−q is the probability that they both happen. So 1−p+1−q, or 2−p−q, is the probability that they either both happen or both fail. But the only other possibility left is that just one of the events happens. So the probability of that is 1−(2−p−q), or p+q−1, as above.

4. Ex. 3.—The probability that a witness A tells the truth is p, the probability that another witness B tells the truth is q, and the probability that they disagree in a statement is r. What is the probability that if they agree, their statement is true?

Let x stand for the hypothesis that A tells the truth, and y for the hypothesis that B tells the truth. Then the hypothesis that A and B disagree in their statement will be represented by x(1−y)+y(1−x), that is, one tells the truth and the other does not. The hypothesis that they agree in their statement is xy+(1−x)(1−y), both truthful or both not; and the hypothesis that they agree in the truth is xy. So we have the following data: Prob. x=p,Prob. y=q,Prob. x(1−y)+y(1−x)=r, and from them we are to find Prob. xyProb. xy+(1−x)(1−y). That is, the chance that both are truthful, out of all the cases in which they agree. But since Prob. x(1−y)+y(1−x)=r, it is clear that Prob. xy+(1−x)(1−y) will be 1−r; so what we have to find is Prob. xy1−r. The compound events that appear are x(1−y)+y(1−x) and xy, so let us assume x(1−y)+y(1−x)=sxy=w}(1) Our data are then Prob. x=p, Prob. y=q, Prob. s=r, and we are to find Prob. w.

On reduction, the system (1) becomes the single equation {x(1−y)+y(1−x)}(1−s)+s{xy+(1−x)(1−y)}+xy(1−w)+w(1−xy)=0; and from this, solving for w and developing, w=x(1−y)(1−s)+y(1−x)(1−s)+sxy+s(1−x)(1−y)+xy2xy−1=10xys+xy(1−s)+0x(1−y)s+10x(1−y)(1−s)+0(1−x)ys+10(1−x)(1−y)s+10(1−x)y(1−s)(2)+0(1−x)(1−y)(1−s). In writing out this development, I have put the coefficient 10 in place of every form equivalent to it (X. 6). Here we have V=xy(1−s)+x(1−y)s+(1−x)ys+(1−x)(1−y)(1−s); and so, passing from logic to algebra, xy(1−s)+x(1−y)sp=xy(1−s)+(1−x)ysq=x(1−y)s+(1−x)ysr=xy(1−s)+x(1−y)s+(1−x)ys+(1−x)(1−y)(1−s).Prob. w=xy(1−s)xy(1−s)+x(1−y)s+(1−x)ys+(1−x)(1−y)(1−s), In each fraction on the first lines, the top is the part of V that contains the letter whose probability is the number underneath; the last line gives what is sought. From these we easily deduce Prob. w=p+q−r2; and so we have Prob. xy1−r=p+q−r2(1−r)(3) for the value sought.

Suppose we now ask, in the same way, for the probability that if A and B agree in their statement, that statement will be false. Then we must replace the second equation of the system (1) with this one: (1−x)(1−y)=w; that is, w now stands for both witnesses being untruthful. The final logical equation will then be w=10xys+0xy(1−s)+0x(1−y)s+10x(1−y)(1−s)+0(1−x)ys+10(1−x)y(1−s)+10(1−x)(1−y)s+(1−x)(1−y)(1−s);(4) and, proceeding as before, we finally deduce Prob. w=2−p−q−r2.(5) So we have Prob. (1−x)(1−y)1−r=2−p−q−r2(1−r)(6) for the value sought here.

These results agree with each other. The joint statement of A and B must certainly be either true or false. So the right-hand sides of (3) and (5) ought to add up to 1. And in fact we have, identically, p+q−r2(1−r)+2−p−q−r2(1−r)=1.

Since the results (5) and (6) are so simple, they could probably be deduced easily by applying known principles. But it should be noted that they do not fall directly within the reach of known methods. The number of data is greater than the number of simple events they involve: here three data, and only two simple events. M. Cournot, in his very able work, “Exposition de la Theorie des Chances," has proposed a way of handling cases like this one. Select from the original premises several different sets of data, each set as large as the number of simple events it involves. Assume that those simple events are independent, and work out their probabilities separately from each set of data. Then compare the different values found in this way for the same quantities, and judge from that how far the assumption of independence is justified. This method can only come near to being correct when the simple events turn out, by that test, to be nearly or quite independent. And in questions of testimony and of judgment, where such a hypothesis is used, it seems doubtful whether actual experience of the ways of men justifies it.

5. Ex. 4.—Observations were made during a period of widespread sickness. They gave a probability p that any house taken at random in a particular district was visited by fever, and a probability q that it was visited by cholera. They also gave a probability r that it escaped both diseases and was not in a defective sanitary condition as regards cleanliness and ventilation. What is the probability that any house taken at random was in a defective sanitary condition?

For any house, let us assign the symbols x,y,z, as follows:

The symbol xto the house being visited by fever.
y” by cholera.
zto its defective sanitary condition.

The events whose probabilities are given are then denoted by x, y, and (1−x)(1−y)(1−z); the event whose probability is sought is z. The third datum is compound, so we assume (1−x)(1−y)(1−z)=w; that is, w is a house with no fever, no cholera, and nothing wrong with its sanitation. Then our data are Prob. x=p,Prob. y=q,Prob. w=r, and we are to find Prob. z. Now, solving for z and developing, z=(1−x)(1−y)−w(1−x)(1−y)=10xyw+00xy(1−w)+10x(1−y)w+00x(1−y)(1−w)+10(1−x)yw+00(1−x)y(1−w)+0(1−x)(1−y)w+(1−x)(1−y)(1−w).(1) The value of V we deduce from this is V=xy(1−w)+x(1−y)(1−w)+(1−x)y(1−w)+(1−x)(1−y)w+(1−x)(1−y)(1−w)=1−w+w(1−x)(1−y); and reducing Vx,Vy,Vw in the same way, we get Vx=x(1−w),Vy=y(1−w),Vw=w(1−x)(1−y); which give the algebraic equations x(1−w)p=y(1−w)q=w(1−x)(1−y)r=1−w+w(1−x)(1−y).(2) As for the terms of the development that carry the coefficient 00, I shall not gather them into a single term. For the sake of variety (XVII. 18), I shall present them in the form 00x(1−w)+00(1−x)y(1−w);(3) each with its own unknown constant. The value of Prob. z will then be Prob. z=(1−x)(1−y)(1−w)+cx(1−w)+c′(1−x)y(1−w)1−w+w(1−x)(1−y).(4)

From (2) and (4) we deduce Prob. z=(1−p−r)(1−q−r)1−r+cp+c′q(1−p−r)1−r, as the expression of the probability required. If in this result we set c=0 and c′=0, we find a lower limit of its value, (1−p−r)(1−q−r)1−r; and if we set c=1, c′=1, we obtain its upper limit, 1−r.

6. Looking at this solution, we can see that the premises chosen were very incomplete. The constants c and c′ show this, and the corresponding terms (3) of the final logical equation show how the gap is to be filled. Since x(1−w)=x{1−(1−x)(1−y)(1−z)}=x,(1−x)y(1−w)=(1−x)y{1−(1−x)(1−y)(1−z)}=(1−x)y, we learn that c is the probability that if a house was visited by fever its sanitary condition is defective. And c′ is the probability that if a house was visited by cholera without fever, its sanitary condition was defective. These are exactly the further facts the data would need to supply.

If the terms of the logical development with the coefficient 00 had been gathered together, as in the direct statement of the general rule, the final solution would have taken this form: Prob. z=(1−p−r)(1−q−r)1−r+c(p+q−pq1−r) with c here standing for the probability that if a house was visited by either or both of the diseases, its sanitary condition was defective. This result is entirely consistent with the former one. Indeed, it can be formally proved that the different forms of solution given in such cases are necessarily equivalent.

The solution above can be checked in particular cases. Take the second form: if c=1 we find Prob. z=1−r, a correct result. For if the presence of either fever or cholera certainly meant a defective sanitary condition, then the probability that a house was in a defective sanitary state would simply equal the probability that it was not found in the category denoted by z, and by the data the probability of that would be 1−r. A general check of the solution would perhaps be difficult.

The constants p, q, and r in this solution are subject to the conditions p+r<=1,q+r<=1. that is, p plus r is at most 1, and so is q plus r.

7. Ex. 5.—Given the probabilities of the premises of a hypothetical syllogism, to find the probability of the conclusion.

Let the syllogism, stripped to its bare form, be as follows:

Major premise:If the proposition Y is true X is true.
Minor premise:If the proposition Z is true Y is true.
Conclusion:If the proposition Z is true X is true.

Suppose the probability of the major premise is p, and that of the minor premise q.

Represent the proposition X by x, and so on, and take c and c′ as arbitrary constants, numbers whose values the data do not fix: c is the probability of Y, and c′ that of Z. The probability of an "if" proposition is the probability that its "then" part is true when its "if" part is. So the data are as follows: Prob. y=c, Prob. xy=cp;Prob. z=c′, Prob. yz=c′q; and from these we are to find Prob. xzProb. z or Prob. xzc′. that is, the probability that X is true when Z is.

Let us assume xy=u,yz=v,xz=w, and then proceed by the usual method to find w as a developed function of y, z, w, and v, the symbols that stand for propositions whose probabilities are given. We find w=uzvy+0u(1−z)(1−v)y+0(1−u)zvy+00(1−u)z(1−v)(1−y)+0(1−u)(1−z)(1−v)y+0(1−u)(1−z)(1−v)(1−y)+ terms whose coefficients are 10; and passing from logic to algebra, uzvy+u(1−z)(1−v)ycp=uzvy+(1−u)zvy+(1−u)z(1−v)(1−y)c′=uzvy+(1−u)zvyc′q=uzvy+u(1−z)(1−v)y+(1−u)zvy+(1−u)(1−z)(1−v)yc=V.Prob. w=uzvy+a(1−u)z(1−v)(1−y)V, where V=uzvy+u(1−z)(1−v)y+(1−u)zvy+(1−u)z(1−v)(1−y)+(1−u)(1−z)(1−v)y+(1−u)(1−z)(1−v)(1−y), Here a is the new arbitrary constant belonging to the single indefinite term. Solving this system of equations gives Prob. w=c′pq+ac′(1−q), and so Prob. xzc′=pq+a(1−q), which is the value required. In this expression the arbitrary constant a is the probability that if the proposition Z is true and Y false, X is true. In other words, it is the probability that if the minor premise is false, the conclusion is true.

This investigation could have been made much simpler by assuming the proposition Z to be true, and then looking for the probability of X. The data would then have been simply Prob. y=q,Prob. xy=pq; and from these we should have found Prob. x=pq+a(1−q). Clearly this way of proceeding would have been allowable in the circumstances. But I have preferred to deduce the solution by applying the method directly, without conditions. The result is one that ordinary reasoning confirms, and indeed one that needs no calculus to obtain. General methods tend to look most cumbersome when they are applied where their help is least needed.

Note that the method above applies equally to the categorical syllogism. And not to the syllogism only, but to every form of deductive reasoning. Given the probabilities attaching separately to the premises of any chain of argument, the method can always find the resulting probability that a conclusion legitimately drawn from those premises is true. I hardly need to remind the reader that the truth of a conclusion and its correctness are different things.

8. One remarkable fact that turns up in such applications deserves special notice. It is this: propositions that are equivalent when true are not necessarily equivalent when they are regarded only as probable. The following example illustrates this principle.

Ex. 6.—Given the probability p of the disjunctive proposition “Either the proposition Y is true, or both the propositions X and Y are false,” required: the probability of the conditional proposition, “If the proposition X is true, Y is true.”

Let x and y stand for the propositions X and Y respectively. Then we have Prob. y+(1−x)(1−y)=p, and from this we are required to find the value of Prob. xyProb. x, the chance that Y is true among the cases where X is. We give the disjunctive proposition a letter of its own: Assumey+(1−x)(1−y)=t.(1) Eliminating y, we get (1−x)(1−t)=0. that is, whenever the disjunctive proposition is false, X is true. So x=00t+1−t; and proceeding in the usual way, Prob. x=1−p+cp.(2) Here c is the probability that if either Y is true, or X and Y are both false, then X is true.

Next, to find Prob. xy, we assume xy=w.(3) Eliminating y from (1) and (3), we get w(1−t)=0; and from this, proceeding as above, Prob. w=cp, with c meaning the same as before. So Prob. xyProb. x=cp1−p+cp, is the probability that the given conditional proposition is true.

Now in pure logic, which as such deals only with truth and falsehood, the disjunctive and conditional propositions above are equivalent. They are true together and false together. Yet the investigation above shows that when the disjunctive proposition has a probability p, the conditional proposition has a different and partly indefinite probability, cp1−p+cp. Still, these expressions are such that when either of them becomes 1 or 0, the other takes the same value. So the results are entirely consistent, and the logical transformation serves to check the formula deduced from the theory of probability.

By a similar analysis the reader will easily prove the reverse. If the probability of the conditional proposition were given as p, that of the disjunctive proposition would be 1−c+cp, where c is the arbitrary probability that the proposition X is true.

9. Ex. 7.—Required: the probability of an event x, when we are given either the first, or the first and second, or the first, second, and third of the following data:

First: the probability that the event x occurs, or that it alone of the three events x, y, z, fails, is p.

Second: the probability that the event y occurs, or that it alone of the three events x, y, z, fails, is q.

Third: the probability that the event z occurs, or that it alone of the three events x, y, z, fails, is r.

Solution of the First Case.

Here we suppose that only the first of these data is given. We then have Prob. {x+(1−x)yz}=p, and we are to find Prob. x. In words: either x happens, or x fails while y and z both happen. Letx+(1−x)yz=s, Then, eliminating yz as if it were a single symbol, we get x(1−s)=0. that is, x never happens without s. So x=01−s=00s+0(1−s), and from this, proceeding by the rule, we have Prob. x=cp,(1) where c is the probability that if either x occurs or it alone fails, it will be the first of these two alternatives that happens. Clearly the limits of the solution are 0 and p.

This solution seems to tell us nothing beyond what plain good sense would have told us. But it is all that the single datum assumed here really entitles us to infer. In the next solution we shall see how adding to our data confines the final solution within narrower limits.

Solution of the Second Case.

Here we take as our data the equations Prob. {x+(1−x)yz}=p,Prob. {y+(1−y)xz}=q. Let us write x+(1−x)yz=s,y+(1−y)xz=t; From the first of these we have, by (VIII. 7), {x+(1−x)yz}(1−s)+s{1−x−(1−x)yz}=0,or(x+x‾yz)s‾+sx‾(1−yz)=0; where for simplicity we write x‾ for 1−x, y‾ for 1−y, and so on. Now, writing out 1−yz in constituents (the three compartments in which y and z are not both present), we have (x+x‾yz)s‾+sx‾(yz‾+y‾z+y‾z‾)=0, an equation made up entirely of positive terms. In the same way we get from the second equation (y+y‾xz)t‾+ty‾(xz‾+x‾z+x‾z‾)=0; and from the sum of these two equations we have to eliminate y and z. To eliminate them, we put in each of the four pairs of values 1 and 0 for y and z, and multiply the results together.

If in that sum we set y=1, z=1, we get the result s‾+t‾.

If in the same sum we set y=1, z=0, we get the result xs‾+sx‾+t‾.

If in the same sum we set y=0, z=1, we get xs‾+sx‾+xt‾+tx‾.

And if, last, in the same sum we set y=0, z=0, we find xs‾+sx‾+tx+tx‾, or xs‾+sx‾+t.

These four expressions are to be multiplied together. The first and third can be multiplied like this: (s‾+t‾)(xs‾+sx‾+xt‾+tx‾)=xs‾+xt‾+(s‾+t‾)(sx‾+tx‾) by (IX. Prop. II.)=xs‾+xt‾+s‾x‾t+sx‾t‾.(2) Next, the second and fourth give, by (IX. Prop. I.), (xs‾+sx‾+t‾)(xs‾+sx‾+t)=xs‾+sx‾.(3) Last, (2) and (3) multiplied together give (xs‾+sx‾)(xs‾+sx‾t‾+xt‾+tx‾s‾)=xs‾+sx‾(sx‾t‾+xt‾+tx‾s‾)=xs‾+sx‾t‾. So the final equation is (1−s)x+s(1−t)(1−x)=0, which says that x never happens without s, and that s never happens with t failing unless x happens. Solved for x, it gives x=s(1−t)s(1−t)−(1−s)=00st+s(1−t)+0(1−s)t+0(1−s)(1−t), and, working with this by the rule, we have, finally, Prob. x=p(1−q)+cpq.(4) Here c is the probability that if the event st happens, x will happen. Now if we form the developed expression of st by multiplying together the expressions for s and t, we find:

c= Prob. that if x; and y happen together, or x and z happen together and y fails, or y and z happen together and x fails, the event x will happen.

Clearly the limits of Prob. x are p(1−q) and p.

This solution is more definite than the first one, since it contains a term that does not carry an arbitrary constant.

Solution of the Third Case.

Here the data are:

Prob. {x+(1−x)yz}=p,
Prob. {y+(1−y)xz}=q,
Prob. {z+(1−z)xy}=r.

As before, let us write x‾ for 1−x, and so on, and assume x+x‾yz=s,y+y‾xz=t,z+z‾xy=u. Reducing these by (VIII. 8) to a single equation, we obtain (x+x‾yz)s‾+sx‾(yz‾+y‾z+y‾z‾)+(y+y‾xz)t‾+ty‾(zx‾+xz‾+x‾z‾)+(z+z‾xy)u‾+uz‾(xy‾+x‾y+x‾y‾)=0.(5)

Instead of eliminating y and z from this equation directly, let us follow (IX. Prop, III.) and assume that the result of the elimination is Ex+E′(1−x)=0, Then E will be found by setting x=1 in the given equation and eliminating y and z from the resulting equation. And E′ will be found by setting x=0 in the given equation and eliminating y and z from the result. First, then, setting x=1, we have s‾+(y+y‾z)t‾+ty‾z‾+(z+yz‾)u‾+uy‾z‾=0, Next, in the left-hand side of this equation we set in turn y=1,z=1,y=1,z=0, and so on, and multiply the results together. We get the expression (s‾+t‾+u‾)(s‾+t‾+u‾)(s‾+t‾+u‾)(s‾+t+u), which is equivalent, since a repeated factor may be written once, to (s‾+t‾+u‾)(s‾+t+u). This is the expression for E. We shall keep it in this form. It has already been shown by example (VIII. 3) that actually reducing such expressions by multiplication is convenient but not necessary.

Again, in (5), setting x=0, we have yzs‾+s(yz‾+y‾z+y‾z‾)+yt‾+ty‾+zu‾+uz‾=0; and from this, by the same process of elimination, we find for E′ the expression (s‾+t‾+u‾)(s+t‾+u)(s+t+u‾)(s+t+u). So the final result of eliminating y and z from (5) is (s‾+t‾+u‾)(s‾+t+u)x+(s‾+t‾+u‾)(s+t‾+u)(s+t+u‾)(s+t+u)(1−x)=0. From this, solving for x, we have x=(s‾+t‾+u‾)(s+t‾+u)(s+t+u‾)(s+t+u)(s‾+t‾+u‾)(s+t‾+u)(s+t+u‾)(s+t+u)−(s‾+t‾+u‾)(s‾+t+u); or, developing the right-hand side, x=00stu+10st‾u+10stu‾+st‾u‾+10s‾tu+0s‾t‾u+0s‾tu‾+0s‾t‾u‾.(6) So, passing from logic to algebra, stu+st‾u‾p=stu+s‾tu‾q=stu+s‾t‾ur=stu+st‾u‾+s‾t‾u+s‾tu‾+s‾t‾u‾.(7) and the probability sought is Prob. x=st‾u‾+cstustu+st‾u‾+s‾t‾u+s‾tu‾+s‾t‾u‾,(8)

To simplify this system of equations, change ss‾ into s,tt‾ into t, and so on; that is, divide every term through by the product of the three barred letters, and let the letters stand for the ratios. After the change, let λ stand for stu+s+t+u+1 . We then have Prob. x=s+cstuλ,(9) with the relations stu+sp=stu+tq=stu+ur=stu+s+t+u+1=λ.(10) From these equations we get stu+s=λp,(11)stu+s=λ−t−u−1,∴λp=λ−u−t−1.u+t=λ(1−p)−1.Similarly,u+s=λ(1−q)−1,ands+t=λ(1−r)−1. The second line comes from the last member of (10): take away t, u and 1 from lambda, and what is left is the top of the first fraction.

From these equations, which give the sums of s, t, u two at a time, we find each one separately: s=λ(1+p−q−r)−12,t=λ(1+q−r−p)−12,u=λ(1+r−p−q)−12.(12) Now, by (10), stu=λp−s. Substitute in this equation the values of s, t, and u just found, and we have {(1+p−q−r)λ−1}{(1+q−p−r)λ−1}{(1+r−p−q)λ−1}=4{(p+q+r−1)λ+1},(13) an equation that determines λ. It is a cubic, an equation of the third degree in lambda. The values of s, t, and u are then given by (12), and putting them into (9) completes the solution of the problem.

10. Here a difficulty arises, and bringing it clearly before the reader has been one purpose of this investigation. How are we to decide which root of the equation above should be taken as the value of λ? I referred to this difficulty at the opening of this chapter, and said that a fuller treatment of it was kept for the next one. The following results are taken from there.

If the data of the problem are to come from a possible experience, the quantities p, q, and r must satisfy the following conditions: 1+p−q−r>=0,1+q−p−r>=0,1+r−p−q>=0.(14) that is, none of these three quantities may be negative. Moreover, the value of λ used in the general solution must satisfy the following conditions: λ>=11+p−q−r,λ>=11+q−p−r,λ>=11+r−p−q.(15)

Now these two sets of conditions are enough to pin down the general solution. It can be shown that the central equation (13) gives only one value of λ that satisfies these conditions, and that value of λ is the one required.

Let 1+p−q−r be the smallest of the three coefficients of λ given above. Then 11+p−q−r will be the largest of those values, and we are to show that above it there is only one value of λ. Let us write (13) in the form {(1+p−q−r)λ−1}{(1+q−p−r)λ−1}{(1+r−p−q)λ−1}−4{(p+q+r−1)λ+1}=0;(16) and call its left-hand side V.

Put λ=11+p−q−r. The first bracket then vanishes, and V becomes −4(p+q+r−11+p−q−r+1)=−4(2p1+p−q−r), which is negative. Let λ=∞; then V is positive and infinite.

Again, d2Vdλ2=(1+p−q−r)(1+q−p−r){(1+r−p−q)λ−1}+ similar positive terms, and this expression, the second derivative of V, is positive between the limits λ=11+p−q−r and λ=∞.

Suppose, then, that we draw a curve, with λ measured along the horizontal axis and V as the height above it. Between the limits specified, that curve will pass from below the axis of λ to above it, and it will always bend upward, its hollow side facing up. So it can cross the axis of λ only once within those limits, and the equation (16) will therefore have only one root in that range.

So the solution is given by (9), with λ the root of (13) that satisfies the conditions (15), and with s,t, and u given by (12). The meaning of c can be found in the usual way.

It appears from all this that the problem is, in every case, more or less indeterminate.

Chapter 19: Of Statistical Conditions

1. By statistical conditions I mean the conditions that must connect the numerical data of a problem if those data are to be consistent with one another, and so be data that real statistical observations could actually have produced. Finding these conditions is an important problem. In this chapter I mean to solve it, at least as far as this work requires. I treat it partly as a subject of inquiry in its own right, and partly as a necessary supplement to the theory of probability, which we have already seen at work to some extent. The two subjects are connected in the following way.

Editor's note: Boole's statistical conditions are the inequalities that any set of observed frequencies must satisfy if the data are consistent. He later called them "conditions of possible experience". In 1989 the philosopher Itamar Pitowsky showed that the Bell inequalities of quantum physics are conditions of exactly this kind: measurements on certain pairs of particles break them, which is why those results cannot be explained by any account in which the particles simply carry their properties with them.

2. There are countless cases, and we met one in the last chapter (Ex. 7), where the solution of a question in probability comes down in the end to solving an algebraic equation of high degree. In such cases the right root has to be picked out by certain conditions. Some of these concern the numbers given in the data; others concern the proper limits of the quantity we are looking for. Sometimes plain reasoning, without any special method, will find such conditions. For instance, suppose there is a probability p that an event A occurs, and a probability q that the same event A and another event B both occur. Then plainly we must have p>=q. that is, p is greater than or equal to q, since the two events cannot happen together more often than the first of them happens at all. But to find such relations in general, we need a method of its own, and that is what we now set out to build.

When we get it from actual experience, the probability of an event is the result of a process of approximation. It is the limit of a ratio: the number of cases in which the event is seen to occur, divided by the whole number of equally possible cases that observation records. We come closer to this limit the more observations we make. Now let the symbol n, placed in front of the expression for any class, stand for the number of individuals in that class: "n of x" means "the number of things in the class x". So, with x standing for men and y for white beings, let us set nx=number of men.nxy=number of white men.nx(1−y)=number of men who are not white; and so on. In this notation n(1) will stand for the number of individuals in the whole universe of discourse, and n(x)n(1), the number of men divided by the number of all individuals, will stand for the probability that an individual picked out of that universe, the one counted by n(1), is a man. If observation has not told us the total values of n(x) and n(1), then the probability in question is the limit that n(x)n(1) approaches as the number of individual observations grows.

In the same way, suppose (as we generally shall in this chapter) that x stands for an observed event of a particular kind. Then n(x) will stand for the number of times that event occurred, n(1) for the number of observed events of all kinds (all equally probable), and n(x)n(1), or its limit, for the probability that the event x occurs.

So it is clear that any conclusions we can draw about the ratios of the quantities n(x), n(y), n(1), and so on, can be turned into conclusions about the probabilities of the events represented by x, y, and so on. For example, suppose we found a relation like this one: n(x)+n(y)<n(1), which says that the number of times the event x occurs and the number of times the event y occurs, added together, are less than the number of possible occurrences, n(1). From it we could deduce the relation n(x)n(1)+n(y)n(1)<1,orProb. x+Prob. y<1. that is, the two probabilities together come to less than 1.

In general, any statistical relation of this kind can be turned into a relation connecting the probabilities of the events concerned. We change n(1) into 1, and every other symbol n(x) into Prob. x.

3. Our plan, then, has two stages. First, we shall work out a method for finding the numerical relations of classes or events, and above all their major and minor limits (the largest and smallest values possible). Second, we shall apply the method to fixing the limits of the solutions of questions in probability.

It is clear that the symbol n is distributive in the way it works: it can be applied term by term. So we have n{xy+(1−x)(1−y)}=nxy+n(1−x)(1−y)nx(1−y)=nx−nxy, and so on. In words, the second line says that the number of men who are not white is the number of men minus the number of white men. The number of things in any class that can be split into separate groups or portions equals the sum of the numbers of things in those separate portions. It is clear, too, that any expression built from the logical symbols x, y, and so on may be developed or expanded in any way the laws of the symbols allow, and the symbol n then applied to each term of the result, without changing the value of the result, provided that any constant multiplier that turns up is placed outside the symbol n. The expression n(1), if it appears, will of course stand for the number of individuals in the universe. Thus, n(1−x)(1−y)=n(1−x−y+xy)=n(1)−n(x)−n(y)+n(xy).Again,n{xy+(1−x)(1−y)}=n(1−x−y+2xy)=n(1)−nx−ny+2nxy). The first line says that the number of things that are neither x nor y is the whole universe, minus the x's, minus the y's, plus the things that are both (which were subtracted twice). In the last line the term 2nxy means twice the number of individuals in the class xy.

4. We now turn to finding the numerical limits of classes whose logical expression is given. In this inquiry two principles are basic, and I shall cite them later as Principle I and Principle II.

First, if every member of a given class has a certain property x, then the total number of individuals in the class x is an upper limit of the number of individuals in the given class. The given class cannot have more members than x has.

Second, a minor limit of the number of individuals in any class y is found by subtracting a major numerical limit of the contrary class, 1−y, from the number of individuals in the universe. If we know that at most so many things are not y, then at least the rest are y.

To illustrate these principles, let us apply them to the following problem.

Problem.—Given, n(1), n(x), and n(y), required the superior and inferior limits of nxy.

That is: given the number of things in the universe, in x, and in y, find the upper and lower limits of the number of things that are both x and y. Our data are the number of individuals in the universe of discourse, the number in the class x, and the number in the class y. We are to find the limits of the number in the class made up of the individuals that belong at once to the class x and to the class y.

By Principle I, this number cannot be more than the number in the class x, and it cannot be more than the number in the class y. So its major limit will be the smaller of the two values n(x) and n(y).

By Principle II, a minor limit of the class xy will be given by the expression n(1)− major limit of {x(1−y)+y(1−x)+(1−x)(1−y)},(1) that is, the whole universe minus the largest possible number of things that are not both x and y. This is because x(1−y)+y(1−x)+(1−x)(1−y) is the complement of the class xy: what it lacks to make up the universe.

Now x(1−y)+(1−x)(1−y)=1−y: the things that are x but not y, together with the things that are neither, are just the things that are not y. So for (1) we have n(1)− major limit of {1−y+y(1−x)}=n(1)−n(1−y)− major limit of y(1−x).(2) The major limit of y(1−x) is the smaller of the two values n(y) and n(1−x). First, let n(y) be the smaller. Then (2) becomes n(1)−n(1−y)−n(y)=n(1)−n(1)+n(y)−n(y)=0.

Second, let n(1−x) be less than n(y). Then major limit of ny(1−x)=n(1−x); and so (2) becomes n(1)−n(1−y)−n(1−x)=n(1)−n(1)+n(y)−n(1)+n(x)=nx+ny−n(1). So the minor limit of nxy is either 0 or n(x)+n(y)−n(1), depending on whether n(y) is less or greater than n(1−x), or, to put the same condition another way, on whether n(x) is greater or less than n(1−y).

Now 0 is necessarily a minor limit of the number in any class, since no class has fewer than no members. So it is enough to keep the second of the two expressions above as the minor limit of n(xy). We have, therefore, Major limit of n(xy)= least of values n(x) and n(y).Minor limit of n(xy)=n(x)+n(y)−n(1). In words: the number of things that are both x and y is at most the smaller of the two numbers, and at least the number of x's plus the number of y's minus the whole universe.21

Proposition I.

5. To express the major and minor limits of a class represented by any constituent of the symbols x, y, z, &c., having given the values of n(x), n(y), n(z), &c., and n(1).

Take first the constituent xyz, the things that are x, y and z all at once.

Clearly the major numerical limit will be the smallest of the values n(x), n(y), n(z).

The minor numerical limit could be worked out as in the problem above. But it can also be drawn from the solution of that problem, like this: Minor limit of n(xyz)=n(xy)+n(z)−n(1).(1) This means that n(xyz) is at least as great as the expression n(xy)+n(z)−n(1). But n(xy) is at least as great as n(x)+n(y)−n(1). So n(xyz) is at least as great as n(x)+n(y)−n(1)+n(z)−n(1),or n(x)+n(y)+n(z)−2n(1). Hence we have Minor limit of n(xyz)=n(x)+n(y)+n(z)−2n(1). that is, the three numbers added together, minus twice the universe.

Carrying this line of reasoning further, we reach the following conclusions.

First, the major numerical limit of the class represented by any constituent is found by putting n in front of each factor of the constituent separately, and taking the smallest of the resulting values.

Second, the minor limit is found by adding all those values together, and subtracting from the result the value of n(1) as many times as there are factors, less one.

So we should have Major limit of nxy(1−z)= least of the values nx, ny, and n(1−z).Minor limit of nxy(1−z)=n(x)+n(y)+n(1−z)−2n(1)=nx+n(y)−n(z)−n(1).

When we work with general symbols, it is perhaps better to regard all the values n(x), n(y), n(1−z) as major limits of n{xy(1−z)}, since in fact it cannot exceed any of them. In what follows I shall speak in this way.

Proposition II.

6. To determine the major numerical limit of a class expressed by a series of constituents of the symbols x, y, z, &c., the values of n(x), n(y), n(z), &c., and n(1), being given.

Clearly one way of finding such a limit would be to form the smallest possible sum of the major limits of the separate constituents. So a major limit of the expression n{xy+(1−x)(1−y)} (the number of things that are either both x and y, or neither) would be found by adding the smaller of the two values nx, ny, supplied by the first constituent, to the smaller of the two values n(1−x), n(1−y), supplied by the second. If we do not know which value is the smaller in each case, we must form all four possible sums, and throw out any that are equal to n(1) or exceed it. In the example above we should have nx()+n(1−x)=n(1).n(x)+n(1−y)=n(1)+n(x)−n(y).n(y)+n(1−x)=n(1)+n(y)−n(x).n(y)+n(1−y)=n(1). Throwing out the first and last of these values, we have n(1)+n(x)−n(y), and n(1)+n(y)−n(x), as the expressions required. Unless nx=ny, one of them will be less than n(1) and the other greater. Of course the smaller must be taken.

When two or more of the constituents share a common factor, such as x, that factor can supply only a single term n(x) to the final expression of the major limit, as Principle I makes obvious: the x's are counted once, however many constituents they appear in. So if n(x) appears as a major limit in two or more constituents, then when we add those limits together we must replace nx+nx by nx, and so on. Take for example the expression n{xy+x(1−y)z}. The major limits of this expression that come straight from addition would be—

1. nx.4. ny+nx.
2. nx+n(1−y).5. ny+n(1−y).
3. nx+n(z).6. ny+nz.

Of these we need keep only the first and the sixth. The second, third, and fourth are greater than the first, and the fifth equals n(1). So the limits are n(x) and n(y)+n(z), and of these two values the second must be taken, supposing it to be less than n(1).

These considerations lead us to the following Rule.

Rule.—Take one factor from each constituent, and put the symbol n in front of it. Add together the terms formed in this way, throwing out every repetition of the same term. The sum obtained is a major limit of the expression, and the smallest of all such sums is the major limit to be used.

So the major limits of the expression xyz+x(1−y)(1−z)+(1−x)(1−y)(1−z) would be n(x)+n(1−y), and n(x)+n(1−z),orn(x)+n(1)−n(y), and n(x)+n(1)−n(z).

Suppose instead we began with n(y), picked from the first term, and took n(x) from the second. Then we should have to take n(1−y) from the third term, and this would give n(y)+n(x)+n(1−y), or n(1)+n(x). But this result exceeds n(1), which is an obvious major limit of every class, so we need not take it into account.

Proposition III.

7. To find the minor numerical limit of any class expressed by constituents of the symbols x,y,z, having given n(x),n(y),n(z)…n(1).

We could do this by applying the preceding Proposition together with Principle II. But the following method does it better.

Take any two constituents that differ from each other in a single factor only, and add them, so that they form a single class term; for example, x(1−y)+xy form x. Carry this kind of combining as far as it will go. That is, pick out of the given series of constituents as many sums of this kind as can be formed, each sum taking in as many constituents as can be gathered into a single term, without caring whether some of those constituents also go into other terms. Then write down these final combined terms, together with any constituents that cannot be combined in this way, as separate terms. The minor limits of those terms, found by Prop. I, will be the minor limits of the given expression, and at most one of those minor limits will be positive at any one time.

For example, from the expression xy+(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y) we can form the combined terms y and 1−x, by adding the first and second terms, and the second and third. So n(y) and n(1−x) will be the minor limits of the given expression. Again, suppose the given expression were xyz+x(1−y)z+(1−x)yz+(1−x)(1−y)z+xy(1−z)+(1−x)(1−y)(1−z), Adding the first four terms we get the single term z; adding the first and fifth we get the single term xy; and adding the fourth and sixth we get the single term (1−x)(1−y). There is no other way of gathering the constituents into single terms, and no constituent is left over that has not been accounted for. The three resulting terms give, as the minor limits of the given expression, the values n(z),n(x)+n(y)−n(1),andn(1−x)+n(1−y)−n(1), or n(1)−n(x)−n(y).

8. The proof of this rule rests on applying the following principles correctly. First, the minor limit of any collection of constituents that can be added together into a single term is plainly the minor limit of that single term. This explains the first part of the rule. Second, take two terms that are separate constituents, or are made up of separate constituents, but cannot be added together into one term. The minor limit of their sum will be the sum of their two minor limits if both are positive. But if one is positive and the other negative, it will equal the positive minor limit alone. For if we added the negative one, the limit would go down: it would be smaller for the sum of two terms than for one term on its own. Now whenever two constituents differ in more than one factor, so that they cannot be added together, their minor limits cannot both be positive. Take the terms xyz and (1−x)(1−y)z, which differ in two factors. The minor limit of the first is n(x+y+z−2), that of the second n(1−x+1−y+z−2), or, 1st. n{x+y−1−(1−z)}.2nd. n{1−x−y−(1−z)}. If n(x+y−1) is positive, then n(1−x−y) is negative, and the second limit must be negative. If n(x+y−1) is negative, the first limit is negative. The same holds for cases with a larger number of factors. In this way it can be shown that, given the way the combined terms are formed under the rule, no two minor limits of separate terms can ever be added together. Either the two terms share some constituent, and then we clearly cannot add their minor limits; or their minor limits are not both positive, and then adding them would be useless.

Proposition IV.

9. Given the respective numbers of individuals comprised in any classes, s, t, &c. logically defined, to deduce a system, of numerical limits of any other class w, also logically defined.

This is the most general problem the chapter means to discuss. The earlier inquiries only lead up to it, and the later ones apply it. So it is worth stating clearly what it is and what it is for.

When we say the classes s, t…w are logically defined, we mean that they are defined well enough for us to write down their symbolic expressions, whether the classes are simple or compound. By the general method of this book, the symbol w can then be found directly as a developed function of the symbols s, t, and so on, in the form w=A+0B+00C+10D,(1) where A, B, C, and D are made up of constituents of s, t, and so on. Read aloud, as in Chapter 6: the compartments gathered in A belong wholly to w; those in B not at all; of those in C some, none, or all may belong to w; and those in D must be empty. How the numerical limits of w can be found from such an expression in the most general way, we shall consider later. For now I only mean to show how far this can be done on the principles set out in the previous propositions, and that is enough for the purposes of this work. To keep things simple, I shall base my argument on the particular development w=st+0s(1−t)+10(1−s)t+00(1−s)(1−t),(2) in which every kind of coefficient appears.

Of the constituent (1−s)(1−t), whose coefficient is 00, the equation tells us that some, none, or all of the class it denotes are found in w. Clearly n(w) will be largest when all the members of the class denoted by (1−s)(1−t) are found in w. And since none of the individuals in the classes denoted by s(1−t) and (1−s)t are found in w, the upper numerical limits of w will be the same as those of the class st+(1−s)(1−t). They are therefore ns+n(1−t) and nt+n(1−s). In the same way, a system of upper numerical limits of the development A+0B+00C+10D can be found from those of A+C by Prop. 2.

Again, by Principle II, any minor numerical limit of w is given by the expression n(1)− major limit of n(1−w), that is, the universe minus the largest possible number of things that are not w. But since the development of w is given by (1), that of 1−w will plainly be 1−w=0A+B+00C+10D. This can be proved directly by the method of Prop. 2, Chap. X. Hence Minor limit of n(w)=n(1)− major limit (B+C)= minor limit of (A+D), by Principle II, since the classes A+D and B+C are supplementary: together they make up the universe. So the minor limit of the right-hand side of (2) would be n(t). Generalizing this line of reasoning, we have the following result:

A system of minor limits of the development A+0B+00C+10D will be given by the minor limits of A+D.

This result can also be seen directly. Of minor numerical limits, the one we want is always the greatest. Now in general we get a higher minor limit by joining the class D to A in the expression of w than we should get otherwise; and various examples in the Logic have shown that this combination is one we are allowed to make.

Finally, the last term of the development of w stands for the equation D=0, the class D must be empty. So clearly n(D)=0. Hence we have Minor limit of n(D)<=0, that is, the lower limit of the number in D must be zero or less. This condition, treated by Prop. 3, gives the conditions the numerical elements n(s), n(t), and so on must satisfy if the problem is to be real, and its data are to contain the results of a possible experience.

So from the term 10(1−s)t on the right-hand side of (2) we should deduce n(1−s)+n(t)−n(1)<=0,∴n(t)<=n(s). that is, the number of t's cannot be greater than the number of s's; which is what the term says, since it forbids anything to be t without being s. These conclusions can be gathered into the following rule.

10. Rule.—Find the expression of the class w as a developed logical function of the symbols s, t, and so on, in the form w=A+0B+00C+10D. Then Maj. lim. w= Maj. lim. A+C.Min. lim. w= Min. lim. A+D. And the necessary numerical conditions among the data are given by the inequality Min. lim. D<=0.

To apply this method to fixing the limits of the solutions of questions in probability, we need only replace, in each of the formulas, n(x) by Prob. x, n(y) by Prob. y, and so on, and finally n(1) by 1. But the application is very important, so it may be worth setting out the chief results of this change in the form of a rule.

11. Given the probabilities of any events s, t, &c., whereof another event w is a developed logical function, in the form w=A+0B+00C+10D, required the systems of superior and inferior limits of Prob. w, and the conditions among the data.

Solution.—The upper limits of Prob. (A+C), and the lower limits of Prob. (A+D), will form two systems of the kind we want. The conditions among the constants in the data will be given by the inequality Inf. lim. Prob. D<=0. that is, the lower limit of the probability of D must be zero or less. In applying these principles we always have Inf. lim. Prob. x1x2…xn= Prob. x1+ Prob. x2…+ Prob. xn−(n−1). that is, the lower limit of the probability that all of a set of events occur together is the sum of their separate probabilities, minus one less than the number of events. Moreover, lower limits can be found only from single terms, either given as such or formed by combining. Upper limits are included in the form ∑ Prob. x, a sum of probabilities, where Prob. x applies only to symbols that are different from one another and taken from different terms of the expression whose upper limit we want. So the upper limits of Prob. xyz+x(1−y)(1−z) are Prob. x,Prob. y+ Prob. (1−z), and Prob. z+ Prob. (1−y). Notice that if in the last case we had taken Prob. z from the first term and Prob. (1−z) from the second (a choice the rule does not forbid), their sum would have been 1. That result would be useless, because it is known à priori: no probability exceeds 1. Clearly we may throw out any limits that do not fall between 0 and 1.

Let us apply this method to Ex. 7, Case III. of the last chapter.

The final logical solution is x=00stu+10st‾u+10stu‾+st‾u‾+10s‾tu+0s‾t‾u+0s‾tu‾+0s‾t‾u‾, where a bar over a letter means "not": t with a bar is "not t". The data are Prob. s=p,Prob. t=q,Prob. u=r.

We shall look for both the numerical limits of x and the conditions connecting p, q, and r. By the rule, the upper limits of x are given by those of stu+st‾u‾, the terms with coefficient 1 or 0/0. They are therefore p,q+1−r,r+1−q. The lower limits of x are given by those of st‾u+stu‾+st‾u‾+s‾tu. the terms with coefficient 1 or 1/0.

We can gather the first and third of these constituents into the single term st‾, and the second and third into the single term su‾. So the lower limits of x must be found separately from the terms s(1−t), s(1−u), (1−s)tu, which give p+1−q−1,p+1−r−1,1−p+q+r−2,or p−q,p−r,and q+r−p−1.

Finally, the conditions among the constants p, q, and r are given by the terms with coefficient 1/0, st‾u,stu‾,s‾tu, from which the rule gives p+1−q+r−2<=0,p+q+1−r−2<=0,1−p+q+r−2<=0.or 1+q−p−r>=0,1+r−p−q>=0,1+p−q−r>=0. These are the limiting conditions used in analysing the final solution in that example. The conditions that limited λ in that solution, however, were found simply from the requirement that the quantities s, t, and u be positive. In all probability, narrower limits for that quantity could have been drawn from the investigation above.

12. The following application comes from an important problem whose solution will be given in the next chapter. We are given Prob. x=c1,Prob. y=c2,Prob. s=c1p1,Prob. t=c2p2, together with the logical equation z=stxy+st‾xy‾+s‾tx‾y+0s‾t‾+10{stxy‾+stx‾y+stx‾y‾+st‾xy+st‾x‾y+st‾x‾y‾+s‾txy+s‾txy‾+s‾tx‾y‾; which we read as before: the constituents with coefficient 1 make up the class z, the one with coefficient 0 lies outside it, and those with coefficient one over zero are combinations that cannot occur at all. We are asked to find the conditions that must hold among the constants c1, c2, p1, p2, and the major and minor limits of z.

First let us look for the conditions among the constants. Attending only to the terms whose coefficients are 10, and grouping their constituents together, we easily form the following terms: s(1−x),t(1−y),sy(1−t),tx(1−s); and no other term can be formed that is not included under these. So the conditions among the constants, one for each of these terms, are n(s)+n(1−x)−n(1)<=0,n(t)+n(1−y)−n(1)<=0,n(s)+n(y)+n(1−t)−2n(1)<=0,n(t)+n(x)+n(1−s)−2n(1)<=0. The first, for example, says that the number of things in the class s, added to the number of things that are not x, is at most the number of things in the whole universe.

Now replace n(x) by c1, n(y) by c2, n(s) by c1p1, n(t) by c2p2, and n(1) by 1. After slight reductions we have c1p1<=c1,c2p2<=c2,c1p1<=1−c2(1−p2),c2p2<=1−c1(1−p1). These, then, are the conditions required among the constants. The first two say that the probability of s cannot exceed the probability of x, nor the probability of t the probability of y.

Again, the major limits of z are the same as those of the expression stxy+s(1−t)x(1−y)+(1−s)t(1−x)y; and if we bear in mind the conditions n(s)<=n(x),n(t)<=n(y), found above, these limits will be found to be n(s)+n(t), or, c1p1+c2p2,n(s)+n(1−x), or, 1−c1(1−p1).n(t)+n(1−y), or, 1−c2(1−p2).

Lastly, to find the minor limits of z: from the constituents whose coefficients are 1 or 10 we easily form the single terms s and t, and no other terms not included under these can be formed, whether by selecting constituents or by grouping them. So for the minor limits of z we have the values c1p1 and c2p2.

13. Note that the method developed above does not always give the narrowest limits that it is possible to find. But in every case, I believe, it limits the solutions of questions in the theory of probability well enough.

The problem of finding the narrowest limits of the number of things in a class can, however, always be reduced to a purely algebraic form. Take up again the equation w=A+0B+00C+10D, and let the highest lower limit of the number of things in w be represented by the formula an(s)+bn(t)…+dn(1), where a,b,c,…d are numerical constants still to be found, and s, t, and so on, are the logical symbols of which A, B, C, D are constituents. Then an(s)+bn(t)…+dn(1)= minor limit of A subject to the condition D=0. So suppose we develop the function as+bt…+d, and reject from the result all the constituents that are found in D. Then the coefficients of the remaining constituents that are also found in A must not, any of them, exceed 1 in value, and the coefficients of the remaining constituents that are not found in A must not, any of them, exceed 0. So we shall have one series of inequalities of the form f<=1, and another of the form g<=0, where f and g are linear functions of a, b, c, and so on (sums of these unknowns, each multiplied by a fixed number). We must then find those values of a,b…d which satisfy all these conditions and at the same time give the function an(s)+bn(t)…+dn(1), its highest value; and that highest value will be the highest minor limit of w. To this we may add the relations, formed in the same way, that determine the relations among the given constants n(s),n(t)…n(1).22

14. The following rather complicated example shows how a solution is limited when the problem contains an arbitrary element. Such an element makes the problem stand for a whole system of problems, which share the same data but are unlimited in what they seek.

Problem.—Of n events x1x2…xn, we know the following:

First, the probability that either the event x1 will occur, or all the events will fail, is p1.

Second, the probability that either the event x2 will occur, or all the events will fail, is p2. And so on for the others.

We are asked to find the probability of any single event, or combination of events, represented by the general function ϕ(x1…xn), or ϕ for short.

In a notation used before, the data of the problem are Prob. (x1+x‾1…x‾n)=p1…Prob. (xn+x‾1…x‾n)=pn. And the probability of ϕ(x1…xn) is what we seek.

Put, in general, xr+x‾1…x‾n=sr,(1)ϕ=w.(2) From these we obtain the combined logical equation of the problem: ∑{(xr+x‾1…x‾n)s‾r+sr(x‾r−x‾1…x‾n)}+ϕw‾+wϕ‾=0.(3) It is a sum of terms each of which must vanish, and it says two things at once: each s stands for exactly its own event, "this x occurs, or all the events fail", and w stands for exactly the event whose probability is sought. From this equation we must eliminate the symbols x1,…xn, and find w as a developed logical function of s1…sn.

Let us write the result of this elimination in the form Ew+E′(1−w)=0; then E will be the result of eliminating the same symbols from the equation ∑{(xr+x‾1…x‾n)s‾r+sr(x‾r−x‾1…x‾n)}+1−ϕ=0.(4) which is what equation (3) becomes when w is 1.

Now E will be the product of the coefficients of all the constituents (taken with respect to the symbols x1,x2…xn) that appear in the development of the left-hand side of this equation. Moreover, ϕ, and so also 1−ϕ, will consist of a series of such constituents, each with 1 for its coefficient. To work out the forms of the coefficients in the development of the left-hand side of (4), it is convenient to arrange them in three groups, as follows.

First, the coefficients of the constituents found in 1−ϕ.

Second, the coefficient of x‾1,x‾2…x‾n, if it is found in ϕ.

Third, the coefficients of the constituents found in ϕ, leaving out the constituent x‾1,x‾2…x‾n.

Plainly these three groups between them take in every coefficient there is.

First, then: the coefficient of any constituent found in 1−ϕ will, in the development of the left-hand side of (4), be of the form 1+ positive terms derived from ∑. So every such coefficient may be replaced by unity, by Prop. I. Chap. IX.

Second: the coefficient of x‾1…x‾n, if it is found in ϕ, will in the development of the left-hand side of (4) be ∑s‾r, or s‾1+s‾2…+s‾n

Third: the coefficient of any other constituent, x1…xi,x‾i+1…x‾n, found in ϕ, will in the development of the left-hand side of (4) be s‾1…+s‾i+si+1…+sn.

Now we see that E is the product of all the coefficients just found. But since the coefficients of the constituents not found in ϕ reduce to 1, E may be taken as the product of the coefficients of just those constituents that are found in ϕ. From the way those coefficients are formed, we get the following rule for finding E. In each constituent found in ϕ, except the constituent x‾1x‾2…x‾n, for x1 write s‾1, for x‾1 write s1, and so on, and add the results; but for the constituent x‾1,x‾2…x‾n, if it occurs in ϕ, write s‾1+s‾2…+s‾n. The product of all these sums is E.

To find E′ we must set w=0 in (3), and eliminate x1,x2…xn from the reduced equation. That equation will be ∑{(xr+x‾1…+x‾n)s‾r+sr(x‾r−x‾1…x‾n)}+ϕ=0.(5) So E′ will be formed from the constituents in 1−ϕ, that is, from the constituents not found in ϕ, in the same way as E is formed from the constituents found in ϕ.

Consider next the equation Ew+E′(1−w)=0. This gives w=E′E′−E.(6)

Now E and E′ are functions of the symbols s1,s2…sn. So the expansion of the value of w will consist of all the constituents that can be formed from those symbols, each with its proper coefficient attached, as fixed by the rule of development.

Moreover, E and E′ are each formed by multiplying factors together, and neither of them can vanish unless one of its own factors vanishes. Again, any factor, such as s‾1…+s‾n, can vanish only when all the terms added together to form it vanish at once, since in development we give these terms only the values 0 and 1. It is also plain that no two different factors can vanish together. For instance, the factors s‾1+s‾2…+s‾n, and s1+s‾2…+s‾n, cannot vanish at the same time: the former cannot vanish unless s‾1=0, or s1=1; but the latter cannot vanish unless s1=0.

First, let us find the coefficient of the constituent s‾1s‾2…s‾n in the development of the value of w.

Assuming all at once that s‾1=1, s‾2=1…s‾n=1, would make the factor s1+s2…+sn vanish, if that factor occurred in E or E′; and under the same assumption no other factor would vanish. But s1+s2…+sn is not a factor of either E or E′. So neither of these quantities can vanish, and therefore the expression E′E′−E is neither 1, 0, nor 00.

So the coefficient of s‾1s‾2…s‾n in the expanded value of w may be represented by 10.

Second, let us find the coefficient of the constituent s1s2…sn. The assumptions s1=1,s2=1,…sn=1 would make the factor s‾1+s‾2…+s‾n vanish. Now this factor is found in E and not in E′ whenever ϕ contains both the constituents x1x2…xn and x‾1x‾2…x‾n. In that case E′E′−E becomes E′E′, or 1. The factor s‾1+s‾2…+s‾n is found in E′ and not in E if ϕ contains neither of the constituents x1x2…xn and x‾1x‾2…x‾n. In that case E′E′−E becomes 0−E, or 0. Last, the factor s‾1+s‾2…+s‾n is contained in both E and E′ if one of the constituents x1x2…xn and x‾1x‾2…x‾n is found in ϕ, and the other is not. In that case E′E′−E becomes 00.

So the coefficient of the constituent s1s2…sn will be 1, 0, or 00, according as ϕ contains both the constituents x1x2…xn and x‾1x‾2…x‾n, or neither of them, or one of them and not the other.

Last, we must find the coefficient of any other constituent, such as s1…si s‾i+1…s‾n.

The assumptions s1=1,…si=1,si+1=0,sn=0 would make the factor s‾1…+s‾i+si+1…+sn vanish. Now this factor is found in E if the constituent x1…xix‾i+1…x‾n is found in ϕ, and in E′ if that constituent is not found in ϕ. In the first case we have E′E′−E=E′E′=1; in the second we have E′E′−E=00−E=0.

So the coefficient of any other constituent s1…si,s‾i+1…s‾n is 1 or 0, according as the matching constituent x1…xix‾i+1…x‾n is or is not found in ϕ.

In practice, then, we may find the value of w as follows. From the given expression of ϕ, reject the constituents x1x2…xn and x‾1x‾2…x‾n, if both or either of them occur in it. In the result, change the symbols x1,x2,…xn into s1,s2,…sn respectively. Give the constituents s1s2…sn and s‾1s‾2…s‾n the coefficients fixed by the special rules for those cases given above, and give every other constituent the coefficient 0. The result will be the value of w as a function of s1,s2,…sn.

As a particular case, let ϕ=x1. We are to find, from the given data, the probability of the event x1.

The symbol x1, expanded in terms of the whole series of symbols x1,x2,…xn, will generate all the constituents of those symbols that have x1 as a factor. Among those constituents will be the constituent x1x2…xn, but not the constituent x‾1x‾2…x‾n.

So in the expanded value of x1 as a function of the symbols s1,s2,…sn, the constituent s1s2…sn will have the coefficient 00, and the constituent s‾1s‾2…s‾n the coefficient 10.

If from x1 we reject the constituent x1x2…xn, the result will be x1−x1x2…xn. Changing x1 into s1 in it, and so on for the rest, we have s1−s1s2…sn as the corresponding portion of the expression of x1 as a function of s1,s2,…sn.

So the final expression for x1 is x1=s1−s1s2…sn+00s1s2…sn+10s‾1s‾2…s‾n+ constituents whose coefficients are 0.(7)

The sum of all the constituents in this expansion whose coefficients are 1, 0, or 00 will be 1−s‾1s‾2…s‾n, that is, everything except the one constituent that cannot occur.

So we have the following algebraic system for finding the probability of x1: Prob. x1=s1−s1s2…sn+cs1s2…sn1−s‾1s‾2…s‾n,(8) where c takes the place of the indefinite coefficient zero over zero, with the relations s1p1=s2p2…=snpn=1−s‾1s‾2…s‾n=λ.(9)

Notice that the relations for finding s1s2…sn are quite independent of the form of the function ϕ. The values of these quantities, once found, will serve for every possible problem with the same data, however much the things those problems seek may vary. The nature of the event, or combination of events, whose probability is sought affects only the form of the function into which the values found for s1s2…sn are to be substituted. From (9) we have s1=p1λ,s2=p2λ,…sn=pnλ. So 1−(1−p1λ)(1−p2λ)…(1−pnλ)=λ. Or, 1−λ=(1−p1λ)(1−p2λ)…(1−pnλ);(10) and from this equation the value of λ is to be found.

Supposing this value found, the probability of x1 will be p1λ−(1−c)p1p2…pnλn1−(1−p1λ)(1−p2λ)…(1−pnλ), or, reducing by means of (10), Prob. x1=p1−(1−c)p1p2…pnλn−1.(11)

Let us next look for the conditions that must hold among the constants p1,p2,…pn, and for the limits of the probability of x1.

Since only one term has the coefficient 10, there is only one condition among the constants, namely Minor limit, (1−s1)(1−s2)…(1−sn)<=0.Or,n(1−s1)+n(1−s2)…+n(1−sn)−(n−1)n(1)<=0.Or,n(1)−n(s1)−n(s2)…−n(sn)<=0.Whencep1+p2…+pn>=1, which is the condition required. In words: the given probabilities, added together, must come to at least 1.

The major limit of the probability of x1 is the major limit of the sum of those constituents whose coefficients are 1 or 00. But that sum is s1.

So Major limit, Prob. x1= major limit s1=p1. The minor limit of the probability of x1 will be the same as the minor limit of the expression s1−s1s2…sn+(1−s1)(1−s2)…(1−sn).

A little attention will show that the different aggregate terms that can be formed from this, each taking in the greatest possible number of constituents, are the following: s1(1−s2),s1(1−s3),…s1(1−sn),(1−s2)(1−s3)…(1−sn).

From these we deduce the following expressions for the minor limit: p1−p2,p1−p3…p1−pn,1−p2−p3…−pn.

So the probability of x1 will not fall short of any of these values, nor exceed the value of p1.

Instead of using these conditions, however, we may make direct use of the principle stated in the proof of the general method in probabilities. The condition that s1,s2,…sn must each be less than 1 requires that λ be less than each of the quantities 1p1,1p2,…1pn. And the condition that s1,s2,…sn must each be greater than 0 requires that λ also be greater than 0. Now p1p2…pn are proper fractions (numbers between 0 and 1) satisfying the condition p1+p2…+pn>1, and it can be shown that the central equation (10) yields only one positive value of λ that is less than each of the quantities 1p1,1p2,…1pn. That value of λ, then, is the one required.

To prove this, let us consider the equation (1−p1λ)(1−p2λ)…(1−pnλ)−1+λ=0.

When λ=0 the left-hand side vanishes, and the equation is satisfied. Let us examine how the left-hand side varies between the limits λ=0 and λ=1p1, supposing p1 to be the greatest of the values p1p2…pn. Calling the left-hand side V, we have, for the rate at which V changes as lambda grows, dVdλ=−p1(1−p2λ)…(1−pnλ)…−pn(1−p1λ)…(1−pn−1λ)+1, which, when λ=0, takes the form −p1−p2…−pn+1, and is negative in value.

Again, we have d2Vdλ2=p1p2(1−p3λ)(1−pnλ)+ &c., a series of terms which, under the restrictions already placed on the value of λ, are all positive.

Last, when λ=1p1, we have V=−1+1p1, which is positive.

From all this it follows that if we draw a curve whose ordinates (heights) show the value of V for each abscissa (distance along the horizontal axis) λ, the curve will pass through the origin, and for small values of λ will lie below the axis. Between the limits λ=0 and λ=1p1 its convexity will be downward, so that it bends upward all the way; and at the far limit 1p1 the curve will be above the axis, its ordinate being positive. It follows from this description that the curve will cross the axis once, and only once, within the limits specified, namely between the values λ=0 and λ=1p1.

So the solution of the problem is given by (11), where the value of λ is the root of equation (10) that lies between 0 and each of 1p1,1p2,…1pn.

The constant c is plainly the probability that, if the events x1,x2,…xn all happen or all fail, they will all happen.

This determination of the value of λ serves for every problem whose data are the same as in the one just considered. As earlier discussions have prepared us to expect, it does not depend on the form of the function ϕ. As another example, let us suppose ϕ= or w=x1(1−x2)…(1−xn)…+xn(1−x1)…(1−xn−1). This amounts to asking for the probability that, of the events x1,x2,…xn, one, and only one, will happen. The value of w will plainly be w=s1(1−s2)…(1−sn)…+sn(1−s1)…(1−sn−1)+10(1−s1)…(1−sn), from which we should have Prob. {x1(1−x2)…(1−xn)…+xn(1−x1)…(1−xn−1)}=s1(1−s2)…(1−sn)…+sn(1−s1)…(1−sn−1)1−(1−s1)…(1−sn)=p1λ(1−p2λ)…(1−pnλ)…+pnλ(1−p1λ)…(1−pn−1λ)λ=p1(1−λ)1−p1λ+p2(1−λ)1−p2λ…+pn(1−λ)1−pnλ This solution illustrates well the remarks made in the introductory chapter (I. 16). The real difficulties of the problem lie in the nature of its data, not in the nature of what it asks. The central equation that determines λ, and the particular discussions that go with it, apply equally to every form the problem can be made to take by varying the interpretation of the arbitrary elements in its original statement.

  1. The above expression for the minor limit of nxy is applied by Professor De Morgan, who seems to have been the first to give it, to the syllogistic form:

    	Most men in a certain company have coats.
	Most men in the same company have waistcoats.
	Therefore some in the company have coats and waistcoats.

    ↩
