  2. I regret the loss of a manuscript, written about four years ago, in which, I believe, this method was worked out at considerable length. What I remember of its contents comes down almost entirely to the impression that the principle of the method was the same as the one described above, and that its sufficiency was proved. The earlier methods of this chapter are, it hardly needs saying, easier, though certainly less general. ↩

Chapter 20: Problems Relating to the Connexion of Causes and Effects

1. The final object of science is to grasp, in every particular case, the relation of cause and effect: to connect the two ends of it in thought in the same order in which they are connected in nature. (How the cause actually does its work, the modus operandi, is unknown to us, and must always remain so.) This treatise has shown that the faculties of the intellect are built with a special reference to that object. There is one sphere of thought that grasps things only as parts of a universe, existing side by side. But there is also a sphere of thought (Chap. XI.) in which things are grasped as links in an unbroken chain, and, as far as we can see, an endless one. Each has its place in an order that connects it both with what went before and with what will follow after. When we contemplate a series like that, we cannot help feeling that the relation of cause and effect deserves first place among all relations.

Here I propose to consider, in their abstract form, some problems that involve this relation. As the nature of the relation would lead us to expect, they are of many different kinds. Suppose we know the probabilities of certain causes, assigned à priori or given by experience, and the probability that each of them goes along with a certain effect. We may be asked to find the probability of that effect: first, absolutely, or second, under given conditions. Some of the earlier problems below are of this kind. On the other hand, we may be asked to find the probability of a particular cause, or of some particular connection among a system of causes, from the effects we have observed and from what we know of how the causes tend, alone or together, to produce such effects. That class of questions will come in a later part of the chapter, and other forms of the general inquiry will be noticed too. I should say one thing. These examples are meant chiefly to illustrate a method, but I have paid no attention to making the method easy or convenient to apply. On the contrary, I have tried, with whatever success, to design them as types of the problems we might expect to meet when we study the relation of cause and effect in its more complex real and visible forms.

2. Problem I.—The probabilities of two causes A1 and A2 are c1 and c2 respectively. The probability that if the cause A1 is present, an event E will go along with it (whether as a result of the cause A1 or not) is p1. The probability that if the cause A2 is present, that event E will go along with it, whether as its result or not, is p2. Moreover, the event E cannot appear when both the causes A1 and A2 are absent. Required, the probability of the event E.23

If the causes A1, A2 exclude one another, the problem becomes a familiar one, and its solution is well known to be Prob. E=c1p1+c2p2; that is, the chance of the first cause times the chance it brings the effect, plus the same for the second. This is a particular case of a basic and very important principle in the received theory of probability. Here I propose to solve the problem without that restriction.

Let us represent The cause A1 by x.The cause A2 by y.The effect E by z. Then we have the following numerical data: Prob. x=c1,Prob. y=c2,Prob. xz=c1p1,Prob. yz=c2p2.(1) (The probability that x and z happen together is the chance of x times the chance that z goes with it, and the same for y.) Next, the problem lays down that if the causes A1, A2 are both absent, the effect E does not occur. That gives us the logical equation (1−x)(1−y)=v(1−z). which says that the cases with neither cause are some of the cases without the effect. Or, eliminating v, z(1−x)(1−y)=0.(2) that is, there is no case of the effect with neither cause present.

Now assume, xz=s,yz=t.(3) so that s stands for the compound event "cause one and the effect together", and t for "cause two and the effect together".

Then, reducing these equations (VIII. 7) and joining the result to (2), we get a single equation that holds everything the problem tells us about the connections: xz(1−s)+s(1−xz)+yz(1−t)+t(1−yz)+z(1−x)(1−y)=0.(4)

From this equation we must find z as a developed logical function of x, y, s, and t, and then deduce its probability from the data, Prob. x=c1,Prob. y=c2,Prob. s=c1p1,Prob. t=c2p2.(5) The point of bringing in s and t is that every datum is now the probability of a single symbol.

Now develop (4) with respect to z, putting x‾ for 1−x, y‾ for 1−y, and so on (a bar over a letter means "not"). We have (xs‾+sx‾+yt‾+ty‾+x‾y‾)z+(s+t)z‾=0,∴z=s+ts+t−xs‾−sx‾−yt‾−ty‾−x‾y‾=stxy+10stxy‾+10stx‾y+10stx‾y‾+10st‾xy+st‾xy‾+10st‾x‾y+10st‾x‾y‾+10s‾txy+10s‾txy‾+s‾tx‾y+10s‾tx‾y‾+0s‾t‾xy+0s‾t‾xy‾+0s‾t‾x‾y+0s‾t‾x‾y‾.(6) Read aloud, this sorts all sixteen compartments of s, t, x, y. Three of them (coefficient 1) are cases where the effect certainly happens. Four (coefficient 0) are cases where it certainly does not. The remaining nine (coefficient 1/0) are combinations the conditions of the problem make impossible.

From this result we find (XVII. 17) the condition V, the sum of all the compartments that are possible at all: V=stxy+st‾xy‾+s‾tx‾y+s‾t‾xy+s‾t‾xy‾+s‾t‾x‾y+s‾t‾x‾y‾=stxy+st‾xy‾+s‾tx‾y+s‾t‾. So, passing from logic to algebra, with u standing for the probability sought, we have the following system of equations. (Each fraction sets the part of V in which a given event occurs against that event's known probability, as the general rule of Chapter XVII directs; the letters now stand for numbers, the unknown probabilities of the simple events once the restriction V is taken away.) stxy+st‾xy‾+s‾t‾xc1=stxy+s‾tx‾y+s‾t‾yc2=stxy+st‾xy‾c1p1=stxy+s‾tx‾yc2p2=stxy+st‾xy‾+s‾tx‾yu=stxy+st‾xy‾+s‾tx‾y+s‾t‾1=V,(7) and from it we must eliminate s, t, x, y, and V, so that only u and the known numbers remain.

To do this we use a familiar property of equal fractions. If we have any series of equal fractions, such as aa′=bb′=cc′…=λ, we know that la+mb+ncla′+mb′+nc′=λ. In words: add any multiples of the numerators, and the same multiples of the denominators, and the new fraction still has the same value. So by subtracting suitable members of the system above from one another we may deduce s‾tx‾yu−c1p1=st‾xy‾u−c2p2=s‾t‾1−u=V; and so, setting the product of the first three members equal to the cube of the last, ss‾2tt‾2xx‾yy‾(u−c1p1)(u−c2p2)(1−u)=V3.(8)

Again, from the system (7), combining its members in another way, we have s‾t‾x‾1−u−c1+c1p1=s‾t‾y‾1−u−c2+c2p2=stxyc1p1+c2p2−u=V, and so, proceeding as before, ss‾2tt‾2xx‾yy‾(1−c1+c1p1−u)(1−c2+c2p2−u)(c1p1+c2p2−u)=V3.(9) The two numerators are the same product of the unknowns. That is the reason for this choice of combinations: when we set the two values of the cube of V in (8) and (9) equal, all of s, t, x, y cancel at once. Equating the values of V3 in (8) and (9), we have (u−c1p1)(u−c2p2)(1−u)={1−c1(1−p1)−u}{1−c2(1−p2)−u}(c1p1+c2p2−u), which can be written more conveniently in the form (u−c1p1)(u−c2p2)c1p1+c2p2−u={1−c1(1−p1)−u}{1−c2(1−p2)−u}1−u.(10)

The value of u can be found from this equation, which contains only u and the data. All that remains is to decide which of its roots we must take.

3. It has been shown (XIX. 12) that if u is to stand for the probability required here, it must be greater than each of the quantities c1p1, c2p2, and smaller than each of the quantities 1−c1(1−p1), 1−c2(1−p2) and c1p1+c2p2. The condition the constants themselves must meet is that each of the last three quantities must be greater than each of the first two. I shall now show that when these conditions are met, the final equation (10) has only one root that falls within the limits assigned. That root will therefore be the value of u we want.

Let us represent the lower limits c1p1, c2p2, by a, b respectively, and the upper limits 1−c1(1−p1), 1−c2(1−p2) and c1p1+c2p2 by a′, b′, c′ respectively. Then the general equation can be written in the form (u−a)(u−b)(1−u)−(a′−u)(b′−u)(c′−u)=0,(11)or(1−a′−b′)u2−{ab−a′b′+(1−a′−b′)c′}u+ab−a′b′c′=0. (The terms in the cube of u cancel, so the equation is really a quadratic.) Call the left-hand side of this equation V. Then we have d2Vdu2=2(1−a′−b′).(12) that is, the rate at which the slope of V changes is a fixed number, the same for every value of u. Now let a be the highest of the lower limits of u, and a′ the lowest of its upper limits, and let us follow how the value of V changes between u=a and u=a′.

When u=a, the form of the left-hand side of (11) shows that V is negative, and when u=a′ it shows that V is positive. Between those limits V changes continuously without becoming infinite, and d2Vdu2 always has the same sign.

So suppose u is the abscissa (the distance along the horizontal axis) and V the ordinate (the height) of a curve in the plane. The curve will pass from a point below the axis of u, at u=a, to a point above the axis of u, at u=a′. It stays continuous on the way, and it always bends in the same direction. A little attention will show that, in these circumstances, it must cross the axis of u once, and only once.

So between the limits u=a, u=a′, there is one value of u, and only one, that satisfies the equation (11). If we trace the curve in thought, it will also appear that the other value of u is less than a when the quantity 1−a′−b′ is positive, and greater than every one of the quantities a′, b′, c′ when 1−a′−b′ is negative. It follows that in solving (11) we must take the positive sign of the square root. We thus find u=ab−a′b′+(1−a′−b′)c′+Q2(1−a′−b′),(13) where Q={ab−a′b′+(1−a′−b′)c′}2−4(1−a′−b′)(ab−a′b′c′).

4. These results can be checked to some extent. First, it is clear that the probability of the event E must in general be greater than the probability that E occurs together with the cause A1, or together with A2. So we must have, as the solution indicates, u>c1p1,u>c2p2.

Again, it is clear that the probability of the effect E must in general be less than it would be if the causes A1,A2 excluded one another. So u<=c1p1+c2p2. that is, u is at most the sum of those two products.

Last, the probability that the effect E fails while the cause A1 is present must, in general, be less than the absolute probability that E fails. So we have c1(1−p1)<=1−u,∴u<=1−c1(1−p1). In the same way, u<=1−c2(1−p2).

So the conditions that limited the general solution are confirmed.

Again, let p1=1, p2=1. This means supposing that whenever either of the causes A1, A2 is present, the event E will occur. Then we have a=c1, b=c2, a′=1, b′=1, c′=c1+c2, and substituting these in (13) we get u=c1c2−c1−c2−1+{(c1c2−c1−c2−1)2+4(c1c2−c1−c2)}−2=c1+c2−c1c2 on reduction=1−(1−c1)(1−c2). Now this is the familiar expression for the probability that at least one cause will be present: one minus the chance that both are absent. In these circumstances that is plainly the probability of the event E.

Finally, suppose that c1 and c2 are very small, so small that their product can be neglected. Then the expression for u reduces to c1p1+c2p2. The smaller the probability of each cause, the smaller, and in a much higher degree, is the probability that the causes occur together. So in the end, as the probabilities go on shrinking, the probability of the event E becomes the same as if the causes excluded one another.

I have dwelt on this solution at some length because it serves, in a way, as a model for those that follow. Some of them are more complex, and without this preparation they might look difficult.

5. Problem II.—Instead of the supposition of the last problem, that the event E cannot happen when both the causes A1, A2 are absent, let us assume that the causes A1, A2 cannot both be absent, and let everything else stay as before. Required, then, the probability of the event E.

Here, in place of equation (2) of the last solution, we have the equation (1−x)(1−y)=0. which says that there is no case in which both causes are missing. The developed logical expression for z turns out to be z=stxy+10stxy‾+10stx‾y+10stx‾y‾+10st‾xy+st‾xy‾+10st‾x‾y+10st‾x‾y‾+10s‾txy+10s‾txy‾+s‾tx‾y+10s‾tx‾y‾+0s‾t‾xy+0s‾t‾xy‾+0s‾t‾x‾y+10s‾t‾x‾y‾; It differs from the development in Problem I only in the last compartment, where neither cause is present: that case is now impossible. The final solution is Prob. E=u; where the quantity u is found by solving the equation (u−a)(u−b)a+b−u=(a′−u)(b′−u)u−a′−b′+1,(1) in which a=c1p1, b=c2p2, a′=1−c1(1−p1), b′=1−c2(1−p2).

The conditions that limit the choice are these. We must choose the value of u that is greater than each of the three quantities a,b, and a′+b′−1, and at the same time smaller than each of the three quantities a′,b′, and a+b.

Exactly as in the last problem, we can show that the quadratic equation (1) has one root, and only one, meeting these conditions. The conditions themselves were found by the same rule as before, except that the minor limit (smallest possible value) a′+b′−1 was found by looking for the major limit of 1−z, the largest possible probability that the effect fails.

I may add that the constants in the data must meet the conditions implied above, namely that each of the quantities a′, b′, and a+b must be greater than each of a, b, and a′+b′−1. Besides these, they must also meet the condition c1+c2>=1, that is, the two chances of the causes must add up to at least one. This too follows from applying the rule.

6. Problem III.—The probabilities of two events A and B are a and b respectively. The probability that if the event A takes place an event E will go along with it is p, and the probability that if the event B takes place, the same event E will go along with it is q. Required, the probability that if the event A takes place the event B will take place; or, vice versâ, the probability that if B takes place, A will take place.

Let us represent the event A by x, the event B by y, and the event E by z. Then the data are— Prob. x=a,Prob. y=b.Prob. xz=ap,Prob. yz=bq. From these we are to find Prob. xyProb. x or Prob. xyProb. y. that is, the probability that both happen, divided by the probability of the one we are told has happened. So the real unknown is the probability of x and y together. Let xz=s,yz=t,xy=w. Eliminating z, we have, after reduction, sx‾+ty‾+syt‾+xts‾+xyw‾+(1−xy)w=0,∴w=sx‾+ty‾+syt‾+xts‾+xy2xy−1=xyst+10xy‾st+10x‾yst+10x‾y‾st+10xyst‾+0xy‾st‾+10x‾yst‾+10x‾y‾st‾+10xys‾t+10xy‾s‾t+0x‾ys‾t+10x‾y‾s‾t+xys‾t‾+0xy‾s‾t‾+0x‾ys‾t‾+0x‾y‾s‾t‾.(1) So, passing from logic to algebra, we take the two compartments with coefficient 1 and divide by the condition V: Prob. xy=xyst+xys‾t‾V, where x, y, s, and t are found from the system of equations xyst+xy‾st‾+xys‾t‾+xy‾s‾t‾a=xyst+x‾ys‾t+xys‾t‾+x‾ys‾t‾b=xyst+xy‾st‾ap=xyst+x‾ys‾tbq=xyst+xy‾st‾+x‾ys‾t+xys‾t‾+xy‾s‾t‾+x‾ys‾t‾+x‾y‾s‾t‾=V. This system has four unknowns besides V, and it is awkward as it stands. The steps that follow are a change of unknowns that makes it manageable. To bring it to a more convenient form, divide every member by x‾y‾s‾t‾, and in the result let xsx‾s‾=m,yty‾t‾=m′,xx‾=n,yy‾=n′. We then find mm′+m+nn′+na=mm′+m′+nn′+n′b=mm′+map=mm′+m′bq=mm′+m+m′+nn′+n+n′+1. Also, Prob. xy=mm′+nn′mm′+m+m′+nn′+n+n′+1. These equations can be reduced to the form mm′+map=mm′+m′bq=nn′+na(1−p)=nn′+n′b(1−q)=(m+1)(m′+1)+(n+1)(n′+1)−1.Prob. xy=mm′+nn′(m+1)(m′+1)+(n+1)(n′+1)−1. Now we bring in two auxiliary quantities, μ and ν (the Greek letters mu and nu), through which the two products in the last denominator are expressed. Assume (m+1)(m′+1)=μν+μ−1,(n+1)(n′+1)=νν+μ−1.(2) Then since mm′+m=m(m′+1)(m+1)m+1=mμ(m+1)(ν+μ−1), and so on for the other numerators of the system, we substitute and multiply each member of the system by ν+μ−1, and find the following results: mμ(m+1)ap=m′μ(m′+1)bq=nν(n+1)a(1−p)=n′ν(n′+1)b(1−q)=1.Prob. xy=(mm′+nn′)(ν+μ−1).(3) Each of these fractions equals 1, so each gives one of the old unknowns in terms of μ or ν. From the system above we have mm+1=apμ, whence m=apμ−ap. In the same way, m′=bqμ−bq,n=a(1−p)ν−a(1−p),n′=b(1−q)ν−b(1−q). So m+1=μμ−ap,n+1=νν−a(1−p), &c. Substitute these values in (2), rewritten in the form ν+μ−1=μ(m+1)(m′+1)=ν(n+1)(n′+1), and we have ν+μ−1=(μ−ap)(μ−bq)μ={ν−a(1−p)}{ν−b(1−q)}ν,(4) Now m, m′, n, n′ have disappeared, and only μ and ν are left to find. Substitute also the values of m, m′, &c. in (3), and we have Prob. xy=[abpq(μ−ap)(μ−bq)+ab(1−p)(1−q){ν−a(1−p)}{ν−b(1−q)}](ν+μ−1)=abpqμ+ab(1−p)(1−q)ν by (4). Now the first equation of the system (4) gives ν+μ−1=μ−ap−bq+apbqμ,(5)∴apbqμ=ν−1+ap+bq. In the same way, ab(1−p)(1−q)ν=μ−1+a(1−p)+b(1−q). Add these two equations together. The left-hand side of the result is exactly the expression we have just found for Prob. xy, so we have Prob. xy=ν+μ+a+b−2. Let us represent Prob. xy by u, and let a+b−2=m. (The letter m is now free for this new use, since the old m has been eliminated.) Then μ+ν=u−m.(6) This gives the sum of μ and ν in terms of u. We next look for a second relation between them. Again, from (5) we have μν=abpq−(ap+bq−1)μ.(7) In the same way, setting the first and third members of (4) equal, we have μν=ab(1−p)(1−q)−{a(1−p)+b(1−q)−1}ν. Let us represent ap+bq−1 by h, and a(1−p)+b(1−q)−1 by h′. Setting the two values of μν above equal, we find hμ−h′ν=ab{pq+(1−p)(1−q)}=ab(p+q−1). Let ab(p+q−1)=l. Then hμ−h′ν=l.(8) Now (6) and (8) are two simple equations in μ and ν, and from them we get μ=h′(u−m)+lm,ν=h(u−m)−lm. Substitute these values in (7), rewritten in the form μ(ν+h)=abpq, and we have (hu−l){h′(u−m)+l}=abpqm2,(9) a quadratic equation whose solution gives u, the value of Prob. xy we are looking for.

The solution can easily be put in the form u=lh′+h(h′m−l)±[{lh′−h(h′m−l)}2+4hh′abpqm2]2hh′. But we may also observe that lh′−h(h′m−l)=l(h+h′)−hh′m=(l−hh′)m, since h=ap+bq−1,h′=a(1−p)+b(1−q)−1, and so h+h′=a+b−2=m, With that simplification we find Prob. xy=lh′+h(h′m−l)±m{(l−hh′)2+4hh′abpq}2hh′.(10) It remains to decide which sign to give the square root. We could settle this by the general method used in the last problem. But it is far easier, and quite enough in this case, to settle the sign by comparing the formula with the answer in some case where we already know it. For instance, if it were certain that the event A is always, and the event B never, accompanied by the event E, then it is certain that the events A and B never happen together. So if p=1, q=0, we ought to have u=0. Now the assumptions p=1, q=0, give h=a−1,h′=b−1,l=0,m=a+b−2. Substituting these in (10), we have Prob. xy=(a−1)(b−1)(a+b−2)±(a+b−2)(a−1)(b−1)2(a−1)(b−1), and this expression is zero when we take the lower sign, the minus. So the final solution of the general problem will be expressed in the form Prob. xyProb. x=lh′+h(h′m−l)−m{(l−hh′)2+4hh′abpq}2ahh′, where h=ap+bq−1,h′=a(1−p)+b(1−q)−1, l=ab(p+q−1),m=a+b−2. The terms in the final logical solution that carry the coefficient 10 are the same as in the first problem of this chapter. So the conditions the constants must meet will be the same, namely ap<=1−b(1−q),bq<=1−a(1−p).24

7. One confirmation that this solution is correct is that the expression we found is symmetrical in the two sets of quantities p, q, and 1−p, 1−q. That is, if we change p into 1−p, and q into 1−q, the expression is unchanged. This can be seen from the equation Prob. xy=ab{pqμ+(1−p)(1−q)ν} which we used on the way to the final result. Now if there are probabilities p, q of the event E, given that we know A or B has occurred, there are also probabilities 1−p, 1−q of the contrary event, that is, of E not occurring in the same circumstances. The data keep the same form whether we count in them the occurrence of E or its failure. So it is clear that the solution ought to be, as it is, a symmetrical function of p, q and 1−p, 1−q.

Let us look at the particular case in which p=1, q=1. We find h=a+b−1,h′=−1,l=ab,m=a+b−2, and substituting, Prob. xyProb. x=−ab+(a+b−1)(2−a−b−ab)−(a+b−2)(ab−a−b+1)−2a(a+b−1)=−2ab(a+b−1)−2a(a+b−1)=b. So it seems that in this case the events A and B are in effect independent of each other: knowing that A has happened leaves the chance of B just what it was. Suppose both are invariably accompanied by some other event E, and suppose we know absolutely nothing about how often E occurs, beyond what can be inferred from this particular connection. That supposition does not set up any dependence between the events A and B themselves. I believe this conclusion agrees with reason, though particular examples may seem at first sight to point the other way. Take two events: first, a particular species of weed being cast up on the seashore; second, a certain kind of zoophyte (a plant-like sea animal, such as a sponge or coral) being cast up there too. Suppose their probabilities had been separately found, and suppose it had also been established that neither could happen except when the waves are stirred up by a storm. Then, I think, we would rightly conclude that the two events were not independent. Picking up a piece of the weed would, presumably, make finding the zoophytes more likely than it would otherwise have been. But I believe this comes from our knowing something else, which is not contained in the conditions of the problem: that a storm is only an occasional phenomenon. Confine the range of observation to a sea that is always churned by storms. Then, I suppose, we would see that the casting up of the weeds and of the zoophytes ought to count as independent events. To put it more generally, there are conditions common to all phenomena, conditions which, we feel, do not affect whether they are independent of one another. So I believe the solution shows this: when a particular condition has held throughout the whole of our recorded experience, it takes on that same character with respect to the class of phenomena that experience has covered.

8. Problem IV.—To illustrate these remarks a little, let us be given, in addition to the data of the last problem, the absolute probability of the event E. The complete system of data is then Prob. x=a,Prob. y=b,Prob. z=c,Prob. xz=ap,Prob. yz=bq, and we are asked to find Prob. xy.

Assuming, as before, xz=s, yz=t, xy=w, the final logical equation is w=xystz+xys‾t‾z‾+0(xy‾st‾z+x‾ys‾tz+xy‾z‾s‾t‾+xyz‾s‾t‾+x‾y‾zs‾t‾+x‾y‾z‾s‾t‾)+ terms whose coefficients are 10.(1) Once the algebraic system has been formed, the eliminations that follow can be simplified by the same changes of unknowns we used in the last problem. The final result is Prob. xy=ab{pqc+(1−p)(1−q)1−c}.(2) The conditions the constants must meet are c>=ap,c>=bq,c<=1−a(1−p),c<=1−b(1−q).

Now if p=1, q=1, we find Prob. xy=abc, where c cannot take any value less than a or b. It follows that if the event E is known to be an occasional one, the fact that it always goes along with the events x and y increases the probability that they happen together, in inverse proportion to how often E itself happens: the rarer the shared companion, the more closely the two are tied. Formula (2) can be checked in a large number of cases. As one particular instance, let q=c. We find Prob. xy=ab.(3) Now the assumption q=c means, by the definition (Chap. XVI.), that the events B and E are independent: the chance of E is the same whether or not B has happened. If B and E are independent, then no relation that may exist between A and E can set up a relation between A and B. So A and B are also independent, as equation (3) above implies.

It can easily be shown from (2) that the value of Prob. z that makes Prob. xy as small as possible is Prob. z=(pq)(pq)+(1−p)(1−q). If p=q, this gives Prob. z=p; a result whose correctness can be shown by the same considerations we applied to (3).

Problem V.—Given the probabilities of any three events, and the probability that all three happen together; required, the probability that any two of them happen together.

Suppose the data are Prob. x=p,Prob. y=q,Prob. z=r,Prob. xyz=m, and the quæsitum is Prob. xy.

Assuming xyz=s, xy=t, we find as the final logical equation t=xyzs+xyz‾s‾+0(xy‾s‾+x‾s‾)+10(sum of all other constituents); and so, in the end, Prob. xy=H−(H2−4pqr‾2−4p‾q‾r‾m)2r‾, where p‾=1−p, &c.H=p‾q‾+(p+q)r‾. This can be checked when p=1, when q=1, when r=0, and so m=0, and so on.

If the condition Prob. z=r had been left out, the solution would still have been definite. We would have had Prob. xy=pq(1−m)+(1−p)(1−q)m1−m; and I may add, as a final confirmation that both results are correct, that they become identical when m=pqr, that is, when the probability of all three together is just the product of their separate probabilities, as it would be for independent events.

9. The following problem is a generalization of Problem I. Its solution is necessarily more complex, but it is reached by a similar analysis.

Problem VI.—Suppose an event can happen only as a result of one or more of certain causes A1,A2,…An. In general, let ci stand for the probability of the cause Ai, and pi for the probability that if the cause Ai exists, the event E will occur. Then, given the series of values of ci and pi, required, the probability of the event E. Let the causes A1,A2,…An be represented by x1,x2,…xn, and the event E by z.25

Then in general we have Prob. xi=ci,Prob. xiz=cipi. that is, for each cause, its own probability, and the probability that it and the event occur together. Further, the condition that E can happen only along with one or more of the causes A1,A2,…An sets up the logical condition z(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn)=0.(1) which says there is no case of the event when every cause is absent.

Now let us assume in general xiz=ti, which can be reduced to the form xiz(1−ti)+ti(1−xiz)=0, This is the pattern for a system of n equations, one for each cause, which together with (1) express the logical conditions of the problem. After the reduction just made we are allowed to add all these equations together, and doing so we have ∑{xiz(1−ti)+ti(1−xiz)}+z(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn)=0,(2) (the sum marked by ∑ running from i=1 to i=n). This single logical equation is enough. Together with the 2n data, represented by the general equations Prob. xi=ci,Prob. ti=cipi,(3) it makes up the material from which we are to find Prob. z.

Let (2) be developed with respect to z. We have [∑{xi(1−ti)+ti(1−xi)}+(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn)]z+∑ti(1−z)=0, and so z=∑ti∑ti−∑{xi(1−ti)+ti(1−xi)}−(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn).(4) We now have to work out the coefficient of every constituent when the right-hand side is developed, and we do it by sorting the constituents into kinds. Any constituent in the expansion of the right-hand side of the equation above will have 2n factors. Of these, n are taken from the set x1,x2,…xn,1−x1,1−x2,…1−xn, and n from the set t1,t2,…tn,1−t1,1−t2…1−tn, and no pairing such as x1(1−x1),t1(1−t1) is allowed, since a thing cannot be both x and not x. Let us first consider the constituents whose t-factor is (1−t1),(1−t2)…(1−tn), where by the t-factor I mean the part taken from the set t1,…1−t1.

We find the coefficient of any such constituent by changing t1,t2,…tn each into 0 in the right-hand side of (4), and then giving x1,x2,…xn the values that the x-factor of the constituent calls for. Now if we simply put for t1,t2,…tn the value 0, the right-hand side becomes 0−∑xi−(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn), and this is zero whatever values, 0 or 1, we then give to x1,x2,…xn. For if those values are not all 0, the term ∑xi is not zero; and if they are all 0, the term −(1−x1)…(1−xn) becomes −1. Either way the denominator is not zero, and so the fraction is. So the coefficients of all constituents that have (1−t1)…(1−tn) as a factor will be 0. And since all the possible x-constituents added together make unity, there will be an aggregate term 0(1−t1)…(1−tn), standing for all of them at once, in the development of z.

Next, consider any constituent whose t-factor is t1t2…tr(1−tr+1)…(1−tn), with r equal to or greater than unity. Putting t1=1,…tr=1,tr+1=0,…tn=0 in the right-hand side of (4), we get the expression rx1…+xr−xr+1…−xn−(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn) Now the only values the symbols can take are 0 and 1. So it is clear that this expression will equal 1 when x1=1…xr=1,xr+1=0,…xn=0, and that for every other combination of values it will take a value greater than unity. So the coefficient 1 will go to all constituents of the final development that have the form x1…xr(1−xr+1)…(1−xn)t1…tr(1−tr+1)…(1−tn), where the x-factor matches the t-factor, while the other constituents that fall under this case will in effect have the coefficient 10. In plain terms: a compartment in which the t's present are exactly the x's present is a case of the event; the other compartments of this kind cannot occur. It is also plain that this reasoning does not depend on the particular arrangement or order of the individual symbols.

So the complete expansion of z will have the form z=∑(XT)+0(1−t1)(1−t2)…(1−tn)+ constituents whose coefficients are 10,(5) where T stands for any t-constituent except (1−t1)…(1−tn), and X for the matching constituent of x1…xn. For instance, if n=2, we shall have ∑(XT)=x1x2t1t2+x1x‾2t1t‾2+x‾1x2t‾1t2, with x‾1, x‾2, &c. standing for 1−x1, 1−x2, &c.; and so z=x1x2t1t2+x1x‾2t1t‾2+x‾1x2t‾1t2(6)+0(x1x2t‾1t‾2+x1x‾2t‾1t‾2+x‾1x2t‾1t‾2+x‾1x‾2t‾1t‾2)+ constituents whose coefficients are 10. Allowing for the difference of notation, this agrees with the developed form of z in Problem I. of this chapter, as it clearly should.

10. To keep things simple, I shall take equation (6) above and draw from it the conditions that determine Prob. z in the particular case where n=2. I shall put them in a form that lets us, by following the same line of reasoning in thought, write down the corresponding conditions for the general case, where n is any whole number at all.

So suppose n=2. The general method (Chap. XVII) tells us what to write. V is the sum of the compartments that the final logical equation allows, and the probability of z is the share of V made up of the compartments in which E occurs. We have V=x1x2t1t2+x1x‾2t1t‾2+x‾1x2t‾1t2+x1x2t‾1t‾2+x1x‾2t‾1t‾2+x‾1x2t‾1t‾2+x‾1x‾2t‾1t‾2.Prob. z=x1x2t1t2+x1x‾2t1t‾2+x‾1x2t‾1t2V, and the conditions that determine x1, t1, &c., are these. Each fraction has on top the part of V that contains a letter whose probability is given, and underneath that given probability; all the fractions are equal to one another and to V: x1x2t1t2+x1x‾2t1t‾2+x1x2t‾1t‾2+x1x‾2t‾1t‾2c1=x1x2t1t2+x‾1x2t‾1t2+x1x2t‾1t‾2+x‾1x2t‾1t‾2c2=x1x2t1t2+x1x‾2t1t‾2c1p1=x1x2t1t2+x‾1x2t‾1t2c2p2=V.

These equations are awkward as they stand, and the next steps only change the unknowns to make them easier to handle. Divide every side of this system of equations by x‾1x‾2t‾1t‾2, and divide the top and bottom of Prob. z by the same quantity. In the results, put x1t1x‾1t‾1=m1,x2t2x‾2t‾2=m2,x1x‾1=n1,x2x‾2=n2;(7)

and we find Prob. z=m1m2+m1+m2m1m2+m1+m2+n1n2+n1+n2+1,and m1m2+m1+n1n2+n1c1=m1m2+m2+n1n2+n2c2=m1m2+m1c1p1=m1m2+m2c2p2=m1m2+m1+m2+n1n2+n1+n2+1,(8) Notice that these expressions nearly factor into products. So if we put (m1+1)(m2+1)=M,(n1+1)(n2+1)=N,(9) we have, after a little simplifying, Prob. z=M−1M+N−1,n1(n2+1)c1(1−p1)=n2(n1+1)c2(1−p2)=m1(m2+1)c1p1=m2(m1+1)c2p2=M+N−1; or, what is the same, m1M(m1+1)c1p1=m2M(m2+1)c2p2=n1N(n1+1)c1(1−p1)=n2N(n2+1)c2(1−p2)=M+N−1.

Now carry out, in thought, the same series of changes and simplifications on the general final logical equation (5), for any number of causes. We get the following expression for Prob. z: Prob. z=M−1M+N−1(10) where M=(m1+1)(m2+1)…(mn+1),N=(n1+1)(n2+1)…(nn+1), and where m1,…,mn,n1,…,nn, are given by the system of equations, m1M(m1+1)c1p1=m2M(m2+1)c2p2…=mnM(mn+1)cnpn=n1N(n1+1)c1(1−p1)…=nnN(nn+1)cn(1−pn)=M+N−1.(11)

To simplify the results still further, we bring in two new auxiliary quantities, μ and ν. Put M+N−1M=1μ,M+N−1N=1ν; so that M=μμ+ν−1,N=νμ+ν−1. Dividing the system (11) through by M in its first half and by N in its second, we find m1(m1+1)c1p1=m2(m2+1)c2p2…=mn(mn+1)cnpn=1μ,n1(n1+1)c1(1−p1)=n2(n2+1)c2(1−p2)…=nn(nn+1)cn(1−pn)=1ν; and solving each of these for its own unknown, m1=c1p1μ−c1p1,…mn=cnpnμ−cnpn; and finally, m1+1=μμ−c1p1,…mn+1=μμ−cnpn,n1+1=νν−c1(1−p1),…nn+1=νν−cn(1−pn). So every one of the unknowns is now written in terms of just two, μ and ν.

Put these values, together with those of M and N, into (9), and we have two equations for μ and ν: μn(μ−c1p1)(μ−c2p2)…(μ−cnpn)=μμ+ν−1,νn{ν−c1(1−p1)}{ν−c2(1−p2)}…{ν−cn(1−pn)}=νμ+ν−1, which can be brought into the symmetrical form μ+ν−1=(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)μn−1={ν−c1(1−p1)}…{ν−cn(1−pn)}νn−1.(12) Finally, the probability sought itself turns out to be very simple: Prob. z=M−1M+N−1=1−ν.(13) So let us put 1−ν=u, the very quantity we want. Then we have μ−u=(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)μn−1={1−c1(1−p1)−u}…{1−cn(1−pn)−u}(1−u)n−1.

If, for simplicity, we write c1p1=a1,cnpn=an,1−c1(1−p1)=b1, &c., the equations above can be written as follows: μ−u=(μ−a1)…(μ−an)μn−1,(14) where μ=u+(b1−u)…(bn−u)(1−u)n−1.(15)

Put this value of μ into (14), and we get an equation that contains only u. Solving it will determine Prob. z, since by (13) Prob. z=u. Such an equation may have several roots, so it remains to find the limits of u, which tell us which root to take.

11. The very same analysis that fixed the limits in the particular case n=2, (XIX. 12) leads us here to the following result. If the quantity u is to stand for the value of Prob. z, it must have as its lower limits the quantities a1,a2,…an, and as its upper limits the quantities b1,b2,…bn, a1+a2…+an. In words: u must be at least as large as every one of the a's, and no larger than any of the b's, nor than the sum of the a's. From this we may infer, à priori, that the equation (14) will always have one root, and only one, that satisfies these conditions. For a practical check, I think it enough to show that the equation (14) has one root, and only one, between the limits a1,a2,…an, and b1,b2,…bn. The proof has three steps: first, that μ grows as u grows; then that the equation's left-hand side is negative at one end of the range and positive at the other; and last, that it grows steadily in between, so that it passes through zero exactly once.

First, let us look at how μ changes in (15) as u runs from a1, which we will suppose is the greatest of its minor limits, to b1, which we will suppose is the least of its major limits. When u=a1, it is clear that μ is positive and greater than a1. When u=b1, we have μ=b1, which is also positive. Between the limits u=a1, u=b1 it can be shown that μ increases with u. To show it, we take the rate at which μ changes with u, its derivative. We have dμdu=1−(b2−u)…(bn−u)(1−u)n−1−(b1−u)(b3−u)…(bn−u)(1−u)n−1…+(n−1)(b1−u)(b2−u)…(bn−u)(1−u)n.(16) Now let b1−u1−u=x1…bn−u1−u=xn. Clearly x1,x2,…xn, will be proper fractions (numbers between 0 and 1), and we have dμdu=1−x2x3…xn−x1x3…xn…−x1x2…xn−1+(n−1)x1x2…xn=1−(1−x1)x2x3…xn−x1(1−x2)x3…xn…−x1x2…xn−1(1−xn)−x1x2…xn.

Now the negative terms on the right-hand side are (if we may borrow the language of the logical developments) constituents formed from the fractions x1,x2,…xn. They are some of the compartments, and all the compartments together add up to exactly 1, so their sum cannot be more than unity. So dμdu is positive, and μ increases with u between the limits stated.

Next, write (14) in the form (μ−a1)…(μ−an)μn−1−(μ−u)=0,(17) and put u=a1. The left-hand side becomes (μ−a1){(μ−a2)…(μ−an)μn−1−1},(18) and this expression is negative. For if we make the same assumption in (15), we find μ−a1=(b1−u)…(bn−u)(1−u)n−1= a positive quantity. At the same time we have (μ−a2)…(μ−an)μn−1=μ−a2μ…μ−anμ, and since the factors on the right-hand side are positive fractions, that side is less than unity. So the bracket in (18) is negative, its first factor is positive, and (18) is negative. Therefore the assumption u=a1 makes the left-hand side of (17) negative.

Second, let u=b1. Then by (15) μ=u=b1, the second term of (17) vanishes, and the left-hand side of (17) becomes positive.

Last, between the limits u=a1 and u=b1 the left-hand side of (17) increases steadily. For its first term, written in the form (μ−a1)μ−a2μ…μ−anμ increases, since μ increases, and with it every factor the term contains. And the negative term μ−u gets smaller as u increases, as we see from its value taken from (15), namely, (b1−u)…(bn−u)(1−u)n−1. So between the limits u=a1, u=b1, the left-hand side of (17) increases steadily, and in doing so passes from a negative value to a positive one. Therefore, between the limits assigned, there is one value of u, and only one, that satisfies the equation.

12. Putting these results together, we arrive at the following solution of the general problem.

The probability of the event E will be the value of u found from the equation μ−u=(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)μn−1,(19) where μ=u+{1−c1(1−p1)−u}…{1−cn(1−pn)−u}(1−u)n−1, the value that lies between the two sets of quantities, c1p1,c2p2,…,cnpn and 1−c1(1−p1),1−c2(1−p2)…1−cn(1−pn), the first set being its lower limits, the second its upper limits.

We may further infer for the general case, as was proved for the particular case of n=2, that the value of u found in this way will not be more than the quantity c1p1+c2p2…+cnpn. That is, the probability of the event is never more than the sum of the chances that each cause occurs and brings it about.

13. Some particular checks follow. In each, we give the data special values for which the answer is known in advance, and see whether the general solution gives it.

First, let p1=1,p2=1,…pn=1. This is to suppose it certain that if any one of the events A1,A2…An happens, the event E will happen. In this case, then, the probability that E occurs will simply be the probability that the events or causes A1,A2…An do not all fail to occur, and so its expression will be 1−(1−c1)(1−c2)…(1−cn): one, minus the chance that every cause is absent.

Now the general solution (19) gives μ−u=(μ−c1)…(μ−cn)μn−1, where μ=u+(1−u)n(1−u)n−1=1. So, 1−u=(1−c1)…(1−cn),∴u=1−(1−c1)…(1−cn), which agrees with the answer worked out à priori above.

Second, let p1=0, p2=0, pn=0: no cause ever brings the event. Then (19) gives μ−u=μ,∴u=0, as it clearly ought to be.

Third, let c1,c2…cn be small quantities, so small that their squares and products may be neglected. Then, expanding the right-hand sides of the equation (19), μ−u=μn−(c1p1+c2p2…+cnpn)μn−1μn−1=μ−(c1p1+c2p2…+cnpn),∴u=c1p1+c2p2…+cnpn.

Now this is what the solution would be if the causes A1,A2…An excluded one another. But the smaller the probabilities of those causes, the nearer they come to excluding one another, since the smaller is the probability that any of them happen together. So the result just obtained is surely the limiting form of the expression for the probability of E.

Fourth, in the particular case of n=2, we can easily eliminate μ from the general solution. The result is (u−c1p1)(u−c2p2)c1p1+c2p2−u={1−c1(1−p1)−u}{1−c2(1−p2)−u}1−u, which agrees with the particular solution found earlier for this case, Problem I.

By the system (19), the solution in general depends on solving an equation of high degree. Even so, it will not be hard in practice. The conditions about the limits let us pick at once a value of u close to the true one, and the forms of the system (19) suit the methods of successive approximation, in which a rough answer is improved step by step.

14. Problem 7.—The data being the same as in the last problem, required the probability that, if any definite and given combination of the causes A1,A2,…An presents itself, the event E will be realized.

Given, then: the probability of each cause, and the probability that the event follows each cause. Sought: the probability that the event follows when the causes appear in one stated combination (say, the first and third present and the rest absent, or any such pattern). The answer is a fraction. Its top is the probability that the combination and the event occur together; its bottom is the probability of the combination.

The causes A1,A2,…An being represented as before by x1,x2,…xn respectively, let the definite combination of them named in the problem be represented by the ϕ(x1,x2…xn), so that the actual occurrence of that combination will be expressed by the logical equation, ϕ(x1,x2,…xn)=1.

The data are Prob. x1=c1,…Prob. xn=cn,Prob. x1z=c1p1,Prob. xnz=cnpn;(1) and the object of the inquiry is Prob. ϕ(x1,x2…xn)zProb. ϕ(x1,x2…xn).(2) We shall look first for the value of the top of this fraction.

As in Problem VI, we give a single letter to each compound event whose probability is known or sought. Let us put x1z=t1…xnz=tn,(3)ϕ(x1,x2…xn)z=w.(4) Or, if for simplicity we shorten ϕ(x1,x2…xn) to ϕ, the last equation will be ϕz=w,(5) and to these we must add the equation x‾1x‾2…x‾nz=0.(6) This says that the event never happens when every cause is absent.

Now any equation xrz=tr of the system (3) can be brought to the form xrzt‾r+tr(1−xrz)=0. Treat (5) in the same way, and add all the results together, and we get the single logical equation Σ{xrzt‾r+tr(1−xrz)}+x‾1…x‾nz+ϕzw‾+w(1−ϕz)=0,(7) from which we must eliminate z, since its probability is not given here, and then find w as a developed logical function of x1,…xn,t1,…tn.

To eliminate z, we set z=1,z=0 in turn in the equation above, and multiply the results together. We have {Σ(xrt‾r+x‾rtr)+x‾1…x‾n+ϕw‾+wϕ‾}×(Σtr+w)=0. Develop this equation with respect to w, and in the result replace ∑tr+1 by 1, as Prop. I. Chap. IX. allows, and we have Ew+E′(1−w)=0; where E=Σ(xrt‾r+trx‾r)+x‾1…x‾n+ϕ‾,E′=Σtr{Σ(xrt‾r+trx‾r)+x‾1…x‾n+ϕ}. And so w=E′E′−E.(8)

We must now develop the right-hand side of this equation with respect to the double series of symbols x1,x2,…xn,t1,t2,…tn; that is, find the coefficient of every compartment of these letters. The easiest way is to sort the compartments of the development into three classes, and find the coefficients proper to each class separately.

First, take the compartments that have t‾1…t‾n as a factor, those in which none of the t-events happens. Setting t1=0…tn=0, we find E′=0,E=Σxr+x‾1…x‾n+ϕ‾. It is clear that whatever values (0,1) are given to the x-symbols, E is not zero. So the fraction (8) is zero, and the coefficients of all compartments that contain t‾1…t‾n are 0.

Second, take the compartments that do not contain the factor t‾1…t‾n, and that are symmetrical with respect to the two sets of symbols x1…xn and t1…tn. By symmetrical compartments I mean those that would stay unchanged if x1 were turned into t1, x2 into t2, &c., and vice versâ. They are the compartments in which each t is present exactly when its x is. The constituents x1…xnt1…tn,x‾1…x‾nt‾1…t‾n, &c., are symmetrical in this sense. For all symmetrical constituents it is clear that ∑(xrt‾r+trx‾r) is zero. For those that do not contain t‾1…t‾n, it is further clear that x‾1…x‾n is zero too, so that E=ϕ‾E′=Σtr(ϕ),w=∑tr(ϕ)∑tr(ϕ)−ϕ‾. For the compartments whose x-factor is found in ϕ, the right-hand side of this equation becomes 1; for those whose x-factor is found in ϕ‾, it becomes 0. So the coefficients of the symmetrical compartments not containing t‾1…t‾n will be 1 when the x-factor is found in ϕ, and 0 when the x-factor is not found in ϕ.

Last, take the compartments that are unsymmetrical with respect to the two sets of symbols, and that do not contain t‾1…t‾n.

Here it is clear that neither E nor E′ can be zero, so the top of the fraction that gives w in (8) must be larger than the bottom. So that value cannot be 1, 0, or 00. In the logical development, then, it must be represented by 10, the mark of a compartment that cannot occur. That, then, is the coefficient of this class of compartments.

15. So the final logical equation, which gives w as a developed logical function of x1,…xn, t1,…tn, will be of the form w=∑1(XT)+0{∑2(XT)+t‾1…t‾n}+10(sum of other constituents),(9) where ∑1(XT) stands for the sum of all symmetrical compartments whose factor X is found in ϕ, and ∑2(XT) for the sum of all symmetrical compartments whose factor X is not found in ϕ. In either case the constituent x‾1…x‾nt‾1…t‾n, if it appears, is thrown out.

Now we pass from logic to algebra. Notice that here, and in all similar cases, the function V, from which we form the algebraic system of equations that determines the values of x1,…xn,t1…tn, does not depend on the nature of any function ϕ that enters not into the data but only into the quæsitum of the problem. The combination we ask about changes the top of the answer, but not the equations that fix the unknowns. So in the present example we have Prob. w=∑1(XT)V,wherein V=∑1(XT)+∑2(XT)+t‾1…t‾n=∑(XT)+t‾1…t‾n.(10) Here ∑(XT) stands for the sum of all symmetrical compartments of the x and t symbols, except the constituent x‾1…x‾n,t‾1…t‾n. This value of V is the same as the one in effect used in solving the last problem, so we can make use of the results found there.

If, then, as in that solution, we put x1t1x‾1t‾1=m1,xntnx‾nt‾n=mn,x1x‾1=n1, &c., we shall get a result that can be written like this: Prob. w=M1M+N−1,(11) where M1 is formed as follows. Throw out of the function ϕ the constituent x‾1…x‾n, if it is there; divide the result by that same constituent x‾1…x‾n; and then change x1x‾1 into m1, x2x‾2 into m2, and so on. The values of M and N are the same as in the last problem. Going back to these, and to the values of m1, m2, &c. that belong with them, we find Prob. w=M1(μ+ν−1), the general values of mr, nr being mr=crprμ−crpr,nr=cr(1−pr)ν−cr(1−pr), and μ and ν being given by solving the system of equations, μ+ν−1=(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)μn−1={ν−c1(1−p1)}…{ν−cn(1−pn)}νn−1. This value of Prob. w is the top of the fraction (2). It remains to find its bottom, the probability of the combination itself.

For this, put ϕ(x1,x2…xn)=v, or ϕ=v; which brings the form ϕv‾+vϕ‾=0.

Put the left-hand side of this equation into (7), in place of the corresponding expression ϕzw‾+w(1−ϕz), and we get as the primary logical equation ∑{xrzt‾r+tr(1−xrz)}+x‾1…x‾nz+ϕv‾+vϕ‾=0, and from this, eliminating z and reducing by Prop. II. Chap. IX., ϕv‾+vϕ‾+∑tr{∑(xrt‾r+trx‾r)+x‾1…x‾n}=0. So v=ϕ+∑tr{∑(xrt‾r+trx‾r)+x‾1…x‾n}2ϕ−1 and developing as before, v=∑1(XT)+t‾1…t‾n∑1(X)+0{∑2(XT)+t‾1…t‾n∑2(X)}+10(sum of other constituents).(12)

Here ∑1(X) stands for the sum of all the compartments found in ϕ, and ∑2(X) for the sum of all the compartments not found in ϕ. These expressions are used in place of ϕ and 1−ϕ only to keep the symmetry.

It follows that ∑1(X)+∑2(X)=1, and, as before, that ∑1(XT)+∑2(XT)=∑(XT). So V will have the same value as before, and we shall have Prob. v=∑1(XT)+t‾1…t‾n∑1(X)V, or, transforming as in the previous case, Prob. v=M1+N1M+N−1,(13) where N1 is formed by dividing ϕ by x‾1…x‾n, and in the result changing x1x‾1 into n1, x2x‾2 into n2, &c.

Now the final solution of the problem is found by giving their values, now determined, to the two terms of the fraction Prob. ϕ(x1,…xn)zProb. ϕ(x1,…xn),orProb. wProb. v. So, by (11) and (13), the common bottom M + N − 1 cancels, and we have Prob. sought=M1M1+N1

A very little attention to how the functions M1 and N1 are formed will show that the process can be made much simpler. In fact we can set out the solution of the general problem as a rule, as follows:

Throw out of the function ϕ(x1,x2…xn) the constituent x‾1…x‾n, if it is in it. In all the remaining compartments, strike out the factors x‾1, x‾2, &c., and in the result change every xr into crprμ−crpr. Call this result M1.

Again, in the function ϕ(x1,x2…xn), replace the constituent x‾1…x‾n, if it is there, by unity. In all the remaining compartments strike out the factors x‾1, x‾2, &c., and in the result change every xr into cr(1−pr)ν−cr(1−pr). Call this result N1.

Then the solution required will be given by the formula M1M1+N1,(14) where μ and ν are found by solving the system of equations μ+ν−1=(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)μn−1={ν−c1(1−p1)}…{ν−cn(1−pn)}νn−1.(15)

We may add that the limits of μ and ν are the same as in the last problem. This could be inferred from the general principle of continuity. But conditions of limitation, which are probably enough, can also be established in other ways.

Thus, from the proof of the general method in probabilities, Chap. XVII. Prop. IV., it appears that the quantities x1,…xn,t1,…tn in the primary system of algebraic equations must be positive proper fractions, numbers between 0 and 1, as probabilities are. Now xr1−xr=nr=cr(1−pr)ν−cr(1−pr). So in general nr must be a positive quantity, and therefore we must have ν>=cr(1−pr). That is, ν is at least as large as each quantity c times one minus p. In the same way, since we have xrtr(1−xr)(1−tr)=mr=crprμ−crpr, we must have in general μ>=crpr.

16. These two classes of conditions are probably enough, taken together, to settle in general which roots of the equations for μ and ν are to be taken. Let us take in particular the case where n=2. Here we have μ+ν−1=(μ−c1p1)(μ−c2p2)μ=μ−(c1p1+c2p2)+c1p1c2p2μ,∴ν=1−c1p1−c2p2+c1p1c2p2μ=1−c1p1−(μ−c1p1)c2p2μ. So, since μ>=c1p1, the last fraction cannot be negative, and we have in general ν<=1−c1p1. In the same way we have ν<=1−c2p2,μ<=1−c1(1−p1),μ<=1−c2(1−p2).

Now it has already been shown that only one value of μ satisfies all the conditions above that concern that quantity, namely μ>=crpr,μ<=1−cr(1−pr), so the solution in this case, at least, is determinate: there is just one answer. And I believe the same method applies, and is enough, in general. But this is a question on which more light would be welcome.

To check the results above, suppose ϕ(x1,…xn)=1: the "combination" is any combination at all, which is in effect the case of the last problem. Now the development of 1 gives all possible compartments of the symbols x1,…xn. Following the Rule, then, we find M1=μn(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)−1=μμ+ν−1−1 by (15).N1=νn{ν−c1(1−p1)}…{ν−cn(1−pn)}−1=νμ+ν−1−1. Putting these into (14), we find Prob. z=1−ν, which agrees with the earlier solution.

Again, let ϕ(x1,…xn)=x1, the case where we know only that the first cause is present. After development and striking out the factors x‾2,…x‾n, this gives x1(x2+1)…(xn+1), and so we find M1=c1p1μn−1(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)=c1p1μ+ν−1 by (15).N1=c1(1−p1)νn−1{ν−c1(1−p1)}…{ν−cn(1−pn)}=c1(1−p1)μ+ν−1. Putting these in, we have Probability that if the event A1 occur, E will occur=p1. And this result is confirmed by the data, which gave exactly this probability. Similar checks could easily be added.

Let us look at the case where ϕ(x1,…xn)=x1x‾2…x‾n+x2x‾1x‾3…x‾n…+xnx‾1…x‾n−1. That is, exactly one of the causes is present. Here we find M1=c1p1μ−c1p1…+cnpnμ−cnpn,N1=c1(1−p1)ν−c1(1−p1)…+cn(1−pn)ν−cn(1−pn); and so we have the following result: Probability that if some onealone of the causes A1,A2…Anpresent itself, the event Ewill follow.}=∑crprμ−crpr∑{crprμ−crpr}+∑cr(1−pr)ν−cr(1−pr)

Notice that this case is quite different from the well-known one in which the fact that the causes A1,…An exclude one another is part of the data. There, it is a condition under which the very observations that fixed the probabilities of A1,A2, &c. were made. Here, the causes may in general occur together, and we only ask what follows on the occasions when just one of them happens to be present.

Last, take the case where ϕ(x1,…xn)=x1x2…xn, that is, where all the causes are present together. Here M1=c1p1…cnpn(μ−c1p1)…(μ−cnpn)=c1p1…cnpnμn−1(μ+ν−1),N1=c1(1−p1)…cn(1−pn){ν−c1(1−p1)}…{ν−cn(1−pn)}=c1(1−p1)…cn(1−pn)νn−1(μ+ν−1). So we have the following result: Probability that if all thecauses A1,…Anconspire, the event E will follow.}=p1…pnνn−1p1…pnνn−1+(1−p1)…(1−pn)μn−1. This expression takes the value 1, as it ought to, when any one of the quantities p1,…pn is equal to 1. If one of the causes present always brings the event, the event is certain.

17. Problem VIII.—Certain causes A1,A2,…An are so restricted that they cannot all fail, and yet can occur only in certain definite combinations, expressed by the equation ϕ(A1,A2…An)=1, and we are given the separate probabilities c1,…cn of these causes, and the corresponding probabilities p1,…pn that an event E will follow if each of them is realized. Required the probability of the event E.

This problem differs from the last one in several ways, but chiefly in this. The restriction expressed by the equation ϕ(A1,…An)=1 is one of the data. It is supposed to be supplied by, or at least to agree with, the very experience from which we learned the numbers in the problem.

Represent the events A1,…An by x1,…xn respectively, and the event E by z. We have Prob. xr=cr,Prob. xrz=crpr.(1) Let us put, in general, xrz=tr, and then combine the system of equations this stands for with the equations x‾1…x‾n=0,ϕ(x1,…xn)=1,or ϕ=1, given in the data: the first says the causes cannot all fail, the second that they occur only in the allowed combinations. In the end we find, as the developed expression of z, z=∑(XT)+0t‾1t‾2…t‾n∑(X),(2) where X stands in turn for each compartment found in ϕ, and T for a matching series of compartments of the symbols t1,…tn; ∑(XT) includes only compartments that are symmetrical with respect to the two sets of symbols.

The method of reduction needed here is so like the one already shown in earlier problems that I shall only set out the results it leads to. We find Prob. z=MM+N(3) with the relations M1c1p1…=Mncnpn=N1c1(1−p1)=Nncn(1−pn)=M+N.(4) Here M is formed by striking out in ϕ(x1,…xn) all the factors x‾1,…x‾n, and changing in the result x1 into m1, xn into mn, and so on; while N is formed by putting into M, n1 for m1, &c. Further, M1 is the part of M that has m1 as a factor, N1 the part of N that has n1 as a factor, and so on.

As an illustration, take the particular case where the causes A1…An exclude one another. Here we have ϕ(x1,…xn)=x1x‾2…x‾n…+xnx‾1…x‾n−1. So M=m1+m2…+mn,N=n1+n2…+nn,M1=m1,N1=n1, &c. Putting these in, we have m1c1p1…=mncnpn=n1c1(1−p1)…=nncn(1−pn)=M+N. Adding the tops and the bottoms of the first set of these equal fractions, we find m1+m2…+mnc1p1+c2p2…+cnpn=M+N, or Mc1p1…+cnpn=M+N. So, by (3), Prob. z=c1p1…+cnpn, a known result: when the causes exclude one another, the chance of the event is the sum of the chances that each cause occurs and brings it.

There are other particular cases in which the system (4) can be solved readily. It is plain, though, that in most cases it would lead to very complicated results. Nor does it seem likely that actual experience will often present a functional relation among causes of the kind assumed in the data of the general problem, except in the particular cases discussed above.

Suppose the general problem had been changed. Instead of the restriction that the causes cannot all fail, suppose the restriction were that the event E cannot occur when all the causes A1…An are absent, the other condition, expressed by the equation ϕ(A1,…An)=1, being kept. Then we should have found as the final logical equation z=∑1(XT)+0∑(X), ∑(X) being, as before, equal to ϕ(x1,…xn), but ∑1(XT) being formed by throwing out of ϕ the particular constituent x1‾…xn‾, if it is there, and then multiplying each x-compartment of the result by the matching t-compartment. It is plain that in the particular case where the causes exclude one another, the value of Prob. z found from this will be the same as before.

18. Problem IX.—Assuming the data of any of the previous problems, let it be required to find the probability that, if the event E presents itself, it will be found together with the particular cause Ar; in other words, to find the à posteriori probability of the cause Ar once the event E has been observed to occur. This is the question of reasoning backward, from an effect to its likeliest cause.

In this case we must find the value of the fraction Prob. xrzProb. z, or crprProb. z, by the data.(1) The top of this fraction is given in the data. In the previous problems the value of Prob. z has been found under different hypotheses about the connection, or lack of connection, among the causes. So it is clear that in all those cases the present problem can be solved definitely, simply by putting into (1) the value of that quantity found there.

If the à priori probabilities of the causes are equal, we have c1=c2…=cr. Then, for the different causes, the value (1) will vary in direct proportion to the quantity pr. Therefore, whatever the nature of the connection among the causes, the à posteriori probability of each cause will be proportional to the probability of the observed event E when that cause is known to exist. The particular case of this theorem in which the causes exclude one another is well known. We then have Prob. xrzProb. z=crpr∑crpr=prp1+p2…+pn, the values of c1,…cn being equal.

In the particular case where the causes exclude one another, we need not bring in the functional symbol ϕ to prove these and similar theorems; and to bring it in is in fact to claim for ourselves the choice of every possible and conceivable hypothesis about how the causes are connected. Even so, in whatever form it is used, the method of this work, applied to problems where the number of data is indefinitely large, must always be somewhat complex. Its orderly unfolding of a problem, first of its logical relations and second of its numerical ones, may or may not make up for the length and the occasional tediousness of its processes; I do not presume to judge. Its chief value is surely its power: the mastery it gives us over questions that would apparently baffle the unaided strength of human reason. For this reason I have not thought it needless to show in this chapter how it applies to problems, some of which may perhaps be found off-putting because of their difficulty, with no prospect of immediate use to recommend them. What further value such inquiries may have, I believe it is impossible for us at present to judge with any confidence.

19. The next problem is much easier to describe than the ones before it.

Problem X.—The probability that a certain natural phenomenon occurs under given circumstances is p. Observation has also recorded a probability a that there exists a permanent cause of that phenomenon, that is, a cause which would always produce the event under the circumstances supposed. If the phenomenon is observed to occur n times in a row under the given circumstances, what is the probability that it will occur the n+1th time? And what, after such observation, is the probability that the permanent cause exists?

First Case.—Let t stand for the existence of a permanent cause, and x1,x2…xn+1 for the successive occurrences of the natural phenomenon.

If the permanent cause exists, the events x1,x2…xn+1 follow from it necessarily. So t=vx1,t=vx2, &c., which says that the cases of the cause are some of the cases of each occurrence. Eliminating the indefinite symbols, we get t(1−x1)=0,t(1−x2)=0,t(1−xn+1)=0. that is, there is no case in which the cause is present and an occurrence fails. Now we are looking for the probability that if the combination x1x2…xn happens, the event xn+1 will happen. In other words, we are looking for the value of the fraction Prob. x1x2…xn+1Prob. x1x2…xn. (the probability of n + 1 occurrences in a row, divided by the probability of n in a row).

We will first find the value of Prob. x1x2…xn. Represent the combination x1x2…xn by w. Then we have the following logical equations: t(1−x1)=0,t(1−x2)=0,…t(1−xn)=0,x1x2…xn=w. Bring the last of these into the form (x1x2…xn)(1−w)+w(1−x1x2…xn)=0, and add it to the others. We get ∑t(1−xi)+x1x2…xn(1−w)+w(1−x1x2…xn)=0,(1) where ∑ runs over all values of i from 1 to n. This is the single logical equation of the data. With it we must join the numerical conditions, Prob. x1= Prob. x2…= Prob. xn=p,Prob. t=a; and our aim is to find the probability of w.

From (1) we have w=∑t(1−xi)+x1x2…xn2x1x2…xn−1=∑(1−xi)+x1x2…xn2x1x2…xn−1t+x1x2…xn2x1x2…xn−1(1−t),(2) after developing with respect to t. This result must now be developed further, with respect to x1,x2,…xn.

If we put x1=1,x2=1,…xn=1, the coefficients of both t and 1−t become 1. If we give the same symbols any other set of values made up of 0s and 1s, the coefficient of t plainly becomes negative, while that of 1−t becomes 0. So the full development of (2) will be w=x1x2…xnt+x1x2…xn(1−t)+0(1−x1x2…xn)(1−t)+ constituents whose coefficients are 10, or equivalent to10. Read aloud: w happens whenever all n occurrences happen, cause or no cause; it does not happen when the cause is absent and the occurrences are not all present; and every other case, such as the cause present with some occurrence failing, is impossible. Here we have V=x1x2…xnt+x1x2…xn(1−t)+(1−x1x2…xn)(1−t)=x1x2…xnt+1−t; (the sum of the constituents that can actually happen), and so, passing from logic to algebra, x1x2…xnt+x1(1−t)p=x1x2…xnt+x2(1−t)p…=x1x2…xnt+xn(1−t)p=x1x2…xnta=x1x2…xnt+1−t.Prob. w=x1x2…xnx1x2…xnt+1−t.

The form of these equations makes it clear that x1=x2…=xn: nothing in them tells one occurrence apart from another. So replace each of these quantities by x, and the system becomes xnt+(1−t)xp=xnta=xnt+1−t,Prob. w=xnxnt+1−t; from which we easily find Prob. w= Prob. x1x2…xn=a+(p−a)(p−a1−a)n−1 If in this result we change n into n+1, we get Prob. x1x2…xn+1=a+(p−a)(p−a1−a)n So we find Prob. x1x2…xn+1Prob. x1x2…xn=a+(p−a)(p−a1−a)na+(p−a)(p−a1−a)n−1(3) as the probability that if the phenomenon has occurred n times, it will also appear the n+1th time. By the method of Chapter XIX. we find that a cannot be larger than p: the chance of a cause that always produces the event cannot exceed the chance of the event itself.

The following checks are obvious.

First, if a=0, the expression reduces to p, as it should. For when it is certain that no permanent cause exists, the successive occurrences of the phenomenon are independent of one another.

Second, if p=1, the expression becomes 1, as it should.

Third, if p=a, the expression becomes 1, unless a=0. Suppose the probability of a phenomenon equals the probability that there exists a cause which, under given circumstances, would always produce it. Then the mere fact that the phenomenon has ever been seen under those circumstances makes it certain that it will appear again under the same ones.

Fourth, as n grows, the expression comes closer and closer to 1. This shows that the probability of the event recurring grows with the number of times it has appeared in succession, a result that agrees with the natural laws of expectation.26

Second Case.—We now want the probability à posteriori that a permanent cause of the phenomenon exists. For this we must find the value of the fraction Prob. tx1x2…xnProb. x1x2…xn (the probability that the cause exists and the n occurrences happen, divided by the probability of the n occurrences), whose denominator we have already found.

To find the numerator, put tx1x2…xn=w, then, going on as before, we get the logical development w=tx1x2…xn+0(1−t). So, passing from logic to algebra, we have at once Prob. w=a, a result we might have foreseen, since when the cause exists the occurrences follow of themselves. Putting these values in for the numerator and denominator of the fraction above, we get the à posteriori probability of a permanent cause: aa+(p−a)(p−a1−a)n−1. Clearly this expression grows as n grows.

I owe to a learned correspondent, whose original contributions to the theory of probability I have mentioned before, the following check of the first of the results above, (3).27

“The whole à priori probability of the event (under the circumstances) being p, and the probability of some cause C which would necessarily produce it, a, let x be the probability that it will happen if no such cause as C exist. Then we have the equation p=a+(1−a)x, whence x=p−a1−a. Now the phænomenon observed is the occurrence of the event n times. The à priori probability of this would be— 1 supposing C to exist,xn supposing C not to exist; whence the à posteriori probability that C exists is aa+(1−a)xn, that C does not exist is (1−a)xna+(1−a)xn. Consequently the probability of another occurrence is aa+(1−a)xn×1+(1−a)xna+(1−a)xn×x, or a+(1−a)xn+1a+(1−a)xn, which, on replacing x by its value p−a1−a, will be found to agree with (3)."

Similar checks could probably be found for the following results too, which were obtained by applying the general method directly.

Under the same circumstances, suppose that out of n occasions the event has happened r times and failed n−r times. The probability that it will happen on the n+1th occasion is a+m(p−a)(p−la1−a)ra+m(p−la)(p−la1−a)r−1 where m=n(n−1)…n−r+11⋅2…r and l=rn.

The probability of a permanent cause (with r less than n) is 0. This is easy to check: a cause that always produces the event cannot exist once the event has failed even once.

Let p be the probability of an event, and c the probability that if it occurs, it will be due to a permanent cause. Then the probability, after n occurrences observed in a row, that it will recur on the n+1th similar occasion is c+(1−c)xnc+(1−c)xn−1, where x=p(1−c)1−cp.

20. It is remarkable that the solutions of the problems above contain no arbitrary element. Looking at the data, we would hardly have expected this. But notice that in all those problems the probabilities of the causes are supposed to be known à priori. Without that assumed piece of knowledge, it seems likely that arbitrary constants, numbers the data leave unfixed, would necessarily appear in the final solution. Some support for this remark comes from a class of problems that has drawn a good deal of attention, and which I shall briefly consider to close.

Astronomers have observed that the heavens contain a large number of double stars, pairs extremely close together. Either these apparent cases of connection have some physical basis or they do not. If they do not, we may regard a double star as the accidental result of a “random distribution" of stars over the sky: that is, a distribution that makes it just as likely for either member of the pair to appear in one spot as in another. If we assume this hypothesis, and if we know how many stars there are of the required brightness, we can work out the probability that two of them will be found close enough together to make the observed phenomenon. In this way Michell, estimating that there are 230 stars in the heavens as bright as β Capricorni, found that the odds are 80 to 1 against such a pair appearing if those stars were scattered at random. What is then required is the probability, once such a pair has been observed, that there is a physical connection between its members.28

Again, according to the French measurements, the sum of the inclinations of the orbits of the ten known planets to the plane of the ecliptic (the plane of the earth's orbit) in the year 1801 was 91∘⋅4187. Laplace works out that, if all inclinations were equally probable, there would be only the extremely small probability .00000011235 that the average of the inclinations would fall within the limit so set. From this he concludes that there is a very high probability in favour of a disposing cause, one that has kept the inclinations of the planets' orbits within such narrow bounds. Professor De Morgan, taking the sum of the inclinations as 92∘, gives the probability above the value .00000012, and infers that “it is 1:.00000012, that there was a necessary cause in the formation of the solar system for the inclinations being what they are." An equally definite conclusion has been drawn from observed agreements between the direction of circular polarization in rock-crystal (quartz, which twists light passing through it one way or the other) and the direction of certain slanting faces in its crystal structure.29,30,31

These problems are all alike. We frame a certain hypothesis, and we can assign, with perfect rigour, the probabilities of its various possible consequences. Now some actual observation turns out to be one of those consequences, and so its hypothetical probability, its probability if the hypothesis is true, is known. From this we are asked to find the probability of the hypothesis we assumed, or of its contrary. In Michell's problem the hypothesis is a “random distribution of the stars,"; the possible consequence, which has been observed, is a close double star. The very small probability of such a result is taken to mean that the probability of the hypothesis is equally small, or at least small to the same degree. And from this people infer a high probability, and, as some think, a definite one, that there is a disposing cause behind the arrangement of the stars. The same remarks apply to the other examples.

21. The general problem, in whatever form it is put, admits only an indefinite solution. Let x stand for the proposed hypothesis, and y for a phenomenon that might occur as one of its possible consequences, whose probability, calculated on the assumption that the hypothesis is true, is p. We are asked for the probability that if the phenomenon y is observed, the hypothesis x is true. The very data of this problem cannot be written down without bringing in an arbitrary element. All we can write is Prob. x=a,Prob. xy=ap;(1) where a is entirely arbitrary, except that it must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. We know how likely the phenomenon is if the hypothesis holds; we are not told how likely the hypothesis was to begin with. If P stands for the conditional probability we want, then P=Prob. xyProb. y=apProb. y.(2) It remains to find Prob. y. Let xy=t; then y=tx=tx+10t(1−x)+0(1−t)x+00(1−t)(1−x).(3) Read aloud: y happens whenever t and x both happen; t without x is impossible; when x happens without t, y does not; and when neither happens, y may or may not. Now note that Prob. x=a and Prob. t=ap, and pass from logic to algebra. We have Prob. y=tx+c(1−t)xtx+1−t, with the relations tx+(1−t)xa=txap=tx+1−t.

From these we easily find Prob. y=ap+c(1−a).(4)

Now go back to (3). We find that c is the probability that if the event (1−t)(1−x) occurs, the event y will occur. But (1−t)(1−x)=(1−xy)(1−x)=1−x.

So c is the probability that if the event x does not occur, the event y will occur.

Putting this value of Prob. y into (2), we get the following theorem:

The calculated probability of any phenomenon y, on an assumed physical hypothesis x, being p, the à posteriori probability P of the physical hypothesis, once the phenomenon has been observed, is given by the equation P=apap+c(1−a),(5) where a and c are arbitrary constants. The first is the à priori probability of the hypothesis; the second is the probability that the event y would appear if the hypothesis were false.

The main conclusion to be drawn from this theorem is that, other things being equal, P rises and falls together with p. So the greater or smaller the probability of the phenomenon when the hypothesis is assumed, the greater or smaller the probability of the hypothesis when the phenomenon has been observed. When p is very small, P is generally small too, unless either a is large or c is small. This gives a second conclusion. If the probability of the phenomenon is very small when the hypothesis is assumed, then the probability of the hypothesis is very small when the phenomenon is observed, unless either the à priori probability a of the hypothesis is large, or the probability of the phenomenon on any other hypothesis is small.

Formula (5) can be checked exactly in various cases, for example when c=0, or a=1, or a=0. But plainly, unless we have some way of fixing the values of a and c, it does not give a definite value of P. Any solution that claims to give one is either wrong in principle or makes some unstated assumption about these arbitrary elements. Mr. De Morgan's solution of Laplace's problem, whether there is a determining cause behind the narrow limits that confine the inclinations of the planets' orbits to the plane of the ecliptic, seems to me to be of the second kind. He found a probability p=.00000012 that the sum of the inclinations would be less than 92∘ if all degrees of inclination were equally probable in each orbit. This able writer then remarks: “If there be a reason for the inclinations being as described, the probability of the event is 1. Consequently, it is 1:.00000012 (i.e. 1:p), that there was a necessary cause in the formation of the solar system for the inclinations being what they are.” Now this is exactly what equation (5) would give if, setting p at the value above, we assumed c=1, a=12. For we would then find P=12p12p+12=p1+p∴1−P:P::1:p.(6) (that is, one minus P is to P as 1 is to p).

Here P is the probability, à posteriori, that all inclinations are equally probable, so 1−P is the probability, à posteriori, that this is not so, or, taking Mr. De Morgan's alternative, that a determining cause exists. Equation (6) therefore agrees with Mr. De Morgan's result. His answer is definite only because he has, without saying so, given the two hypotheses equal chances to begin with, and supposed that a determining cause would make the observed result certain.

22. But are we entitled to give a and c particular values? I am strongly inclined to think we are not. The question matters less in this particular case than in where it leads. In the accepted applications of the theory of probability, arbitrary constants do not appear openly. But in the case above, and in many others approved by the highest authorities, some hidden fixing of their values has been attempted. This has given the results of the theory, especially on questions of causation, an air of definite precision. On the one hand, that precision has seemed to raise the power and widen the province of numbers even beyond their ancient claim to rule the world. On the other hand, it has provoked vigorous protests against their intrusion into regions where conjecture is the only basis for inference. When problems like these are treated by the method of this work, arbitrary constants appear in the solutions. That very fact seems to show that a definite solution is impossible, and to mark the point where inquiry ought to stop. We do have the means of interpreting those constants: each one is the probability of something we could learn only from experience. But the experience they point to is as far beyond our reach as the experience that would make any attempt at a solution unnecessary in the first place.32

Another difficulty attends these questions, one that is perhaps built into the very make-up of our faculties. It is the difficulty of defining exactly what we mean by Order. We have no trouble detecting the signs of order, except in very complicated cases, and we do not hesitate to credit it with an almost necessary basis in causes working under Law. But to assign it a standard of numerical value would be a vain, not to say presumptuous, undertaking. Yet the attempt must be made before we can hope to weigh accurately the probabilities of different possible constitutions of the universe, and so fix the elements on which alone a definite solution of these problems could rest.33

23. The most common way of trying to escape the necessary arbitrariness in the solution of probability problems that rest on insufficient data goes like this. Take some element whose real probability is unknown, and give it every possible degree of probability. Suppose that these degrees of probability are themselves equally probable. Then treat them as so many distinct causes of the observed phenomenon, and apply the theorems that cover an effect due to one of a number of equally probable causes that exclude one another (Problem 9). For instance, suppose the sun has been observed to rise after a certain interval of darkness m times in a row. On the accepted principles, the probability that it will rise again under the same circumstances is worked out as follows. Let p be any unknown probability between 0 and 1, and let c (infinitesimal and constant) be the probability that the probability of the sun's rising after an interval of darkness lies between the limits p and p+dp. (So every possible value of the sun's chance of rising is treated as equally likely.) Then the probability that the sun will rise m times in a row is c∫01pmdp; and the probability that he will do this and then rise again, which is the same thing as rising m+1 times in a row, is c∫01pm+1dp, So the probability that if he rises m times in a row, he will rise the m+1th time, is c∫01pm+1dpc∫01pmdp=m+1m+2, the known and generally accepted solution.

This solution usually rests on a supposed likeness between the problem and that of drawing balls from an urn holding a mixture of black and white balls, where every possible ratio between the numbers of the two colours is assumed to be equally probable. And it is remarkable that two or three different hypotheses lead to the same final result. Suppose, for instance, that the balls are finite in number and those drawn are not put back; or that they are infinite in number, whether those drawn are put back or not. Then, if m drawings in a row have produced only white balls, the probability of a white ball at the m+1th drawing is m+1m+2.34

It has been said that the principle behind this and similar applications is the equal distribution of our knowledge, or rather of our ignorance: we assign equal degrees of probability to different states of things we know nothing about, and on the very ground that we know nothing about them. I believe, however, that this is an arbitrary way to proceed. Cases may occur, and one has just been given, in which different hypotheses lead to the same final conclusion. But those cases are exceptions. For this very problem, the memoir cited shows that one hypothesis, namely that the balls are finite in number and not put back, leads to a different conclusion. And it is easy to see that there are other hypotheses, which follow the principle of the “equal distribution of knowledge or ignorance” just as strictly, and which would also lead to conflicting results.

24. For instance, let a sunrise be represented by drawing a white ball from a bag holding an infinite number of balls, each either black or white. And let the principle assumed be that all possible constitutions of the system of balls are equally probable. By a constitution of the system I mean an arrangement that gives every ball in the system a definite colour, black or white. Let us then look for the probability that if m white balls are drawn in m drawings, a white ball will be drawn in the m+1th drawing.

First, suppose there are μ balls, and assign the symbols x1,x2,…xμ to them as follows. Let xi stand for the event that the ith ball of the system is white; the proposition that says this is so is xi=1. In the same way the compound symbol 1−xi stands for the ith ball being black. Clearly the constituents formed from the whole set of symbols x1,x2,…xμ then stand for the possible constitutions of the system of balls, as to black and white. There are 2μ such constitutions, so, by the hypothesis, the probability of each will be 12μ. This is the value we would get if, in the expression for any constituent, we put for each of the symbols x1,x2,…xμ the value 12. So the probability of any event that can be written as a series of such constituents will be found by putting the value 12 for each of these symbols in that expression.

Now the larger μ is, the less likely it is that a ball which has been drawn and put back will be drawn again. As μ approaches infinity, this probability approaches 0.
