That being so, the state of the balls actually drawn can be written as a logical function of m of the symbols x1,x2,…xμ, and therefore, by development, as a series of constituents of those m symbols. So its probability will be found by putting the value 12 for each of the symbols, whether in the undeveloped or the developed form. But this is exactly the substitution we would need to make, and all we would need to make, if we knew à priori that the probability of a white ball at each drawing was 12.

It follows that if the number of balls is infinite, and all constitutions of the system are equally probable, the probability of drawing m white balls in a row will be 12m, and the probability of drawing m+1 white balls in a row 12m+1; so the probability that, after m white balls have been drawn, the next drawing will give a white one will be 12. In other words, in this case past experience does not affect future expectation at all. The same principle of evenly spread ignorance, applied to constitutions of the bag instead of to proportions of colours, gives an answer of one half, not the rule above.

25. It may be satisfying to check this result by ordinary methods. To do so, we shall find:

First: The probability of drawing r white balls and p−r black balls in p trials, from a bag holding μ balls, each ball being put back after it is drawn, and all constitutions of the system being equally probable à priori.

Second: The value this probability takes when μ becomes infinite.

Third: The probability that follows from this, that if m white balls are drawn in a row, the m+1th ball drawn will be white too.

Take the probability that r white balls and p−r black ones will be drawn in p trials from an urn holding μ balls, each ball put back after each trial, and all constitutions of the system, as defined above, equally probable. It equals the sum of the probabilities of the same result on the separate hypotheses that there are no white balls in the urn, 1 white ball, and so on up to μ white balls. So it is the sum of the probabilities of this result on the hypothesis that there are n white balls, with n running from 0 to μ.

Now suppose there are n white balls. The probability of drawing a white ball in a single drawing is nμ, and the probability of drawing r white balls and p−r black ones in some particular order in p drawings is (nμ)r(1−nμ)p−r But there are as many such orders as there are ways of choosing r things out of p things. So the total probability of drawing r white balls in p drawings from the system of μ balls, of which n are white, is p(p−1)…(p−r+1)1⋅2…r(nμ)r(1−nμ)p−r(1) Again, the number of constitutions of the system of μ balls in which exactly n balls are white is μ(μ−1)…(μ−n+1)1⋅2…n, and the number of possible constitutions of the system is 2μ. So the probability that exactly n balls are white is μ(μ−1)…(μ−n+1)1⋅2…n2μ, Multiplying (1) by this expression, and adding up the products from n=0 to n=μ, we get p(p−1)…p−r+11⋅2…r∑n=0n=μμ(μ−1)…(μ−n+1)1⋅2…n2μ(nμ)r(1−nμ)p−r,(2) as the total probability that, from a system of μ balls whose constitutions are all equally probable, r white balls will come out in p drawings. Now ∑n=0n=μμ(μ−1)…(μ−n+1)1⋅2…n⋅2μ(nμ)r(1−nμ)p−r=∑n=0n=μμ(μ−1)…(μ−n+1)1⋅2…n2μ(nμ)r(1−nμ)p−rεnθ…(θ=0)=12μ(Dμ)r(1−Dμ)p−r∑n=0n=μμ(μ−1)…(μ−n+1)1⋅2…nεnθ=12μ(Dμ)r(1−Dμ)p−r(1+εθ)μ,(3) where D stands for the symbol ddθ, so that ϕ(D)εnθ=ϕ(n)εnθ. (The trick is this: multiplying each term by the exponential, which equals 1 when theta is 0, lets the powers of n be produced by differentiating, and then the sum can be done all at once by the binomial theorem.) But by a known theorem, tm=1+Δ0mt+Δ20m1⋅2t(t−1)+Δ30m1⋅2⋅3t(t−1)(t−2).∴Dm(1+εθ)μ={1+Δ0mD+Δ20m1⋅2D(D−1)+ &c.}(1+εθ)μ. On the right-hand side let εθ=x; then Dm(1+εθ)μ=(1+Δ0mxddx+Δ20m1⋅2x2d2dx2+ &c.)(1+x)μ, since D(D−1)…(D−i+1)=xi(ddx)i.

On the right-hand side of this equation, carry out the differentiations and put x=1 (since θ=0). We get Dm(1+εθ)μ=μ(Δ0m)2μ−1+μ(μ−1)1⋅2(Δ20m)2μ−2+ &c. The last term on the right-hand side of this equation will be μ(μ−1)…(μ−m+1)Δm0m1⋅2…m2μ−m=μ(μ−1)…(μ−m+1)2μ−m; since Δm0m=1⋅2…m. When μ is large, this term is bigger than all the others, and as μ approaches infinity it becomes infinitely great compared with them. And since, moreover, it takes the form μm2μ−m, we have, passing to the limit, Dm(1+εθ)μ=μm2μ−m=(μ2)m2μ. So if ϕ(D) stands for any function of the symbol D that can be expanded in a series of rising powers of D, we have ϕ(D)(1+εθ)μ=ϕ(μ2)2μ,(4) if θ=0 and μ=∞. Strictly speaking, this means that the ratio of the two sides of the equation above comes closer and closer to equality as μ increases towards infinity, θ being equal to 0. In words: when the bag is enormous, every D may simply be replaced by half the number of balls.

By means of this theorem, the last line of (3) reduces to the form 12μ(12)r(1−12)p−r2μ=(12)p. So (2) gives p(p−1)…(p−r+1)1⋅2…r(12)p, as the probability that, from an urn holding an infinite number of black and white balls, all constitutions of the system being equally probable, r white balls will come out in p drawings. This is exactly what we would get if each ball drawn were as likely to be white as black.

So, putting p=m, r=m, the probability that all the balls in m drawings will be white is (12)m, and the probability that this will happen and that the m+1th drawing will also give a white ball is (12)m+1. So the probability that, if the first m drawings give only white balls, the m+1th drawing will also give a white ball, is (12)m+1÷(12)m=12; and in general, any proposed result will have the same probability as if it were an even chance whether each drawing gave a white ball or a black one. This agrees with the conclusion we reached before.

26. These results only illustrate one fact: when hypothesis is used to make up for missing data, the solutions will in general vary with the hypotheses assumed. So the question remains, only in a sharper form, whether the principles of the theory of probability can guide us in choosing such hypotheses. I have already said that I am convinced they cannot, and other reasons besides those given above strengthen that conviction. Here is one. Sometimes, when the method of this work has given a definite solution of a problem, the same method also gives an equally definite solution when one of the data, say Prob. x=p1 is left out. But I have not been able to find any way of deriving the second solution from the first by integration with respect to p, taken as varying within the limits fixed by Chap. XIX. Yet, I believe, this derivation would be possible if the principle discussed in Art. 23 were valid. Still, it is with some hesitation that I differ on these points from mathematicians in general, and above all from the English writer who has entered most fully into the spirit and methods of Laplace. And I venture to hope that a question second in importance to none in the theory of probability will receive the careful attention it deserves.

Editor's note: The rule Boole examines here, that after m sunrises the chance of another is m plus one over m plus two, is Laplace's "rule of succession". The question behind Boole's objection, whether ignorance can be expressed by spreading probability evenly over the possibilities, is the question of "prior probabilities", and it still divides statisticians. Bayesian methods assign such priors, often in Laplace's way, while others, like Boole, refuse to assign them unless the evidence supplies them. His bag of balls shows why the choice matters: spreading ignorance evenly over the proportions of colours gives Laplace's rule, while spreading it evenly over the colours of the individual balls gives an answer that experience never changes.

  1. It is easy to imagine how experience might supply data like these. Opposite the window of the room where I write there is a field that can be flooded from two causes, distinct from each other but able to act together: floods from the upper sources of the River Lee, and tides from the ocean. Suppose that observations made on N separate occasions have given these results. On A occasions the river was swollen by freshets (sudden rises from rain or melting snow), and on P of those occasions the field was flooded, whether from this cause or not. On B occasions the river was swollen by the tide, and on Q of those occasions the field was flooded, whether from this cause or not. Suppose, then, that the field cannot be flooded when both these causes are absent, and that we are asked to find the total probability that it will be flooded. Here the elements a, b, p, q of the general problem stand for the ratios AN,PA,BN,QB, or rather for the values those ratios approach as the number N is increased without end. ↩

  2. The numerator was originally “(a−1)b−1)(a+b−2)…”, and was fixed in 2004 by Distributed Proofreaders. ↩

  3. It may be proper to mention that I put the above problem before mathematicians in the Cambridge and Dublin Mathematical Journal, Nov. 1851, with the following remarks: “The motives which have led me, after much consideration, to adopt, with reference to this question, a course unusual in the present day, and not upon slight grounds to be revived, are the following:—First, I propose the question as a test of the sufficiency of received methods. Secondly, I anticipate that its discussion will in some measure add to our knowledge of an important branch of pure analysis. However, it is upon the former of these grounds alone that I desire to rest my apology. “While hoping that some may be found who, without departing from the line of their previous studies, may deem this question worthy of their attention, I wholly disclaim the notion of its being offered as a trial of personal skill or knowledge, but desire that it may be viewed solely with reference to those public and scientific ends for the sake of which alone it is proposed.” I think it right to add that publishing the problem led to some interesting private correspondence, but did not bring out a solution. ↩

  4. Since we can neither go back into infancy nor remember it, we cannot say how far results like the one above explain the confidence with which young children link events they have once seen together. But we may guess, in general, that the strength of their expectations comes from two things: the need to draw inferences, which is part of their rational nature, and the narrow but vivid experience on which that faculty works. Hence their habit of treating every kind of sequence as cause and effect. A little friend of mine, on being put to bed, was heard to ask his brother the pertinent question, "Why does going to sleep at night make it light in the morning?" The brother, who was a year older, was able to answer that it would be light in the morning even if little boys did not go to sleep at night. ↩

Chapter 21: Probability of Judgments

1. I take it that the previous chapters have explained well enough this treatise's general method for solving questions in the theory of probability. Here I propose to take up one of its practical applications, chosen from the wide field of social statistics: namely, estimating the probability of judgments. Judged by its immediate results, this application is perhaps not the best I could have chosen. One of the first conclusions it leads to is that any data experience alone can give us are necessarily insufficient for the most important aim of the inquiry. But the method does all that properly lies within its scope. It sets clearly before us the necessity of hypotheses to supplement the data of experience, and it lets us deduce with rigour the consequences of any hypothesis we may adopt. It is also worth remarking that hypotheses are more justifiable in questions about the conduct of our own species than in questions like those at the close of the previous chapter. Our general experience of human nature comes to the aid of scanty and imperfect statistical records.

2. The elements that enter into problems about criminal trials (Boole's "criminal assize", the courts where serious crimes were tried before a jury) are these:

First, the probability that a particular member of the jury will form a correct opinion on the case.

Second, the probability that the accused person is guilty.

Third, the probability that he will be condemned, or that he will be acquitted.

Fourth, the probability that his condemnation or acquittal will be just.

Fifth, the way the jury is made up: how many members it has, and what majority it needs.

Sixth, the data that experience supplies, such as the relative numbers of cases in which juries reached a unanimous decision, or reached particular majorities; the number of cases in which decisions were reversed by higher courts; and so on.

Again, the questions we are considering can be either direct or inverse. In the direct questions, we suppose we already know, à priori, the probability that each member of the court decides correctly, or the probability that the accused is guilty, and we seek the probability of a decision of a particular kind, or with a definite majority. In the inverse problems, we start from the data experience supplies and must find some element that cannot be observed directly, though it stands to those data as cause to effect. An example is finding, from the records of a court's decisions, the probability that a member of the court will judge correctly. This kind of problem is the most difficult and the most important of the whole series, and it is the one I shall chiefly attend to here.

3. The direct problems in the list above are not hard to solve. Suppose there is only one juryman. Let k be the probability that the accused person is guilty; x the probability that the juryman will form a correct opinion; X the probability that the accused person will be condemned. Then: kx= probability that the accused party is guilty, and that thejuryman judges him to be guilty.(1−k)(1−x)= probability that the accused person is inno-cent, and that the juryman pronounces him guilty.

These are the only two cases in which a verdict of guilty can be given: a guilty man rightly judged, or an innocent man wrongly judged. They also exclude one another. So we have X=kx+(1−k)(1−x).(1)

In the same way, suppose there are n jurymen, whose separate probabilities of judging correctly are x1,x2,…xn. The probability of a unanimous verdict of guilty will be X=kx1x2…xn+(1−k)(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn). In words: either the accused is guilty and every juryman judges rightly, or he is innocent and every juryman judges wrongly. So if the separate probabilities x1,x2…xn are all equal, and each is written x, we have X=kxn+(1−k)(1−x)n.(2) In this last case, the probability that the accused person is guilty, given a unanimous verdict against him, will be kxnkxn+(1−k)(1−x)n that is, the share of the unanimous convictions that are convictions of guilty men. All these results assume that the events whose probabilities are written k, x1, x2, and so on, are independent. As far as we are concerned, however, that assumption is contained in the fact that these events are the only ones whose probabilities are given.

The probability of a condemnation by a given number of votes can be found on the same principles. Suppose a jury of three persons, whose separate probabilities of deciding correctly are x, x′, x″. The probability X2 that the accused person will be declared guilty by two of them will be X2=k{xx′(1−x″)+xx″(1−x′)+x′x″(1−x)}+(1−k){(1−x)(1−x′)x″+(1−x)(1−x″)x′+(1−x′)(1−x″)x}, that is: either he is guilty and exactly two of the three judge rightly, or he is innocent and exactly two judge wrongly. If x=x′=x″, this reduces to 3kx2(1−x)+3(1−k)x(1−x)2.

By the same reasoning, let Xi be the probability that the accused person will be declared guilty by i votes, out of a jury of n persons whose separate probabilities of judging correctly are equal, and written x. Then Xi=n(n−1)…(n−i+1)1⋅2…i{kxi(1−x)n−i+(1−k)xn−i(1−x)i}.(3) The fraction in front counts the ways of choosing which i jurors vote guilty. Suppose we want the probability of condemnation by a definite majority a, that is, by a more votes for guilty than against. Then we simply have i−a=n−i, so that i=n+a2, and this must be put into the formula above. Of course a can only take values that make i a whole number. If n is even, those values are 0, 2, 4, and so on; if odd, 1, 3, 5, and so on, as is obvious anyway.

The probability of a condemnation by a majority of at least a given number of votes m is found by adding together the following probabilities, each found as above, namely:

First, the probability of a condemnation by an exact majority m;
Second, the probability of condemnation by the next greater majority m+2;

and so on, the last term of the series being the probability of a unanimous condemnation. So the probability of condemnation by a majority of at least 4 out of 12 jurors (that is, by at least 8 votes to 4) would be X8+X9…+X12, the values of these terms being given by (3), after putting n=12 in it.

4. Suppose that instead of a jury we are considering a simple deliberative assembly of n persons, each of whom judges correctly with probability x. Then the formulas above are replaced by others, made somewhat simpler by leaving out the quantity k, since there is no accused person whose guilt is in question.

The probability of a unanimous decision is X=xn+(1−x)n. In words, all are right or all are wrong.

The probability that i members out of the whole number agree is Xi=n(n−1)…(n−i+1)1⋅2…i{xi(1−x)n−i+xn−i(1−x)i}.(4)

There is no need to say more about investigations of this kind. Condorcet, Laplace, Poisson and other writers have pursued them a good way. In particular, they have worked out the methods of calculation and reduction needed when n and i are large numbers. Plainly the whole inquiry is highly speculative. The values of x and k cannot be found by direct observation. We can only presume that both must generally be greater than 12. We can presume that the first, x, the juror's chance of judging rightly, must rise as public intelligence advances. And the second, k, the chance that an accused person is guilty, must depend a great deal on the earlier steps in the working of the law, the steps by which people suspected of crime are brought before their country's courts. Poisson remarked that in times of revolution, as during the Reign of Terror in France, the value of k may fall far below 12, if political offences are counted. The history of Europe in days nearer our own would probably confirm this remark. It would show that the wild licence of democracy is not the only thing that brings the innocent to be accused.

Laplace assumes that all values of x from x=12, to x=1, are equally probable. He thus rules out the supposition that a juryman is more likely to be wrong than right. But within the limits to which the probability of an individual's judging correctly is confined, he assumes we have no reason to prefer one value of x to another. This hypothesis is entirely arbitrary, and it would be pointless to examine its consequences here.

Poisson seems to have been the first to try to infer the values of x and k from experience. In the six years from 1825 to 1830 inclusive, 11016 people were accused of crimes against the person before the courts of France, and 5286 were condemned. Each jury had 12 members, and the verdict was given by a simple majority. If we assume these numbers are large enough for estimating probabilities, the probability that an accused person would be condemned by a simple majority is the fraction 528611016, or .4782. So we should have the equation X7+X8…+X12=.4782,(5) that is, the chance of 7 or more votes for guilty, with the general expression for Xi given by (3) after putting n=12 in it. In 1831 the law was changed to require a majority of at least four for condemnation. That year 2046 people were tried for crimes against the person, and 743 were condemned. So the probability that a person would be condemned by that majority was 7432046, or .3631. So we should have X8+X9…+X12=.3631.(6)

Assume the values of k and x were the same in 1831 as in the six years before. Then the two equations (5) and (6) let us find their values approximately. In this way Poisson found k=.5354,x=.6786.

For crimes against property in the same periods, he found by a similar analysis k=.6744,x=.7771.

In each case, solving the system (5) (6) leads to two values of k and two values of x, one of each pair greater than 12 and the other less. It was assumed that in each case the larger value should be preferred, since it was thought more probable that an accused person is guilty than innocent, and more probable that a juryman forms a correct opinion on the evidence than a wrong one.

5. Poisson's data, especially those for the year 1831, are plainly too imperfect for us to put much confidence in these values of x and k. I introduce them here chiefly for the sake of the method. During the six years 1825-30, or any similar period, it would have been possible to record the number of condemnations given by each possible majority of votes. Had no reasons of policy forbidden it, the values of the several elements X8,X9,…X12 might then have been found accurately. This is where the idea of the general problem arises, of which Poisson's is a particular case. From this system of data, which seems to give more equations than there are unknowns, how are we to find the values of x and k? Poisson and every other writer on the subject adopted the hypothesis that the events whose probabilities are written x and k are absolutely independent. If we keep that hypothesis, we are led to a system of five equations of the type (3). Then we must either pick out of them whichever pair of equations seems most advantageous, or combine all the equations of the system by the method of least squares (the standard way of finding the values that fit a set of slightly inconsistent equations best). One might doubt whether the method of least squares strictly applies to such cases, especially if different chosen pairs of the equations gave very different values of x and k. M. Cournot has considered a somewhat similar problem. From the records of individual votes in a court of four judges, he sets out to find each judge's separate probability of a correct verdict. To find the elements x, x′, x″, x‴, he obtains eight equations, which he divides into two sets of four. He remarks that if the values of x, x′, x″, x‴ found from the two sets disagreed considerably, this might be taken as a sign that the hypothesis that the judges' opinions are independent did not hold in that particular case. The principle of this way of investigating was mentioned in (XVIII. 4).

6. I now apply the method of this treatise to the class of problems just described. I shall ask, first, whether the records of courts and deliberative assemblies can, alone, give any information about the probabilities that their individual members judge correctly. It will appear that they cannot. So I shall ask, second, what kind and amount of hypothesis, since some hypothesis is necessary, best suits the actual data.

Proposition I.

From the mere records of the decisions of a court or deliberative assembly, it is not possible to deduce any definite conclusion about the correctness of the individual judgments of its members.

This Proposition may seem to express only what plain good sense already tells us. Still, it is of some interest to show that it can be rigorously proved. Suppose a deliberative assembly of n members, and make no hypothesis at all about whether their judgments depend on one another or are independent. Use the logical symbols x1,x2,…xn according to the following definition. Let the general symbol xi stand for the event that the ith member, Ai, of the court gives a correct opinion. We shall treat the values of Prob. x1, Prob. x2,…Prob. xn, that is, each member's probability of being right, as the quæsita of a problem. Next we must look into how the data of that problem could possibly be expressed.

Now those data are the probabilities of events that can be expressed by definite logical functions of the symbols x1,x2,…xn. Let X1,X2,…Xm stand for these functions, and let the actual system of data be Prob. X1=a1,Prob. X2=a2,Prob. Xm=am. From the very nature of the case, it can be shown that X1,X2,…Xm are functions that stay unchanged if we change x1,x2,…xn in them into 1−x1,1−x2,…1−xn respectively. That is, they stay the same if every member who was right is made wrong and every member who was wrong is made right. For example, suppose the record shows that the votes were unanimous in a certain proportion of cases. If the cases are numerous enough, this fixes the probability of an event, and that event is expressed by the logical function x1x2…xn+(1−x1)(1−x2)…(1−xn), which says that either all are right or all are wrong; and this function satisfies the condition just stated. Again, suppose the record shows that in a certain proportion of cases the vote of one member, say A1, differed from that of all the other members of the court. The event whose probability this gives is expressed by the function x1(1−x2)…(1−xn)+(1−x1)x2…xn; that is, either he alone is right or he alone is wrong; and this too satisfies the condition. Agreement of opinion may be agreement in truth or in error. When opinions are divided, either side may be right or wrong. So clearly any particular state of the assembly, whether of agreement or of difference of opinion, is expressed by a logical function of the symbols x1,x2,…xn that involves the negative symbols 1−x1,1−x2,…1−xn in just the same way. But the records of assemblies do not claim to say which set of opinions was right and which was wrong. So the functions X1,X2,…Xm must all be of the kind just described.

7. Now, following the general method to find the value of Prob. x1, we should first set the functions X1,…Xm equal to a new set of symbols t1,…tm. From the equations so formed, X1=t1,X2=t2,…Xm=tm, we should eliminate the symbols x2,x3,…xn, the other members, and then find x1 as a developed logical function of the symbols t1,t2,…tm, which stand for the events whose probabilities are given. Let the result of this elimination be Ex1+E′(1−x1)=0;(1) where E and E′ are functions of t1,t2,…tm. Then x1=E′E′−E.(2)

Now the functions X1,X2,…Xm are symmetrical with respect to the symbols x1,…xn and 1−x1,…1−xn. So it is clear that in the equation (1), E′ must be the same as E: nothing in the data can tell "right" from "wrong". So (2) gives x=E0, and clearly the only coefficients that can appear in the development of the right-hand side of this equation are 00 and 10. The first appears whenever the values given to t1,…tm, in finding the coefficient of a constituent, make E=0. The second, or something equivalent to it, appears in every other case. So we can write the development in the form x1=00C+10D(3) where C and D are constituents, or sums of constituents, of the symbols t1,t2,…tm. In words: the compartments C are left wholly indefinite, and the compartments D cannot occur at all. Passing then from logic to algebra, we have Prob. x1=cCC=c, since the function V of the general Rule (XVII. 17) here reduces to C. So the value of Prob. x1 is entirely arbitrary, except that it must not go beyond the limits 0 and 1. In the same way, the individual values of Prob. x2, …Prob. xn are arbitrary. It does not follow that these arbitrary values are free of any necessary conditions connecting them, conditions that depend on the data. Looking for such conditions, however, properly belongs to the methods of Chap. XIX.

If we go back to the final logical equation and ask what c means, we get nothing but a restatement of the original problem. For C and D together include all the possible constituents of t1,t2,…tm, so C+D=1; and since D carries the coefficient 10, it is clear that if we put into it, in place of t1,t2,…tm, their expressions in terms of x1,x2,…xn, we should get D=0. So the same substitution would give C=1. Now by the rule, c is the probability that if the event written C happens, the event x1 will happen. Since C equals 1, and so covers every possible case, c must be read as the absolute probability that the event x1 happens. That is, it is simply the probability we set out to find, and the data have told us nothing about it.

It may be of interest to work out the actual form of the final logical equation in a particular case. Suppose, then, that the data come from records of events that are distinct and exclude one another. For instance, let the numerical data a1,a2,…am be the probabilities of distinct and definite majorities. Then the logical functions X1,X2,…Xm exclude one another, and so must satisfy the conditions X1X2=0,…X1Xm=0,X2Xm=0, &c. that is, no two of these majorities can happen at once. So we have t1t2=0,t1tm=0, &c. In these circumstances it can easily be shown that the developed logical value of x1 will be x1=00(t‾1t‾2…t‾m+t1t‾2…t‾m…+tmt‾1…t‾m−1)+ constitutents whose coefficients are 10. In this equation t‾1 stands for 1−t1, and so on.

These investigations apply just as well when the data of a problem are the probabilities of a jury's verdicts, as far as agreement and disagreement of opinion are concerned. Let the logical symbol w stand for the event, or state of things, that the accused person is guilty. Then the functions X1, X2 …Xm of this problem are such that nothing in them would change if we turned w,x1,x2…xn into w‾,x‾1,x‾2,…x‾n all at once. That is, the record looks the same if the accused were innocent instead of guilty and every juror's judgment were reversed. So the final logical value of w, like those of x1,x2,…xn, will come out in the same form (3), and the same general conclusion follows from it.

It is therefore established that from mere statistical records nothing can be inferred about how often a particular judge or counsellor is right, about the guilt of a particular person, or about the merits of a disputed question. If such things can be brought within the reach of science at all, it must be in one of two ways. Either some assumed test of truth gives us new data, or some hypothesis about whether individual judgments are connected or independent justifies a new form of the investigation. In examining the results of different hypotheses, the following general Proposition will be important.

Proposition II.

8. Given the probabilities of the n simple events x1,x2,…xn, namely: Prob. x1=c1,Prob. x2=c2,…Prob. xn=cn;(1) and also the probabilities of the m−1 compound events X1,X2,…Xm−1, namely: Prob. X1=a1,Prob. X2=a2,…Prob. Xm−1=am−1;(2) where the latter events X1…Xm−1 are distinct and exclude one another. Required, the probability of any other compound event X.

In this proposition we suppose that X1,X2,…Xm−1, and X as well, are functions of the symbols x1,x2,…xn alone. Also, since the events X1,X2,…Xm−1 exclude one another, we have X1X2=0,…X1Xm−1=0,X2X3=0, &c.;(3) the product of any two members of the system being zero. Now assume X1=t1,Xm−1=tm−1,X=t.(4) Then t must be found as a logical function of x1,…xn,t1,…tm−1.

Now by (3), t1t2=0,t1tm−1=0,t2t3=0, &c.;(5) all the products of two of t1,…tm−1 being zero. So in the developed expression for t, the only constituents that can have 1, 0, or 00 for their coefficients are those containing one of the following factors, namely: t‾1t‾2…t‾m−1,t1t‾2…t‾m−1,…t‾1…t‾m−2tm−1;(6) where t‾1 stands for 1−t1, and so on. In words, either none of the events t happens, or exactly one of them does. What remains is to find the part of each constituent that involves the symbols x1…xn, together with the matching coefficients.

Since Xi=ti (where i is any whole number from 1 to m−1 inclusive), it is clear that Xit‾1…t‾m−1=0, from the very make-up of the functions: whichever of the given events X we take, it cannot happen while every t fails, since each t is one of those events. So any constituent included in the left-hand side of this equation would have 10 for its coefficient.

Now let Xm=1−X1…−Xm−1;(7) that is, let the last event be "none of the others". Then it is clear that those constituents which contain t‾1…t‾m−1 as a factor, and yet have coefficients of the form 1, 0, or 00, must be included in the expression Xmt‾1…t‾m−1. Now Xm can be split into two parts, namely XXm and (1−X)Xm. The first is the sum of the constituents of Xm that are found in X; the second is the sum of those that are not found in X. In the developed expression of t, which is equivalent to X, the coefficients of the constituents in the first part, XXm, will clearly be 1, while those of the second part, (1−X)Xm, will be 0. So the elements we have just considered will contribute to the development of t the terms XXmt‾1…t‾m−1+0(1−X)Xmt‾1…t‾m−1. Again, since X1=t1, while X2t1=t2t1=0, and so on, it is clear that the only constituents containing t1t‾2…t‾m−1 as a factor that have coefficients of the form 1, 0, or 00 will be included in the expression X1t1t‾2…t‾m−1; and reasoning as before, we see that this will contribute to the development of t the terms XX1t1t‾2…t‾m−1+0(1−X)X1t1t‾2…t‾m−1.

Going on in this way with the remaining terms of (6), we arrive at the final expression for t, t=XXmt‾1…t‾m−1+XX1t1t‾2…t‾m−1…+XXm−1t‾1…t‾m−2tm−1+0(1−X)Xmt‾1…t‾m−1+0(1−X)X1t1t‾2…t‾m−1+ &c.(8)+terms whose coefficients are 10.

Notice that in this expression XXm stands for the sum of the constituents that X and Xm have in common. That sum is actually obtained by multiplying X and Xm together, by the rules of the calculus of logic.

In passing from logic to algebra, we shall write (XXm) for what this product becomes when, after doing the multiplication, or picking out the common constituents, we give the symbols x1,…xn a numerical meaning. On this understanding we shall have, by the general Rule (XVII. 17), Prob. t=(XXm)t‾1…t‾m−1+(XX1)t1t‾2…t‾m−1…+(XXm−1)t‾1…t‾m−2tm−1V,(9)V=Xmt‾1…t‾m−1+X1t1t‾2…t‾m−1…+Xm−1t‾1…t‾m−2tm−1(10) and so the relations that determine x1,…xn,t1,…tm−1 will be of the following type (with i running from 1 to n), (xiXm)t‾1…t‾m−1+(xiX1)t1t‾2…t‾m−1…+(xiXm−1)t‾1…t‾m−2tm−1ci=X1t1t‾2…t‾m−1a1…=Xm−1t‾1…t‾m−2tm−1am−1=V.(11)

From this system we shall next eliminate the symbols t1,…tm−1, the auxiliary quantities, so as to be left with equations in the probabilities alone.

We have t1t‾2…t‾m−1=a1VX1,t‾1…t‾m−2tm−1=am−1VXm−1.(12)

Putting these values into (10), we find V=Xmt‾1…t‾m−1+a1V…+am−1V. So t‾1…t‾m−1=(1−a1…−am−1)VXm.

Now let am=1−a1…−am−1,(13) that is, the probability that none of the given compound events happens. Then we have t‾1…t‾m−1=amVXm.(14) Now use (12) and (14) to reduce equation (9), and also the equation formed by setting the first line of (11) equal to the symbol V; and write Prob. X for Prob. t. We get Prob. X=a1(XX1)X1+a2(XX2)X2…+am(XXm)Xm,(15)a1(xiX1)X1+a2(xiX2)X2…+am(xiXm)Xm=ci;(16) where Xm and am are given by (7) and (13). Read aloud, (15) says: take each of the given compound events in turn; find what share of it falls within X; weight that share by the given probability of the event; and add. These equations contain the direct solution of the problem. In (16) we have the type of n equations (formed by giving i the values 1,2,…n in turn), from which the values of x1,x2,…xn will be found. Those values, put into (15), give the value of Prob. X as a function of the constants a1, c1, and so on.

One conclusion that follows from this solution deserves notice. Suppose the probabilities of the compound events X1,…Xm−1 are just what they would be if the events x1,…xn were entirely independent, with the given probabilities c1,…cn. Then the probability of the event X will be the same as if it were calculated on that same hypothesis, that the events x1,…xn are absolutely independent. For on that hypothesis, taking x1=c1, xn=cn in the numerical system would give X1=a1, Xm=am, and then (15) and (16) would give Prob. X=(XX1)+(XX2)…+(XXm),(17) (xiX1)+(xiX2)…+(xiXm)=ci.(18)

But since X1+X2…+Xm=1, it is clear that the right-hand side of (17) is formed by taking all the constituents contained in X and giving them an algebraic meaning. A similar remark applies to (18). So those equations give, respectively, Prob. X (logical)=X (algebraic),xi=ci. In words: the probability of the event X is just its logical expression read as algebra, and each x is simply its given probability.

So if X=ϕ(x1,x2,…xn), we have Prob. X=ϕ(c1,c2,…cn), which is the result we wanted to show.

It would also follow that if the quantities c1,…cn were not fixed, and no hypothesis were made that they share a common average value, the system (15) (16) would be satisfied by giving those quantities any values x1,x2,…xn that satisfy the equations X1=a1…Xm−1=am−1,X=a, supposing the value of the element a, like the values of a1,…am−1, to be given by experience.

9. Before we apply the general solution (15) (16) to the question of the probability of judgments, it will help to make one transformation. Let the data be x1=c1…xn=cn,namely,Prob. X1=a1…Prob. Xm−2=am−2; that is, we are given the probability of each simple event, and the probabilities of all the compound events except the last two. Let it be required to find Prob. Xm−1, whose unknown value we will write as am−1. Then in (15) and (16) we must change

X into Xm−1,Prob. X into am−1,
Xm−1 into Xm−2,am−1 into am−2,
Xm into Xm−1+Xm,am into am−1+am;

With these changes made, we note that (Xm−1Xr)=0 except when r=m−1, and that it is then equal to Xm−1. (The compound events exclude one another, so the event sought has nothing in common with any of the others, and everything in common with itself.) The equations (15) (16) then give am−1=(am−1+am)Xm−1Xm−1+Xm,(19) a1(xiX1)X1…+am−2(xiXm−2)Xm−2+(am−1+am)(xiXm−1+xiXm)Xm−1+Xm=ci.(20) Now from (19) we find Xm−1am−1=Xmam=Xm−1+Xmam−1+am, and because of this the last term of (20) can be brought to the form am−1(xiXm−1)Xm−1+am(xiXm)Xm. With these reductions, the system (17) and (18) can be replaced by the following symmetrical one: Xm−1am−1=Xmam,(21) a1(xiX1)X1+a2(xiX2)X2…+am(xiXm)Xm=ci.(22) These equations, together with (7) and (13), let us find am−1 as a function of c1…cn,a1…am−2, the numbers we suppose experience supplies. We now turn to applying them.

Proposition III.

10. Given any system of probabilities drawn from recorded cases of unanimity, or of a stated numerical majority, in the decisions of a deliberative assembly; required, on a certain definite hypothesis, the mean probability that a member of the assembly judges correctly.

How the probabilities of unanimous decisions, and of particular numerical majorities, may be found from experience was indicated earlier in this chapter. Using the notation of Prop. I., we shall represent the events whose probabilities are given by the functions X1,X2,…Xm−1. The very nature of the case has shown that these events exclude one another, and that the functions which represent them are symmetrical with respect to the symbols x1,x2,…xn. (Symmetrical here means that the functions are unchanged if the members are relabelled: a record of votes says how many voted each way, not who.) We go on using those symbols in the same sense as in Prop. I.: by xi we mean the event that the ith member of the assembly forms a correct opinion.

Now the data that experience gives us directly are these: Prob. X1=a1,Prob. X2=a2…Prob. Xm−2=am−2,(1) Prob. Xm−1=am−1.(2) Here X1…Xm−1 are functions of the logical symbols x1,…xn, and to the probabilities of the events those symbols stand for we shall assign one and the same undetermined value c. That is, every member has the same probability of judging rightly, and we do not yet know what it is. So we shall have Prob. x1=Prob. x2…=Prob. xn=c.(3)

We saw in Prop. I. that the direct data (1) (2), with no hypothesis to help them, only lead us back to a restatement of the problem. On the other hand, suppose we followed the methods of Laplace and Poisson. We would then use the system (3) alone as the data for this work's method, and only at the end compare the results with the experimental system (1) (2). Plainly we would then be relying wholly on a doubtful hypothesis: that the members' judgments are independent of one another. We ought not to rely on that hypothesis wholly; but we cannot do without it altogether, or without something equivalent in its place. So let us examine what follows from a limited independence of the individual judgments, with the limits set by the data that seemed to be surplus. From the system (1) (3), let us use the method of this work to find Prob. Xm−1; then, comparing the result with (2), let us find c. Even here we claim an arbitrary power of choosing which datum to hold back. But Prop. I. makes it plain that something of this kind cannot be avoided if we want a definite solution at all. As for the principle of choice, I believe the equation (2) held back for the final comparison should be the one that, because of the size of its number am−1, is judged the most important of the first series of data that experience supplies.

Now, since the events denoted by the functions X1,X2,…Xm−1 exclude one another, the concluding equations of the previous proposition apply. Because those functions are symmetrical, and because the set of values denoted by ci has been reduced to a single value c, the equations represented by (22) all become the same equation. The values of x1,x2,…xn become equal and may be replaced by a single value x, and we have simply Xm−1am−1=Xmam,(4)a1(xX1)X1+a2(xX2)X2…+am(xXm)Xm=c.(5) Here is how the solution these equations point to is carried out.

The functions X1,…Xm−1 and the values a1,…am−1 are given in the data. So first we have Xm=1−X1…−Xm−1,am=1−a1…−am−1. In words: the last event is "anything else that can happen", and its probability is whatever is left over after the recorded ones.

From each of the functions X1,X2,…Xm, given or found in this way, we must pick out the constituents that contain a particular symbol, such as x1, as a factor. This fixes the functions (xX1), (xX2), &c. Then in all the functions we must change each of x1,x2,…xn into x. Or we may look at it another way. Any algebraic function Xi in the system (4) (5) expresses the probability of the event denoted by the logical function Xi, on the supposition that the logical symbols x1,x2,…xn stand for independent events, all with the same probability x. On the same supposition, (xXi) would stand for the probability that one particular event of the series x1,x2,…xn occurs together with Xi: that a given member judges rightly and the vote falls out as that function describes. Once the forms of Xi, (xXi), &c. are known, the equation (4) gives the value of x, and this value, put into (5), gives the value of the element c we want. The solution will offer two values, one greater than 12 and the other less. The greater must be chosen whenever, on general grounds, we think it more likely that a member of the assembly will judge correctly than incorrectly.

Here, then, on the assumed principle that the largest of the values, am−1, is held back for the final comparison in the equation (2), we have a definite solution of the problem. The same form of solution still applies if some other equation of the system is held back in place of (2) on some other ground, such as its being more accurate.

11. Let us examine how far this choice of which datum to hold back has affected the final solution. Clearly the equation (5) does not depend on the choice at all. Nor does the right-hand side of (4). Had we held back the function X1 instead of Xm−1, the equation for finding x would have been X1a1=Xmam,(6) but the value of x found from it would still have to be put into the same final equation (5). We know that if the events x1,x2,…xn really were independent, the equations (4), (6), and all the others of which they are examples, would turn out equivalent, and the value of x given by any one of them would be the true value of c. This gives us a way of checking (5). For if that equation is correct, then in these circumstances it ought to be satisfied by taking c=x. In other words, the equation a1(xX1)X1+a2(xX2)X2…+am(xXm)Xm=x(7) ought, when solved, to give the same value of x as the equation (4) or (6). And this is the case. For since, by hypothesis, X1a1=X2a2…=Xmam, we have, by a known theorem (when several fractions are equal, each equals the sum of their tops over the sum of their bottoms), X1a1=X2a2…=Xmam=X1+X2…+Xma1+a2…+am=1. (The last step holds because the events together cover every possibility, so both sums are 1.) So, on putting a1 for X1, &c., (7) becomes (xX1)+(xX2)…+(xXm)=x which is a mere identity: the chance that a given member judges rightly, added up over every possible outcome of the vote, is simply the chance that he judges rightly.

So whenever the events x1,x2,…xn really are independent, the system (4) (5) is correct, and it does not depend on the arbitrary first step of the process that produced it. When those events are not independent, the final system of equations will contain an arbitrary element, setting aside the principle of choice stated above. But the fact that the equation (5) keeps the same form whichever datum is held back suggests that the solution is less arbitrary than the solutions to which the hypothesis of the complete independence of the individual judgments would lead us. Working out the limits of the value of c, as they depend on the limits of the value of x, would settle such points.

These considerations raise a question. The equation (7) is symmetrical with respect to the functions X1,X2,…Xm; it is free from any arbitrary element; and it is strictly exact when the events x1,x2,…xn really are independent. Might it not be accepted as a mean general solution of the problem? The proper way to decide this, I think, would be to find out whether the value of x it gives would generally fall within the limits of the value of c, as determined by the systems of equations of which the system (4), (5), is the type. It seems likely that under ordinary circumstances it would. Apart from such considerations, however, we may regard (7) as itself expressing a certain principle of solution. On this principle, we treat X1,X2,…Xm as exclusive causes of the event whose probability is x (causes that never act together). We accept the probabilities of those causes, a1,a2,…am, from experience. But we form the conditional probabilities of the event, given each of those causes, (xX1)X1,(xX2)X2, &c. (XVII. Prop I.) on the hypothesis that the individual judgments are independent, and so arrive at the equation (7). I believe, however, that this is a less rigorous way to proceed than the one used in the general solution, though in practice it may be the more convenient.

12. It only remains to give the particular forms that the algebraic functions Xi, (xXi), &c. in the equations above take when the logical function Xi stands for the event that r members of the assembly vote one way and n−r members the other way. Clearly, in this case the algebraic function Xi expresses what the probability of that event would be if the events x1,x2,…xn were independent, with a common probability measured by x. So by Art. 3 we should have Xi=n(n−1)…(n−r+1)1⋅2…r{xr(1−x)n−r+xn−r(1−x)r}. The fraction in front counts the number of ways of choosing which r members make up the one side. Under the same circumstances, (xXi) would stand for the probability of the compound event in which one particular member of the assembly judges correctly and, along with that, the voting falls out as just described. It would therefore be the probability that a particular member votes correctly while, of the other n−1 members, r−1 vote correctly; or that the same member votes correctly while, of the other n−1 members, r vote incorrectly. (In the first case he is one of the r, and that side is right; in the second he is among the rest, the n minus r, and the r are the ones in error.) So (xXi)=(n−1)(n−2)…(n−r+1)1⋅2…r−1xr(1−x)n−r+(n−1)(n−2)…(n−r)1⋅2…rxn−r(1−x)r.

Proposition IV.

13. Given any system of probabilities drawn from recorded cases of unanimity, or of a stated numerical majority, in the decisions of a criminal court of justice; required, on hypotheses similar to those of the last proposition, the mean probability c of correct judgment for a member of the court, and the general probability k of guilt in an accused person.

The solution of this problem differs only slightly from that of the last, and can be referred to the same general formulas, (4) and (5), or (7). Note that since there are now two elements, c and k, to be found, we must hold back two of the functions X1,X2,…Xm−1 for final comparison, say X1, and Xm−1. We then use for the data either the remaining m−3 functions, or the two sets X2,X3,…Xm−1, and X1,X2,…Xm−2, one for each. In either case we suppose there must be at least two independent original data. If the equation (7) alone is used, in this case it will give two equations, which may be written: a1(xX1)X1+a2(xX2)X2…+am(xXm)Xm=x,(1)a1(kX1)X1+a2(kX2)X2…+am(kXm)Xm=k.(2) The first is about a juror's judging rightly, the second about the prisoner's being guilty. These equations are to be used in the following way. Let x1,x2,…xn stand for the events that the members of the court, respectively, form a correct opinion. Let w also stand for the event that the accused is guilty. With these symbols we can express in logic the functions X1,X2,…Xm−1, whose probabilities are given, and also the function Xm. Then from the function X1 pick out the constituents that contain, as a factor, some one particular symbol of the set x1,x2,…xn, and also the constituents that contain w as a factor. In both results change each of x1,x2,…xn into x, and w into k. These results give (xX1) and (kX1): the probability that a given juror judges rightly and the verdict falls out as the first recorded event describes, and the probability that the accused is guilty and the verdict falls out so. Make the same changes throughout, and the system (1), (2) will determine x and k, on the particular hypothesis involved.

14. From these investigations we may gather the following facts and conclusions.

First, from the mere records of agreement and disagreement in the opinions of any body of men, no definite numerical conclusions can be drawn, either about the probability that an individual member of the body judges correctly, or about the merits of the questions put before it.

Second, such conclusions may be drawn on several distinct hypotheses: first, on the usual hypothesis that individual judgments are completely independent; second, on certain definite modifications of that hypothesis that the actual data justify; third, on a distinct principle of solution, suggested by the common form that turned up in the solutions obtained from those modifications.

Last, whatever doubt may attach to the final results comes not from any imperfection in the method, which adapts itself equally to every hypothesis, but from the uncertainty of the hypotheses themselves.

It seems likely, however, that even with the widest range of hypotheses consistent with taking all the data of experience into account, the results would differ only slightly, and that their mean values could be found with great confidence by the methods of Prop. III. Of those methods I would be inclined to prefer the first. Once such a principle of mean solution has been agreed on, other considerations suggest that the values of c and k (the chance that a member judges rightly, and the chance that a person brought to trial is guilty) would stay nearly constant for courts and assemblies with a definite constitution, governed in their deliberations by fixed rules. They would be subject only to a small, slow change over the centuries, depending on the progress of knowledge and of justice among mankind. At present there are few data, if any, suitable for finding them.

Chapter 22: On the Nature of Science, and the Constitution of the Intellect

1. By the constitution of a system I mean the sum of the causes and tendencies that produce its observed character when they work without interference, under the conditions the system seems to be adapted to. We judge that adaptation by studying the circumstances in which the system acts most freely, produces its most harmonious results, or in some other way fulfils the apparent design of its construction. In some cases we know clearly the causes on which a system's working depends, and its conditions and its end as well. That is the most perfect kind of knowledge we can have of any subject. In other cases we know the causes at work only partly or imperfectly. Even so, we can work out to some extent the laws by which they act, and beyond that we can discover general tendencies and infer a further purpose. This, I think, is how people have rightly concluded that there is a moral faculty in our nature. They have not concluded it because we understand the particular instruments it works by, as we connect the eye with the faculty of sight. Nor have they concluded it because people agree on universal rules of conduct. They have concluded it for this reason. The feeling of moral approval or disapproval shows itself, in one form or another, in everyone. And wherever human progress can be seen, wherever a society is neither standing still nor hurrying to decay, that feeling tends to attach itself to certain kinds of actions, by common consent, and in a way that points to both permanence and law. Always and everywhere, the appearance of Order gives a presumption, not measurable but real (XX. 22), that some end or purpose is being fulfilled, and that there is a ground of orderly causation behind it.

2. The particular question of the constitution of the intellect has drawn the efforts of speculative minds in every age; that hardly needs saying. It appeals to the desire for knowledge, which the greatest masters of ancient thought believed to be inborn in our species. And it adds to the ordinary strength of that motive a human and personal interest. A real devotion to truth is seldom one-sided in its aims. It urges us to range over the fair fields of observing the outside world, and it forbids us to neglect the study of our own faculties. Even in ages most given over to material interests, part of the current of thought has been turned inward. The desire to understand that by which we understand everything else has been baffled only to be renewed.

This persistence would probably not have lasted among sincere seekers after truth if most of them had been convinced that such speculations are hopelessly barren. We may suppose they felt something like this. Some error and uncertainty always comes with partial information, and will always cling to the results of these inquiries; but a residue of real knowledge may still remain. The contradictions we meet are more often in the words than in the things. Above all, even probable conclusions take on an interest and a value here from their subject, which makes them worth a place beside the more definite and more splendid results of physical science. These considerations seem to me perfectly legitimate. Many of the problems about the nature and constitution of the mind must be presumed insoluble. But there are others on which we can reach a limited but not doubtful knowledge, and others again on which we can reach the conclusions of a highly probable analogy. Day and night do not meet at a sharp edge. They are separated by a twilight zone, through which the light of the one fades gradually into the darkness of the other. In the same way, every region of positive knowledge is surrounded by a debatable, speculative territory, over which it spreads some of its influence and its light. So there may be questions about the constitution of the intellect that cannot be settled absolutely in the present state of knowledge, and yet receive enough reflected light to make their probable answer not hard to find. And there may be questions about the nature of science, and even about particular truths and doctrines of science, on which anyone who accepts the general principles of this work cannot help forming definite opinions, perhaps different from those usually held today. In what follows I will sum up some of the more definite conclusions established in the earlier parts of this treatise. Then I will point out one or two trains of thought, connected with the general aims just mentioned, which those conclusions seem to me fitted to suggest.35

3. Among the conclusions about the intellectual constitution that may count as positive knowledge, we may list the scientific laws of thought and reasoning on which the general methods of this treatise are built, together with the principles (Chap. V.) that have governed how they are applied. Here are some of them. The division of the domain of thought into two spheres, distinct but existing side by side (IV. XI.). The subjection of the operations of the intellect within those spheres to one common system of laws (XI.). The general mathematical character of those laws, and their actual expression (II. III.). How far those laws are akin to the laws of thought in the domain of number, and the point where they part from them. The commanding place, among all the subjects of thought that logic deals with, of the two limiting conceptions of the universe and of eternity. The relation of those conceptions to the fundamental conception of unity in the science of number. These results, and many like them, are not to be ranked as merely probable or analogical conclusions. They have a right to be counted as truths of science. Whether we call them metaphysical or not makes no difference. The evidence they rest on is of a different kind from that of physical science, but it is not inferior in value to any evidence that can be brought for the general truths of physical science.

Again, it is agreed that all the more exact forms of knowledge advance in a certain order. Every branch of physical science begins with observation. It moves on, by comparing facts, to a likely guess at the law that connects them. It tests that guess by new experiments, designed so that, if the guess is sound, they will raise its probability without limit. And finally, once the law of the phenomenon is settled with enough confidence, the search for causes crowns the inquiry, carried on by the right mixture of hypothesis and deduction. The particular faculties and laws whose nature this work has examined play their part in this advancing order of knowledge. So it is clear that if we want to study impartially either the nature of science, or the constitution of the intellect in its relation to science, no part of these two series of truths should be treated in isolation. Above all, truths that in any way supplement each other should be considered in their bearing on each other and in their connection.

4. Take, then, the need for an experimental basis for all positive knowledge, and set it beside the existence and the peculiar character of the system of mental laws, principles and operations this book has studied. Together they throw light on some important questions that still largely divide the world of speculative thought. From the particular facts experience gives us, how do we reach the general propositions of science? What is the nature of those propositions? Are they simply collections of experience, or does the mind supply some connecting principle of its own? In a word, what is the nature of scientific truth, and what grounds the confidence with which it asks to be accepted?

It must be clear that no single, general answer can be given to questions like these. In some cases they do not even need discussing. We all know cases in which a general proposition merely states, per enumerationem simplicem (by simply counting the cases), a fact established by actual observation of every case the proposition covers. On that ground the astronomer asserts that all the known planets move from west to east around the sun. But there are also cases in which a general proposition is assumed because it has been observed true in particular instances, and that truth is then extended to instances not observed. No principle of purely deductive reasoning can justify that step. When Kepler concluded, from a great many observations of the planet Mars, that it moves in an ellipse, his conclusion was larger than his premises, larger indeed than any premises mere observation could supply. What further element, then, is needed to give such generalizations even a provisional validity? It is the ability, built into our nature, to recognize Order, together with the presumption, however we come by it, that the phenomena of Nature are connected by a principle of Order. Without these, the general truths of physical science could never have been found. Grant that the method this sets up can lead us only to probable or approximate results. All that follows is that most of the generalizations of physical science have only a probable or approximate truth. Our hold on knowledge is secure for this reason: wherever such conclusions truly represent the way Nature is made, our confidence in them is confirmed without limit, and soon cannot be told apart from certainty. The principle I have just named as the basis of inductive reasoning also lets us settle the much-disputed question of whether reasoning needs general propositions. The logician says that no conclusion can be deduced from particular premises. Modern writers of high reputation have argued that all reasoning goes from particular truths to particular truths. Their example is this: when we conclude from the fact that certain members of a class have a property that some other member has it too, we need not first establish the intermediate general conclusion that all the members of the class have it. Whether or not that is so, the principle of order or analogy on which the reasoning proceeds must be either stated or grasped as a general truth, or the final conclusion has no validity. In this form, at least, the need for general propositions as the basis of inference is confirmed. And I believe that need is implied by the very existence, and still more by the particular nature, of the faculties whose laws this work has investigated. For if we analyze the process of reasoning carefully, we find that it sets aside everything peculiar to the individual the conclusion is about, and attends only to the properties that define that individual as a member of the class.

5. Besides the general propositions we get by induction from the compared facts of experience, there are others that belong to the domain of what is called necessary truth. The general propositions of arithmetic are of this kind, and so are the propositions stating the laws of thought on which the general methods of this treatise are founded. These propositions can not only be verified strictly in particular instances; they are made plain in all their generality by studying particular instances. Then there are general propositions that express necessary truths but cannot be exactly verified, because our senses are imperfect. Some, if not all, of the propositions of geometry are like this; but geometry is not the only place where such propositions are found. The question of their nature and origin is a very old one. It is more closely bound up with the inquiry into the constitution of the intellect than any other I have mentioned, so it is fair to consider it here. Among the opinions most widely held on the subject are these. Some have held that propositions of this class exist in the mind independently of experience, and that the conceptions they are about are the imprints of eternal archetypes, the original patterns of things. Plato filled his ideal world with such archetypes, though he thought of them as having a reality of which all the objects of sense are only a faint shadow or dim hint. Others, in various ways, have argued the opposite. They have said that the things such propositions are about are copies of individual objects of experience; or that they are mere names; or that they are themselves individual objects of experience, so that the propositions about them are only partly true, because those objects are imperfect. Last, some have said that they are products of the intellect, formed by abstraction from our sense perceptions of individual things, but formed so as to become what individual things never can be, subjects of science: that is, subjects about which exact and general propositions can be asserted. And there are perhaps still other views, in some of which the element of the senses dominates, and in others the element of the intellect, or the ideal.

Now suppose we take the last of the views just mentioned (I do not propose to consider either the purely ideal view or the purely nominalist one, which holds that general terms are mere names). And suppose we ask what, in the sense described, are the proper objects of science: the objects about which its propositions are true with no mixture of error. I believe only one answer can be given. Neither the individual objects of experience, nor, in all probability, the mental images they call up, have any strict claim to that title. It seems certain that nowhere in nature or in art do we meet anything that agrees exactly with the geometrical definition of a straight line, a triangle or a circle, though the difference may be too small for the senses to detect. And it is at least doubtful whether we can form a perfect mental image, or conception, that agrees with the definition any more exactly. But it is not doubtful that such conceptions, however imperfect, point to something beyond themselves; and as we approach that something step by step, all imperfection tends to disappear. The perfect triangle, square or circle does not exist in nature. It escapes all our powers of picturing it in the mind, and it is presented to our thought only as the limit of a process of abstraction that never ends. Yet, by a wonderful faculty of the understanding, it can be made the subject of propositions that are absolutely true. So the domain of reason turns out to be larger than the domain of imagination. If anyone thinks that we can picture to ourselves, with strict accuracy, the scientific elements of form, direction, size and the rest, then for that person these things, as we actually conceive them, will be the proper objects of science. But I think the fairer opinion is that an incurable imperfection clings to every attempt we make to grasp these elements precisely. In that case all we can say is this. External objects in reality, or the conceptions of our imagination through abstraction, approach certain limiting states, which perhaps are never actually reached. The closer they come to those states, the closer the general propositions of science about those things or conceptions come to absolute truth, and the actual departure from it tends to disappear. To some extent the same remarks apply to the physical sciences too. What have been called the “fundamental ideas” of those sciences, such as force, polarity, crystallization and so on, are not, as I see it, products of the intellect independent of experience; nor are they mere copies of external things. On the one hand, they need experience as their necessary starting point. On the other, they need the power of abstraction to form them, exercised in obedience to some general faculty or disposition of our nature, which always prompts us to search for order and fits us to recognize it. So we study the effects of gravitation on the motions of the heavenly bodies approximately, by reference to the limiting supposition that the planets are perfect spheres or spheroids. We work out approximately the path of a ray of light through the atmosphere by a process that sets aside every disturbing effect of temperature. And this is the order of proceeding in all the higher paths of human knowledge. What is remarkable about these processes of the intellect is the disposition, and the matching ability, to rise from the imperfect pictures given by the senses, and from the variety of individual experience, to the perception of general, and perhaps unchanging, truths. Wherever this disposition and this ability come together, each series of connected facts in nature can hint at an order more exact than the one it directly shows. For it can serve as the ground and the occasion for using those powers whose task is to grasp general truths: truths that are indeed exemplified in a world of changing phenomena, but never exemplified perfectly.36,37

6. The ultimate laws of thought are mathematical in form. Put that truth beside the fact that we can make mistakes, and it gives ground for some remarkable conclusions. If we looked at the scientific truth alone, we might be led to infer an almost exact parallel between the operations of the intellect and the movements of external nature. Imagine someone well versed in physical science, but not used to reflecting on the nature of his own faculties, who is told that the laws of those faculties have been proved to be mathematical. Once his first disbelief had passed, he would probably come away with the impression that the order of thought must therefore be as necessary as the order of the material universe. We know that in natural science the absolute connection between the starting point and the end point of a problem, shown in mathematical form, is a fitting symbol of the physical necessity that binds effect to cause. The necessary sequence of states and conditions in the inorganic world, and the necessary connection of premises and conclusion in the exact proofs we apply to it, seem to run side by side. It might be asked which of the two has the first claim to the word “necessary”: the observed constancy of Nature, or the unbreakable connection of propositions in all valid reasoning about her works. Historically we would perhaps give the first claim to the former; philosophically, to the latter. But the fact of the connection cannot be disputed, and the analogy it points to is obvious.

If the laws of valid reasoning, then, were obeyed without exception, there would be a very close parallel between the operations of the intellect and those of external Nature. Both would be subject to laws mathematical in form and expression, and subject with absolute obedience; and that would stamp one common character on both. The reign of necessity over the intellectual world and the physical world would be equally complete and universal.

But it is not so. The observation of external Nature bears ever stronger witness that uniform working and unvarying obedience to appointed laws hold throughout her whole domain. The slightest attention to the processes of the intellectual world shows us a different state of things. The mathematical laws of reasoning are, strictly speaking, the laws of right reasoning only, and they are actually broken again and again. Error, which has no place in the material system, takes up a large place here. We must accept this as one of those ultimate facts whose origin it is not the business of science to determine. We must admit that there exist laws which even the rigour of their mathematical form does not protect from being broken. We must grant them an authority whose essence is not power: a supremacy that the analogy of the unbreakable order of the natural world does nothing to help us understand.

Because the distinction just pointed out is real, it does not depend on any particular views we may hold about other parts of the mind's constitution. If we regard the intellect as free, and this seems to be the view most in keeping with the general spirit of these speculations, then its freedom must be set against the rule of necessity, not against the existence of a certain rightful supremacy of truth. The laws of correct inference can be broken, but they exist no less truly for that. And they keep the same character and authority if we adopt the hypothesis of necessity in its most extreme form. Let it be granted that the laws of valid reasoning, as this work determines them (or, more generally, as they would finally appear at the end of an exhaustive analysis), form only a part of the system of laws that governs the actual processes of reasoning, right or wrong. Let it be granted that if we knew that system completely, we would see that the whole working of the intellect is necessary, just as the movements of the inorganic world are necessary. And let it finally be granted, as a consequence of this hypothesis, that incorrect reasoning, or error, wherever it appears, comes from other laws interfering with the laws that produce right reasoning. Even so, it would remain true that among the laws of the intellect there are some set apart from the rest by a special character, namely this. Every movement of the intellectual system carried out under their direction alone is right; and every interference with them by other laws is not just interference, but violation. We cannot help feeling that this would give the laws in question a character of distinction and of rank above the rest. They would seem all the more clearly to point to a final purpose that is not always fulfilled, and to hold an authority that is built in and rightful, but does not always command obedience.

A little thought will show that there is nothing like this in the government of the world by natural law. The realm of inorganic Nature allows neither preferences nor distinctions. We cannot pick out some of her laws from the rest and declare that they alone deserve obedience, or that they alone are charged with carrying out her highest purpose. On the contrary, all her laws seem to stand on the same level; and the more we know of them, the more their united action seems necessary to the harmony of the system, and, so far as we can understand it, to its general design. Consider the most striking departures from apparent order in the inorganic world: the disturbances of the planets in their orbits, the interruption of crystallization when a foreign force intrudes, and others of the same kind. It hardly needs saying how often these either merge into the idea of some higher scheme of order, or lose their abnormal look to a more attentive and better-informed eye. Only one explanation of these facts can be given, namely that the distinction between true and false, between correct and incorrect, exists in the processes of the intellect, but not in the realm of physical necessity. As we go up from the lower stages of living things to the higher level of conscious intelligence, this contrast gradually dawns on us. Wherever life appears, the rule of rigid law gives way to some degree before that mysterious principle of activity. So, although the bodies of the animal kinds follow certain general types, those types are always realized imperfectly, perhaps in relation to the highest standards of beauty and proportion. Art in our day swings between two choices. One is the exact imitation of individual forms. The other is the effort, by abstracting from all such forms, to reach the idea of an ideal grace and expression that perhaps never appears perfectly in any earthly shape. Again, there are the purposeful adaptations by which species, without giving up their type, become fitted to new conditions or new homes. These come about only slowly; but they seem to come about not by the fated power of outside circumstances, but by an energy called forth from within. So life in all its forms can be contrasted with the passive fixity of inorganic nature. But the perfection of the types in which life takes bodily form is to some degree an ideal thing, and we cannot define exactly the highest excellence of form and adaptation they suggest. So the contrast here is less sharp than the contrast between the processes of the intellect and those of the purely material world. For the definite, technical character of the mathematical laws that govern both of these throws into stronger light the basic difference between the kinds of authority those laws exercise in governing them.

7. There is one more case, connected with the general aims of this chapter, in which comparing truths or facts drawn from different sources suggests an instructive train of thought. It consists in comparing the laws of thought, in their scientific expression, with the actual forms that physical speculation in early ages, and metaphysical speculation in every age, have tended to take. I want to draw attention here to two illustrations in particular.

First, it has been shown (III. 13) that there is a scientific connection between the conception of unity in number and the conception of the universe in logic. They hold the same relative place in their two systems, and they obey the same formal laws. Now think of the Greek mind in its early stage of activity, a stage no less marked, and perhaps no less necessary, in the progress of the human intellect than the age of Bacon or of Newton. The great problems of Nature were then beginning to open up, while the means of observation were still lacking and its necessity was not understood. To that mind, the terms “Universe” and “The One” seem to have meant almost the same thing. The first aim of philosophy was to say what that unity was, of which all existence was thought to be a manifestation. Thales looked for this fundamental unity in water. Anaximenes and Diogenes took it to be air. Hippasus of Metapontum and Heraclitus of Ephesus declared that it was fire. Parmenides, less definite or less confident in his views, simply declared that all existing things were One. Melissus said that the Universe was infinite, incapable of change or motion, One, like itself, and that motion did not exist but only seemed to. Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, following perhaps in the steps of his fellow citizen Hermotimus, looked for the cause of the world and of its order in Intelligence; and to the reflective mind of Aristotle his spirit seemed sober next to the rashness of earlier speculation. The pantheistic leaning (the belief that God and the whole of things are one) that ran through many of these speculations shows plainly in the words of Xenophanes, the founder of the Eleatic school, who, “surveying the expanse of heaven, declared that the One was God.” There are perhaps few, if any, of the ways in which unity can be conceived that we do not find applied in these ancient doctrines: unity in the abstract, as numerical or as rational; unity in the concrete, as a passive substance, or as a central and living principle. The writings of Aristotle, which I have mainly drawn on, are full of allusions of this kind; yet of most of the people who once gave themselves to such speculations, the very names have probably been lost. It is a strange truth, but a telling one. Nature, in everything but the face of the heavens, must have looked like little more than a scene of unexplained disorder; popular belief was scattered among its many gods. And yet the idea of a first unity, if only in a crude, material form, struck the deepest root of all, and lived on in many a thoughtful heart through the chill of a lifelong disappointment and an endless search! Second, the law of thought expressed by an equation of the second degree, which this treatise has called the law of duality, is just as closely allied to the leaning of ancient thought toward the kinds of philosophical speculation known as dualism (the view that everything comes from two opposed principles).
